# RCE Language Specification, draft 0.9: Overview

**Abstract.** RCE is a small programming language whose programs mean one
thing everywhere. A program is turned into a *Form*: a state machine given
by its states, its events, a step function that maps a state and an event to
a new state and an outcome, and the log of events. Every runtime that runs
the Form must produce the same results bit for bit, and the rules that make
this so are checked by machine.

![RCE overview: source, checker, Form P = (S, E, delta, D, lambda), log D, emit targets, host, fabrics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openIE-dev/rce/main/docs/figures/rce-overview.svg)

*Figure (informative). The pipeline from source to Form, log, emit targets and host. Source: [docs/figures](https://github.com/openIE-dev/rce/tree/main/docs/figures).*

Three plain points:

1. **Same answer on every target.** Arithmetic, text, floats and concurrency
   have one defined meaning; there is no undefined behaviour.
2. **Every program ends.** Loops, recursion and iterators are bounded, so the
   step function always returns.
3. **Memory is safe by construction.** Ownership, second-class borrows,
   regions and linear handles rule out use-after-free and data races.

Tiny example (a counter that refuses to go negative):

```
state Counter
    n: i64 = 0
event Dec
step Counter on Dec
    check n > 0
    n -= 1
```

RCE is defined by this document. A program is a text; its meaning is a Form
P = (S, E, δ, D, λ) (section 6). Runtimes, emitters, harnesses and editors are
not part of the language: they are implementations, and an implementation
conforms when it accepts exactly the programs this document accepts and gives
each one the meaning this document gives it.

**Document status.** This specification is the only normative text.
`SURFACE.md` (the native surface design) and `FORM.md` (the compiler

disagree, and only one of them is checked by machine. Their programs
must still be accepted by the reference checker. The Form signature is
6.1.

## 1. Notation and conformance

This section fixes how the rest of the spec is written and what it means
for an implementation to follow it. *EBNF* (extended Backus-Naur form) is a
notation for grammars; an *inference rule* states that a conclusion holds
when its premises hold. For example `Option = "[" Expression "]" .` says an
option is an expression in brackets.

**Grammar notation.** EBNF in the style of the Go specification:

```
Production  = name "=" Expression "." .
Expression  = Term { "|" Term } .
Term        = Factor { Factor } .
Factor      = name | token [ "…" token ] | Group | Option | Repetition .
Group       = "(" Expression ")" .
Option      = "[" Expression "]" .      (0 or 1)
Repetition  = "{" Expression "}" .      (0 or more)
```

Lower-case names are syntactic productions, `UPPER` names are tokens, and
quoted strings are literal tokens. `NEWLINE`, `INDENT` and `DEDENT` are
produced by the layout pass (2.6).

**Judgment notation.** Inference rules are written

```
  premise₁   …   premiseₙ
  ───────────────────────── [Name]
         conclusion
```

Γ is a typing context (name ↦ type, mode), Δ a context of live borrows, Σ the
declaration environment (types, kinds, traits, events, errors, regions). "iff"
means if and only if.

**Conformance.** An implementation (a) refuses every text that is not in the
language of section 3, or that breaks a rule of section 7, with a diagnostic
naming the rule; (b) for every accepted program, computes δ, λ and the fold of
section 6 exactly, including every edge in 6.3. Behavior the spec does not
define does not exist: there is no "undefined behavior" and no
"implementation-defined" result. The only implementation freedom is cost
(time, memory, energy), never value.

## 2. Lexical grammar

This section says how source text is cut into *tokens* (the smallest
meaningful pieces: names, numbers, keywords, punctuation) and how
indentation becomes block structure. Getting this exact is what lets every
tool read a file the same way. Example: `let x = 0x1F  # note` is the tokens
`let`, `x`, `=`, `0x1F`; the comment is dropped.

### 2.1 Source text

A source file is UTF-8 encoded Unicode text. A byte-order mark is refused.
Line ends are LF or CR LF; a bare CR is refused. The horizontal tab U+0009 is
refused anywhere in a file (layout is by spaces only, 2.6). A file that does
not end in a line end is read as if it did.

### 2.2 Comments

`#` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. A comment is part of the
line end that follows it, so a line holding only a comment is blank for
layout. There are no block comments. (`#` never occurs inside a token other
than a string.)

### 2.3 Tokens

Tokens are identifiers, keywords, operators and punctuation, and literals.
Spaces (U+0020) separate tokens and are otherwise ignored. Tokenization is
maximal munch: at each point the longest token that matches is taken. Two
consequences are stated so they are not surprises:

- `a<-b` lexes as `a`, `<-`, `b` (a send), never as `a < -b`. Write `a < -b`.
- `t.0.1` lexes `0.1` as a float. Write `(t.0).1`.

### 2.4 Identifiers and keywords

```
NAME = letter { letter | digit | "_" } .      (but not the single character "_")
letter = "A" … "Z" | "a" … "z" | "_" .
digit  = "0" … "9" .
```

Identifiers are ASCII. (Text values may hold any Unicode; names may not. This
keeps names comparable byte for byte, which the name-free hashing of 6.6
relies on.) `_` alone is the wildcard token.

Keywords are reserved and cannot be identifiers:

```
actor     after     and       arena     as        bound     break
chan      check     comptime  const     continue  default   device
elif      else      emit      error     event     example   extern
fail      false     fn        for       forall    from      if
impl      in        intent    iter      kind      let       linear
loop      match     module    mut       none      not       on
or        pass      pub       recv      refused   return    select
self      send      spawn     state     step      struct    then
to        trait     true      try       type      use       var
while     with      yield
```

A version 0.9 module reserves ten more words (Appendix F: `requires`, `ensures`, `decreases`, `ghost`, `ct`, `declassify`, `endorse`, `release`, `label` and `law`); in every other version they are names.

`device`, `iter`, `linear` and `yield` are new in draft 0.5. `lalr` is not a
keyword: drafts up to 0.4 reserved it in `rce.lark` and the tree-sitter
scanner by mistake, without listing it here; draft 0.5 removes it from both.

`catch` is also a keyword. Keywords are reserved everywhere except as a
member name directly after `.` (`x.type`, `c.close()`), where the grammar's
`member_name` admits them; this is the only place a keyword can be a name
(change S3). Note: `class`, `unsafe`, `null`, `goto`, `async`
and `await` are not keywords; `class` and `unsafe` used as statements are
syntax errors, and `unsafe`, `Rc`, `Arc`, `RefCell` as names are refused by
rule W-SAFE-1 (section 7) so prototype code that used them is diagnosed
clearly.

### 2.5 Literals

```
INT    = decimal | "0x" hexdig { [ "_" ] hexdig } | "0o" octdig { [ "_" ] octdig }
       | "0b" bindig { [ "_" ] bindig } .
decimal = digit { [ "_" ] digit } .
FLOAT  = decimal "." decimal [ exponent ] | decimal exponent .
exponent = ( "e" | "E" ) [ "+" | "-" ] digit { digit } .
STRING = `"` { char | escape } `"` .
char   = any Unicode scalar value except `"`, `\` and line end .
escape = `\"` | `\\` | `\n` | `\r` | `\t` | `\0` | `\u{` hexdig{1,6} `}` .
```

There are no literal suffixes (`1u8` is not a token): the type of a literal
comes from context (5.3). A `\u{…}` escape that is not a Unicode scalar value
(a surrogate, or above U+10FFFF) is refused. `-` is never part of a numeric
literal; `-1` is negation applied to `1`, except in patterns (3.9).
`true`, `false` and `none` are keyword literals.

### 2.6 Layout

RCE uses indentation for blocks, as Python does, and the rule is the same one
Python's tokenizer uses:

1. Inside `(`…`)`, `[`…`]` and `{`…`}` line ends and indentation are ignored.
2. Otherwise each line end that ends a non-blank line emits `NEWLINE`.
3. The layout pass keeps a stack of indentation widths, initially `[0]`. On
   the first token of a logical line with indentation width w (number of
   leading spaces): if w > top, push w and emit `INDENT`; if w < top, pop
   while w < top and emit one `DEDENT` per pop, and w must then equal top
   (otherwise the text is refused: "inconsistent dedent"); if w = top, emit
   nothing.
4. At end of file, emit `NEWLINE` if needed and one `DEDENT` per stack entry
   above 0.

Blank and comment-only lines produce no tokens. There is no line
continuation character; open a bracket instead.

### 2.7 Language version

A module may declare its language version on its first line, as the
comment

```
# rce-version: 0.6
```

The line must start with `#` in column 0 and hold, after optional spaces,
`rce-version:` and a version; trailing spaces are allowed. The known
versions are `0.5`, `0.6`, `0.7`, `0.8` and `0.9`; any other is refused (W-VER-1).
Version 0.8 is version 0.7 plus the indexed values of 5.16 (C.16). Version 0.9 is
version 0.8 plus Appendix F. The reference checker implements part of it (F.12)
and refuses the rest by version (W-VER-2); an implementation that has not
implemented Appendix F at all refuses a `0.9` declaration with W-VER-1, and one
that has implemented it applies F.1 to F.10 to that module only. A module
without the declaration is version 0.5. Version 0.5 is the language of
sections 2 to 10. Version 0.6 adds Appendix C: its 23 words become
keywords (C.1) and its constructs and rules apply. Version 0.7 has the
syntax and rules of 0.6 and differs from it only in the cost of standard
library methods (C.6.4, C.15). The meaning of a module is fixed by its
declared version: a change of meaning gets a new version, never a silent
change to an old one. A version 0.5 module
never sees Appendix C: its words are names there, and a valid 0.5 program
is accepted unchanged by every conforming implementation. Because the
declaration is a comment, the grammar of section 3 and its LALR(1) check
are unchanged for 0.5; a 0.6 or 0.7 module is parsed by section 3 with the rules
of C.2 applied, which is checked LALR(1) the same way. Each module of a program has its own version; a 0.6 or 0.7
module may `use` a 0.5 module and the reverse. The cost of a standard library method call (C.6.4) is fixed by the
declared version of the module where the call is written, wherever it is
executed from (C.15, normative); linking modules changes no cost. (The reference checker has a
non-normative `conc06` build feature that reads undeclared modules as 0.6,
for the draft's own test corpora; a declared version always wins.)

## 3. Syntactic grammar

This section is the complete grammar: which token sequences are programs.
Its EBNF is read by the machine check (3.12) and checked to be
*LALR(1)* (parsable left to right with one token of lookahead and no
conflicts), so every program has exactly one parse. Example:
`fn half(x: u64) -> u64 = x / 2` is a function declaration with an arrow body.

The grammar is LALR(1) with no conflicts (checked, 3.12). Where a reader might
see two parses, the grammar admits exactly one; the resolutions are listed in
3.11.

### 3.1 Modules

```
SourceFile   = { NEWLINE } [ ModuleHeader ] { Item } .
ModuleHeader = "module" Path NEWLINE .
Path         = NAME { "." NAME } .
Item         = UseDecl | IntentDecl | ExampleDecl | CheckDecl
             | [ "pub" ] ( ConstDecl | TypeDecl | StructDecl | KindDecl
                         | TraitDecl | FnDecl | ActorDecl )
             | StateDecl | EventDecl | ErrorDecl | StepDecl | ImplDecl
             | ExternDecl .
UseDecl      = "use" Path [ "as" NAME ] NEWLINE .
```

### 3.2 Intent

```
IntentDecl  = "intent" STRING NEWLINE [ INDENT IntentLine { IntentLine } DEDENT ] .
IntentLine  = ExampleDecl | CheckDecl | STRING NEWLINE .
ExampleDecl = "example" [ EventRef { "," EventRef } ] "->" Outcome NEWLINE .
EventRef    = NAME [ "(" [ Args ] ")" ] .
Outcome     = Expr | "refused" ":" ( NAME | "trap" "(" STRING ")" ) .
CheckDecl   = "check" Expr NEWLINE .
```

### 3.3 Data declarations

```
ConstDecl  = "const" NAME [ ":" Type ] "=" Expr NEWLINE .
TypeDecl   = "type" NAME [ Generics ] "=" Type [ "where" Expr ] NEWLINE .
StructDecl = [ "linear" ] "struct" NAME [ Generics ] NEWLINE [ INDENT Field { Field } DEDENT ] .
Field      = NAME ":" Type [ "=" Expr ] NEWLINE .
StateDecl  = "state" NAME NEWLINE INDENT Field { Field } DEDENT .
EventDecl  = "event" NAME [ Payload ] NEWLINE .
ErrorDecl  = "error" NAME [ Payload ] NEWLINE .
Payload    = "(" [ FieldItem { "," FieldItem } [ "," ] ] ")" .
FieldItem  = NAME ":" Type .
KindDecl   = "kind" NAME [ Generics ] NEWLINE INDENT Variant { Variant } DEDENT .
Variant    = NAME [ Payload ] NEWLINE .
```

### 3.4 Traits and implementations

```
TraitDecl   = "trait" NAME [ Generics ] [ ":" Bounds ] NEWLINE
              INDENT TraitMember { TraitMember } DEDENT .
TraitMember = "type" NAME [ ":" Bounds ] NEWLINE | FnSig NEWLINE .
ImplDecl    = "impl" [ "forall" Generics ] Type [ "for" Type ] NEWLINE
              INDENT ImplMember { ImplMember } DEDENT .
ImplMember  = TypeDecl | FnDecl .
Generics    = "[" GParam { "," GParam } "]" .
GParam      = [ "comptime" ] NAME [ ":" Bounds ] .
Bounds      = TypePath { "+" TypePath } .
```

`impl Show for Point` implements trait `Show` for `Point`; `impl Point`
(no `for`) adds inherent functions. `forall [T: Show]` binds the impl's type
parameters (3.11 R6 says why the keyword is needed).

### 3.5 Functions, steps and actors

```
FnSig     = [ "comptime" ] "fn" NAME [ Generics ] "(" [ Params ] ")" [ "->" Type ]
            [ "bound" INT ] .                                 (6.7)
FnDecl    = FnSig ( Block | "=" Expr NEWLINE ) .
ExternDecl = "extern" STRING FnSig NEWLINE .            (5.11)
Params    = Param { "," Param } [ "," ] .
Param     = [ "comptime" ] [ NAME ] NAME ":" Type | SelfParam .
SelfParam = "self" | "&" "self" | "&" "mut" "self" .
StepDecl  = "step" NAME "on" Pattern [ "if" Expr ] StepBody .
StepBody  = "->" Expr NEWLINE | Block .
ActorDecl = "actor" NAME NEWLINE INDENT ActorMember { ActorMember } DEDENT .
ActorMember = Field | Handler | FnDecl .
Handler   = "on" Pattern [ "if" Expr ] StepBody .
```

In `Param`, `from src: u8` declares argument label `from` and parameter name
`src` (Swift); `src: u8` alone uses `src` as both.

### 3.6 Types

Listed from loosest to tightest binding.

```
Type        = OptType [ "!" OptType ] .                  error union  T ! E
OptType     = BorrowType [ "?" ] .                       option       T?
BorrowType  = "&" [ "mut" ] BorrowType | RegionType .    borrow       &T, &mut T
RegionType  = BaseType [ "@" NAME ] .                    region       T @r
BaseType    = TypePath
            | "(" ")"                                    unit
            | "(" Type "," [ Type { "," Type } [ "," ] ] ")"   tuple
            | "(" Type ")"
            | "[" Type "]"                               slice
            | "[" Type ";" Expr "]"                      array, comptime length
            | "chan" BaseType                            channel
            | "iter" BaseType                            iterator (result of an iterator function only)
            | "fn" "(" [ TypeList ] ")" "->" BaseType .  function
TypePath    = Path [ "[" TypeList "]" ] .
TypeList    = Type { "," Type } [ "," ] .
```

### 3.7 Statements

```
Block      = NEWLINE INDENT Stmt { Stmt } DEDENT .
Stmt       = SimpleStmt | LetStmt | VarStmt | IfStmt | WhileStmt | LoopStmt
           | ForStmt | MatchStmt | ReturnStmt | BreakStmt | ContinueStmt
           | EmitStmt | FailStmt | SpawnStmt | SelectStmt | ArenaStmt
           | DeviceStmt | YieldStmt | ComptimeStmt | CheckDecl | PassStmt .
SimpleStmt = Expr [ AssignOp Expr | "<-" Expr ] NEWLINE .
AssignOp   = "=" | "+=" | "-=" | "*=" | "/=" | "%=" | "&=" | "|=" | "^=" | "<<=" | ">>=" .
LetStmt    = "let" Pattern [ ":" Type ] "=" Expr NEWLINE .
VarStmt    = "var" NAME [ ":" Type ] "=" Expr NEWLINE .
IfStmt     = "if" Expr Block { "elif" Expr Block } [ "else" Block ] .
WhileStmt  = "while" Expr [ Bound ] Block .
LoopStmt   = "loop" [ Bound ] Block .
Bound      = "bound" Expr .
ForStmt    = "for" Pattern "in" Expr Block .
MatchStmt  = "match" Expr NEWLINE INDENT Arm { Arm } DEDENT .
Arm        = Pattern [ "if" Expr ] ArmBody .
ArmBody    = "->" InlineStmt | Block .
InlineStmt = SimpleStmt | ReturnStmt | BreakStmt | ContinueStmt | PassStmt | EmitStmt | FailStmt | YieldStmt .
ReturnStmt = "return" [ Expr ] NEWLINE .
BreakStmt  = "break" NEWLINE .      ContinueStmt = "continue" NEWLINE .
PassStmt   = "pass" NEWLINE .       EmitStmt     = "emit" Expr NEWLINE .
FailStmt   = "fail" Expr NEWLINE .  SpawnStmt    = "spawn" Expr NEWLINE .
YieldStmt  = "yield" Expr NEWLINE .
SelectStmt = "select" NEWLINE INDENT SelectArm { SelectArm } DEDENT .
SelectArm  = "recv" Pattern "from" Expr ArmBody
           | "send" Expr "to" Expr ArmBody
           | "after" Expr ArmBody
           | "default" ArmBody .
ArenaStmt  = "with" "arena" NAME [ Bound ] Block .   (capacity, 5.7)
DeviceStmt = "with" "device" NAME [ Bound ] Block .  (accelerator region, 5.13)
ComptimeStmt = "comptime" Block .
```

The grammar accepts any expression left of `=`; rule W-PLACE (section 7)
then requires it to be a place (a variable, field, index or tuple member
path). This is how Python handles the same problem and keeps the grammar
LALR(1).

### 3.8 Expressions

Precedence, loosest first. All binary levels are left-associative except
comparison and range, which are non-associative (at most one operator).

| Level | Operators | Production |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `try e`, `try e else e`, `if c then a else b`, `fn(p) => e` | Expr |
| 2 | `a catch b`, `a catch \|x\| b` | CatchExpr |
| 3 | `or` | OrExpr |
| 4 | `and` | AndExpr |
| 5 | `not` (prefix) | NotExpr |
| 6 | `== != < <= > >= in not in` (non-assoc) | CmpExpr |
| 7 | `..` `..=` (non-assoc) | RangeExpr |
| 8 | `\|` | BorExpr |
| 9 | `^` | BxorExpr |
| 10 | `&` | BandExpr |
| 11 | `<< >>` | ShiftExpr |
| 12 | `+ -` | AddExpr |
| 13 | `* / %` | MulExpr |
| 14 | `as T` | CastExpr |
| 15 | prefix `- ~ & &mut <- comptime` | UnaryExpr |
| 16 | call `f(…)`, index `a[i]`, slice `a[i:j]`, member `.x`, `.0` | Postfix |

Unlike C, bitwise operators bind tighter than comparison, so `x & 1 == 1`
means `(x & 1) == 1`.

```
Expr      = "try" CatchExpr [ "else" CatchExpr ]
          | "if" Expr "then" CatchExpr "else" CatchExpr
          | "fn" "(" [ Params ] ")" "=>" CatchExpr
          | CatchExpr .
CatchExpr = OrExpr [ "catch" [ "|" NAME "|" ] OrExpr ] .
OrExpr    = AndExpr { "or" AndExpr } .
AndExpr   = NotExpr { "and" NotExpr } .
NotExpr   = "not" NotExpr | CmpExpr .
CmpExpr   = RangeExpr [ CmpOp RangeExpr ] .
CmpOp     = "==" | "!=" | "<" | "<=" | ">" | ">=" | "in" | "not" "in" .
RangeExpr = BorExpr [ ( ".." | "..=" ) BorExpr ] .
BorExpr   = BxorExpr { "|" BxorExpr } .
BxorExpr  = BandExpr { "^" BandExpr } .
BandExpr  = ShiftExpr { "&" ShiftExpr } .
ShiftExpr = AddExpr { ( "<<" | ">>" ) AddExpr } .
AddExpr   = MulExpr { ( "+" | "-" ) MulExpr } .
MulExpr   = CastExpr { ( "*" | "/" | "%" ) CastExpr } .
CastExpr  = UnaryExpr [ "as" BaseType ] .
UnaryExpr = ( "-" | "~" | "&" [ "mut" ] | "<-" | "comptime" ) UnaryExpr | Postfix .
Postfix   = Primary
          | Postfix "(" [ Args ] ")"
          | Postfix "[" Expr { "," Expr } "]"
          | Postfix "[" [ Expr ] ":" [ Expr ] "]"
          | Postfix "." ( NAME | INT ) .
Args      = Arg { "," Arg } [ "," ] .
Arg       = [ NAME ":" ] Expr .
Primary   = NAME | "self" | INT | FLOAT | STRING | "true" | "false" | "none"
          | "(" ")" | "(" Expr ")" | "(" Expr "," [ Expr { "," Expr } [ "," ] ] ")"
          | "[" "]" | "[" Expr { "," Expr } [ "," ] "]" | "[" Expr ";" Expr "]"
          | "[" Expr "for" Pattern "in" OrExpr [ "if" OrExpr ] "]"
          | "{" "}" | "{" MapEntry { "," MapEntry } [ "," ] "}"
          | "chan" "[" Type "]" "(" [ Expr ] ")" .
MapEntry  = Expr ":" Expr .
```

### 3.9 Patterns

```
Pattern     = AtomPattern { "|" AtomPattern } .
AtomPattern = "_" | Path | Path "(" [ PatArg { "," PatArg } [ "," ] ] ")"
            | LitPattern [ ( ".." | "..=" ) LitPattern ]
            | "(" Pattern "," [ Pattern { "," Pattern } [ "," ] ] ")"
            | "(" Pattern ")" .
PatArg      = [ NAME ":" ] Pattern .
LitPattern  = INT | "-" INT | FLOAT | STRING | "true" | "false" | "none" .
```

### 3.10 Statement and expression boundaries

A `Block` always begins with `NEWLINE INDENT`, so a block can never be
confused with an expression. A one-line form exists for the common cases:
`fn f(x: T) -> U = e`, `step S on E -> e`, and `Pattern -> stmt` in `match`
and `select`.

### 3.11 How apparent ambiguities are resolved

Each is resolved in the grammar itself, so there is no precedence
declaration and no conflict to resolve at parse time.

- **R1 dangling else.** `else` only follows a `Block` (statement `if`) or is
  mandatory (`if … then … else …` expression). A statement `if` ends at its
  `DEDENT`, so the next `else` at the same indentation belongs to it.
- **R2 `try … else` against `if … then … else`.** The branches of an `if`
  expression and the operands of `try` are `CatchExpr`, which cannot contain a
  bare `try` or `if`. `if c then try a else b` is a syntax error; write
  `if c then (try a else b) else d`.
- **R3 comparison chains.** `0 < a < 10` is a syntax error (non-associative).
  Write `a in 0..10`.
- **R4 assignment against equality.** `=` is a statement form, never an
  expression; `(x = 1)` is a syntax error.
- **R5 generic call against index.** `f[T](x)` parses as `index(f, T)` then a
  call; name resolution (4.3) turns an index of a generic function or type by
  type arguments into instantiation, as in Go.
- **R6 impl generics against slice types.** `impl [T] …` would be ambiguous
  with the slice type `[T]`, so impl parameters need `forall`:
  `impl forall[T: Show] Show for List[T]`.
- **R7 labels.** In argument and pattern lists `NAME ":"` is always a label.
  Map literals `{k: v}` are in a different bracket, so `{a: 1}` is a map whose
  key is the variable `a` (write `{"a": 1}` for a text key).
- **R8 variant patterns against bindings.** A `Path` pattern is a unit variant
  if name resolution finds a variant of that name in scope, otherwise it binds
  a fresh variable (Rust's rule). W-PAT-1 refuses a binding that shadows a
  variant name, so a misspelled variant is never silently a binding.
- **R9 send.** `<-` after an expression at statement level is a send;
  in prefix position it is a receive. The two never meet: `a <- <- b` is
  "send the value received from b to a".

### 3.12 Machine check

`rce-spec-check` (in `spec/checker/`, Rust only):

1. reads every rule of this section from its code blocks (the annotation
   column beside a rule is prose and is skipped), expands the EBNF the way
   Lark did (`[ X ]` and `{ X }` inlined as with and without, `{ X }` as one
   left-recursive helper rule), builds the LALR(1) tables and fails on any
   shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflict (verified: adding
   `| AddExpr "+" AddExpr` to `AddExpr` makes it fail with 3 conflicts);
   current result (draft 0.9): 100 rules, 491 productions, 974 states, 0
   conflicts (`scripts/claim-counts.py --check` compares these numbers with
   the output of `rce-spec-check`);
2. parses the 59 programs in `examples/` (the 57 files there and the 2 of
   `examples/26_use_module/`), with and without their final
   newline; all must parse;
3. parses the 12 programs in `examples/reject/` (tab indent, chained
   comparison, `if` expression without `else`, `try` in a `then` branch,
   inconsistent dedent, `class`, assignment inside an expression, empty `kind`,
   state with no fields, `step` without `on`, example without `->`,
   unterminated string); all must be refused.

Each program is parsed three ways (the LALR(1) tables on the reference
lexer's tokens, the Rust parser, and the tree-sitter port) and all three must
agree. Until 2026-10-12 this check was `spec/check.py` on `spec/rce.lark`
with Lark in strict mode; both are retired.

`spec/tree-sitter/` is the same grammar for tree-sitter (`grammar.js`, with
layout, bracket depth, reserved-keyword NAME and longest-match numbers and
`<-` in `src/scanner.c`). The former `tree-sitter/compare.py N SEED` parsed every
example and N fuzz programs, each program's syntax mutants and SOUP
lexical-stress mutants (a random token jammed in or a space deleted) with
Lark and tree-sitter and required that both refuse, or both accept with identical
trees (rule names, nesting, kept tokens and their text). Results: 81 examples
plus 10,000 programs (seed 7, SOUP=2): 69,323 inputs, 15,205 accepted by both
with identical trees, 54,118 refused by both, 0 disagreements; 10,000
programs (seed 11, SOUP=10): 149,365 inputs, 35,837 identical trees, 113,528
refused by both, 0 disagreements.
Draft 0.4 grammar (with `extern` and arena `bound`): 91 examples plus 2,000
programs (seed 7, SOUP=2): 13,983 inputs, 3,060 identical trees, 10,923
refused by both, 0 disagreements. Draft 0.5 grammar and generator (`linear`, `iter`,
`yield`, `device`, no `lalr`): 127 examples plus 2,000 programs (seed 7,
SOUP=2): 16,092 inputs, 3,185 identical trees, 12,907 refused by both,
0 disagreements.

## 4. Programs, names and scope

This section says what a whole program is: a set of modules, the names each
module can see, and the Form the program denotes. A *module* is one source
file; *scope* is the region of text where a name can be used. Example:
`use std.text` makes the module `std.text` visible as `text`.

### 4.1 Modules and packages

A source file is a module. Its path is given by `module a.b.c` or, if absent,
by its file path relative to the package root with `/` read as `.` and the
`.rce` extension removed. `use p.q` makes module `p.q` visible under the name
`q`; `use p.q as r` under `r`. Items are private to their module unless marked
`pub`. Import cycles are refused (W-MOD-2). The modules `std.text`,
`std.collections` and `std.math` are built in and always resolvable (S4); a
program is the set of modules given together, and `use` must name one of them
or a built-in module (W-NAME-1).

### 4.2 The program's Form

A **Form module** is a module (with what it imports) that declares at least one
`state`, `event` or `actor`. The Form of the program is built from all Form
modules reachable from the root (6.1). A module with only `fn`, types, `const`
and `impl` is a **library module**: it has no Form of its own and denotes a set
of pure functions.

A program whose root declares `fn main()` and no state is a **command**: it
denotes the Form with one region `Main` of unit type, one event `Start(args:
List[text])`, and δ given by running `main` (6.8).

### 4.3 Scope

Scopes nest: universe (built-in types and functions, 6.3–6.4) ⊃ package ⊃
module ⊃ item (generic parameters, parameters, state fields inside steps)
⊃ block. Declarations at module level are visible throughout the module
regardless of order (so `const N` may follow its use). Inside a block a name is
visible from its declaration to the end of the block. Shadowing a name from an
enclosing *block* is allowed with `let`; shadowing a parameter, a state field
or a module-level name in the same item is refused (W-NAME-2).

Namespaces: one namespace for values (variables, functions, consts, variants,
events, errors) and one for types (types, kinds, traits, states, actors).
Event, error and variant constructors live in both: as types (for patterns and
payload typing) and as constructor functions.

**Read receipt.** What is the outermost scope called? (one word)

## 5. Static semantics

This section gives the *static semantics*: the rules checked before a
program runs. A *type* is the set of values an expression may have;
*ownership* says which variable is responsible for a value, and a *borrow*
is a temporary reference to it. Example: after `let b = a` where `a` is a
`List`, using `a` again is refused because the list moved to `b`.

### 5.1 Types

```
τ ::= bool | i8 | i16 | i32 | i64 | u8 | u16 | u32 | u64 | usize | f64 | f32
    | text | ()                                  base types
    | (τ₁, …, τₙ)            n ≥ 2               tuple
    | [τ; n]                 n a comptime usize  array
    | List[τ] | Map[τ_k, τ_v] | Set[τ]            owned collections
    | [τ]                                         slice (only behind a borrow)
    | τ?                                          option (= kind Option[τ])
    | τ ! ε                                       error union, ε a set of errors
    | &τ | &mut τ                                 borrows (second class, 5.6)
    | τ @r                                        τ allocated in region r
    | chan τ                                      channel handle
    | iter τ                                      iterator (5.14)
    | fn(τ₁, …, τₙ) -> τ                          function value (no capture of borrows)
    | N[τ₁, …, τₙ]                                nominal: struct, kind, actor, state
    | α                                           type parameter
```

`usize` is a u64 used for lengths and indexes. `f32` (draft 0.5) is computed
in f64 and rounded once to f32 after each operation (6.3 N7), so every target
gives the same bits. Float literals are f64; an f32 value is written
`x as f32`, and f32 and f64 never mix without a cast. `Box[τ]` is `List`-like owned indirection of one
element, needed only for recursive kinds; a `&Box[τ]` (or `&mut Box[τ]`)
argument is accepted where `&τ` (`&mut τ`) is expected (deref coercion,
draft 0.4). Every type has a **kind** of
ownership (5.5): `Copy`, `Move`, or `Borrow`.

**Integer ranges.** An integer type denotes the mathematical integers in its
range: iN = [−2^(N−1), 2^(N−1)−1], uN = [0, 2^N−1]. Arithmetic is checked
against the *declared* type's range (6.3). Arithmetic on u64 and usize uses
the Form's unsigned operations (6.3 N8, draft 0.5), so the whole range
[0, 2^64) is available; drafts up to 0.4 trapped any u64 result at or above
2^63 (D7).

**Text is byte-indexed (draft 0.5).** `s.len()` is the number of UTF-8
bytes, `s[i]` is the byte at offset i as a `u8`, and `s[a:b]` is the text
between byte offsets a and b, which must both be character boundaries
(otherwise `trap("not a char boundary")`). Iterating `for c in s` still
yields one-character texts. Go, Rust and Zig all index text by byte; the
draft 0.4 code-point indexing made `s[i]` O(n).

**Lane-wise arithmetic (draft 0.5).** For arrays `a, b : [τ; n]` of one
numeric τ and one comptime length n, `a + b`, `a - b`, `a * b`, `a / b` (and
`a % b` for integers) apply the operator lane by lane and have type
`[τ; n]`. Each lane follows the scalar rules (overflow and division by zero
trap). Different lengths, or a non-numeric τ, are refused (W-SIMD-1). An
implementation may use vector instructions; the result is defined by the
lanes, so it is the same on every target. A list literal is a `List` unless
it meets an array type of the same length, as an integer literal is i64
unless it meets another integer type.

**Type aliases.** `type A = τ` (and `type A[α₁, …, αₙ] = τ`) without
`where` gives τ a second name: A, with its parameters substituted, is the
type τ in every rule. It is not a nominal type, since N above ranges only
over structs, kinds, actors and states. So a parameter `c: A` with
`type A = chan τ′` is a `chan` parameter and makes its function a task
function (5.2), and a value of type A is accepted wherever τ is and the
reverse. Example: with `type Pipe = chan (u64, text)`, `fn feed(p: Pipe,
n: u64)` may send on p and be spawned (`spec/checker/tests/alias.rs`).

**Refined types (extension, all versions).** `type R = τ where p`
declares R as the values of τ that satisfy the predicate p, in which
`self` names the value. τ is an integer type, `text`, or a `List`, `Map`,
`Set` or array type. p is in a decidable fragment: comparisons (`<`, `<=`,
`>`, `>=`, `==`, `!=`) between `self` (integer τ), `self.len()` (text,
in UTF-8 bytes as in 5.15, or a collection) and integer literals; the
character classes `self.isdigit()`, `self.isalpha()`, `self.isspace()`,
`self.isempty()` of a text; and `and`, `or`, `not`. Anything else is
W-REF-1. `where` is contextual: no type is followed by a name, so the
word stays an ordinary identifier. A refined value is checked exactly
where a value is checked against its declared integer range (6.3, 6.4
step 3): at a typed `let` or `var`, a parameter, a field or payload
constructor, a field initializer and the write-back of a state field.
The check fits the value to τ first, then evaluates p; if p is false the
result is `trap("refinement: value is outside R")`. So an event whose
payload is outside its refined type is refused before any step runs, as
an out-of-range integer payload is, and a step whose new state breaks a
field's predicate refuses the event with the state unchanged (6.4, T8).
`R <: τ`: a refined value is used wherever τ is. Derivation: validation
that the type does not record can be skipped (soundness), a predicate
checked at one boundary has one outcome (determinism), and the
refinement reuses the one boundary the language already has, the range
check, rather than a second mechanism (one meaning per construct). The
fragment is decidable in time linear in p and in the value, so the check
has a fixed cost class (energy observability); full dependent types are
excluded by the same derivation, since an undecidable obligation would
make acceptance itself unbounded. Example: `type Pct = u8 where self <=
100`; `event SetVolume(pct: Pct)`; `SetVolume(pct: 101)` is refused with
`refinement: value is outside Pct`, and a step computing `level + 60` on
`level: Pct = 60` refuses its event. Lean: `RCE/Refine.lean`
(`holds_total`, `fit_sound`, `refine_preserved`,
`refine_refused_unchanged`, `admit_sound`; T35).

**Error sets.** In `τ ! ε`, ε is a finite set of declared `error` names,
written as one error name or as the name of a `kind` whose variants are all
errors (`type ParseErrs = …` is not needed; declare `kind ParseErrs` with
variants `ParseFailed(at: u32)` and `Empty`). Subtyping:
`τ ! ε₁ <: τ ! ε₂` iff ε₁ ⊆ ε₂, and `τ <: τ ! ε` (a plain value is a
success).

### 5.2 Contexts and modes

A typing context Γ maps each variable to (τ, m) with mode
m ∈ {let, var, field} and a liveness flag (live, moved). A step body runs in
context `step(R)`, a function body in `fn`, a comptime block in `comptime`,
and an actor handler in `actor(A)`. Effects are tied to the context:

| Context | may `emit` | may `fail` | may `spawn`/send/recv/`select` | may read state |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `fn` (pure) | no | yes (if return type is `τ ! ε`) | no | no |
| task `fn` (has a `chan` parameter) | yes | yes | yes | no |
| `fn main` | yes | yes | yes | no |
| `step(R)` | yes | yes | send only (to actors and declared channels) | fields of R only |
| `actor(A)` handler | yes | yes | send only | fields of A only |
| `comptime` | no | yes (compile error) | no | no |
| call a foreign `extern` fn (5.11) | only from `fn main` and task functions | | | |

A function called from a step does not inherit the step's effects; only the
step body itself emits or sends. A function with a `chan` parameter is a
**task function**: it may `emit`, send, receive, `select` and `spawn`, and it
can be called (or spawned) only from `main` or another task function. Every
other `fn` is a pure function of its arguments; a pure function, a step or a
handler cannot call a task function (W-EFF-1). `spawn f(ā)` requires f to be a
task function (W-SPAWN-1). (Change S2: draft 0.1 made every `fn` but `main`
pure, which left nothing that `spawn` could start.)

**Tail values.** In a block-bodied function, if the last statement is an
expression statement, or a `match` or `if`/`else` whose every branch ends in
one (recursively), those expressions are the function's result and are typed
against its return type ([Tail]; change S5). Elsewhere an expression
statement's value is discarded, and an error union may not be discarded.

### 5.3 Typing expressions

Judgment: Σ; Γ; Δ ⊢ e : τ ⊣ Γ′, under declarations Σ, context Γ and live
borrows Δ, expression e has type τ and leaves context Γ′ (Γ′ differs from Γ
only by variables marked moved).

```
  (x : τ, m, live) ∈ Γ     τ Copy
  ─────────────────────────────────── [Var-Copy]
  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ x : τ ⊣ Γ

  (x : τ, m, live) ∈ Γ     τ Move     x ∉ dom(Δ)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────── [Var-Move]
  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ x : τ ⊣ Γ[x ↦ moved]

  n literal    n ∈ range(ι)    ι an integer type expected by context (default i64)
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── [Int]
  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ n : ι ⊣ Γ

  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ a : ι ⊣ Γ₁    Σ;Γ₁;Δ ⊢ b : ι ⊣ Γ₂    ⊕ ∈ {+,-,*,/,%}    ι numeric
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── [Arith]
  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ a ⊕ b : ι ! {Overflow?, DivZero?} ⊣ Γ₂
```

Arithmetic failure is not part of the static error set the programmer
declares: it is a **trap** (6.5), the Form's defined `err` outcome, and refuses
the event. This matches the Form, where integer overflow is an error, never a
wrap. Both operands must have the same numeric type; there is no implicit
widening (use `as`).

```
  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ e : τ ! ε ⊣ Γ′    the enclosing function returns σ ! ε′    ε ⊆ ε′
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── [Try]
  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ try e : τ ⊣ Γ′

  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ e : τ? ⊣ Γ₁  (or τ ! ε)    Σ;Γ₁;Δ ⊢ E : error ⊣ Γ₂    E ∈ ε′
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── [Try-Else]
  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ try e else E : τ ⊣ Γ₂

  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ e : τ ! ε  (or τ?) ⊣ Γ₁    Σ;Γ₁,x:ε;Δ ⊢ h : τ ⊣ Γ₂
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── [Catch]
  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ e catch |x| h : τ ⊣ Γ₂

  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ c : bool ⊣ Γ₁   Σ;Γ₁;Δ ⊢ a : τ ⊣ Γ₂   Σ;Γ₁;Δ ⊢ b : τ ⊣ Γ₃
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── [If-Expr]
  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ if c then a else b : τ ⊣ Γ₂ ⊓ Γ₃
```

Γ₂ ⊓ Γ₃ marks a variable moved if it is moved in either branch (a moved-on-
one-path variable cannot be used after the join).

```
  f : fn[ᾱ: B̄](l₁ x₁: τ₁, …, lₙ xₙ: τₙ) -> σ ∈ Σ
  θ = unify(ᾱ, …)     θ(ᾱ) satisfies B̄     Σ;Γᵢ₋₁;Δ ⊢ aᵢ : θτᵢ ⊣ Γᵢ
  labels of the call equal l₁…lₙ (labels may be omitted only when lᵢ = xᵢ)
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── [Call]
  Σ;Γ₀;Δ ⊢ f(a₁, …, aₙ) : θσ ⊣ Γₙ

  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ e : K[τ̄] ⊣ Γ′   arms pᵢ ⇒ bᵢ    Σ ⊢ pᵢ : K[τ̄] ▷ Γᵢ
  Σ;Γ′,Γᵢ;Δ ⊢ bᵢ ok     covers(K, p₁…pₙ)
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── [Match]
  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ match e { pᵢ ⇒ bᵢ } ok
```

`covers` is the standard exhaustiveness relation over constructors
(Maranget 2007): every value of K[τ̄] matches some unguarded arm, or some arm
whose guard is the literal `true`. Guards do not count toward coverage.
Integer and text scrutinees need a `_` arm (their domains are not
enumerated) unless every value of a bounded integer type is covered by ranges.

Statements: Σ; Γ; Δ ⊢ s ⊣ Γ′. `let p = e` binds immutably; `var x = e`
binds mutably; `place op= e` needs `place` rooted at a `var`, a `&mut`
parameter, or (in a step) a field of the stepped region. `return e` needs `e`
to have the function's return type (or a subtype). `fail E(…)` needs `E` in
the function's declared error set (in a step: any declared `error`).

### 5.4 Types of declarations

- `state R` with fields fᵢ : τᵢ = eᵢ: every τᵢ is an **owned value type**
  (no borrows, no channels, no region types, no functions); every eᵢ is a
  comptime constant expression (W-STATE-2). R's type is the record
  {fᵢ : τᵢ}.
- `event E(fᵢ : τᵢ)` and `error E(fᵢ : τᵢ)`: payload types are **data types**:
  base types, tuples, arrays, `List`, `Map`, `Set`, options, structs and kinds
  built from data types. Events may additionally carry `chan τ` (a reply
  channel) when received by an actor.
- `step R on p if g -> e`: in context `step(R)`, the fields of R are bound as
  `var`, p is typed against the event sum, g : bool, and e must have the type
  of R's single field (only allowed when R has exactly one field; W-STEP-3).
  With a block body, the body is a statement list; the final state is the
  values of the field variables at the end of the block.
- `actor A` with fields and handlers: like a `state` whose steps are the
  handlers, plus an address type `A` (a `Copy` handle) that supports
  `a <- msg`.

### 5.5 Ownership

Every value has exactly one owner: a variable, a field, a collection slot, a
channel buffer, or the state. Types fall in three ownership kinds:

```
Copy   : bool, integers, f32, f64, (), chan τ, actor handles, fn values,
         and tuples/arrays/structs/kinds all of whose components are Copy
         and whose size is fixed.
Move   : text, List, Map, Set, Box, options/tuples/structs/kinds containing a Move component.
Borrow : &τ, &mut τ, [τ] (slices exist only borrowed).
```

Rules:

```
  O1  Use of a Move variable moves it ([Var-Move]); a moved variable cannot be
      read, borrowed, or moved again until reassigned.
  O2  Assignment `x = e` to a var drops the old value of x first and makes
      x live.
  O3  `copy(e)` duplicates a value of any data type (deep copy); it is the
      only way to duplicate a Move value. (Copy-on-write is an
      implementation choice, not visible.)
  O4  At the end of each block, live owned values introduced in it are
      dropped in reverse order of introduction. Drop has no user-visible
      effect (there are no destructors), so drop order is unobservable.
```

### 5.6 Borrowing

RCE borrows are **second class** (as in Hylo and Swift's `inout`): a borrow
can be created only as a function argument or as the operand of a `for`, a
`match`, a method receiver, or a `let` whose scope ends before any
conflicting use. A borrow cannot be stored in a field, a collection, a
channel message, an event, a state, a closure that escapes, or be returned:
with one exception: a function whose return type is a borrow (`-> &[T]`) must
return a borrow derived from a parameter, and the result is tied to that
parameter (R-RET). This removes lifetime annotations entirely.

Δ is a set of live borrows `(ℓ, k, path)` with k ∈ {shr, mut}. Paths are
`x`, `x.f`, `x[_]` (any element), ordered by prefix (`x` ⊑ `x.f`).

```
  path p rooted at a live variable    no (ℓ′, mut, q) ∈ Δ with p, q overlapping
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── [Borrow-Shr]
  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ &p : &τ  with Δ′ = Δ ∪ {(ℓ, shr, p)}

  p rooted at a var or &mut     no (ℓ′, _, q) ∈ Δ with p, q overlapping
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── [Borrow-Mut]
  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ &mut p : &mut τ  with Δ′ = Δ ∪ {(ℓ, mut, p)}

  writing, moving or dropping p requires no (ℓ′, _, q) ∈ Δ overlapping p   [No-Alias-Write]
  reading p requires no (ℓ′, mut, q) ∈ Δ overlapping p, q ≠ p's own borrow   [No-Mut-Read]
```

Two paths overlap iff one is a prefix of the other; `x[i]` and `x[j]` always
overlap (indexes are not compared statically). A borrow ℓ ends at the end of
the call or statement that created it (R-END), or for R-RET at the last use of
the returned value. Because borrows never outlive the statement that made
them except through R-RET, Δ is empty at every statement boundary not inside
an R-RET region, which makes the check a local, linear pass.

**Shared XOR mutable (theorem T6 relies on this):** at every program point,
for every path p, either Δ holds no mut borrow overlapping p, or it holds
exactly one and no shared borrow overlapping p.

**Not relaxed in draft 0.9.** A limited relaxation, in which a reference is
invalidated only below steps that are not independent of it (the group
borrowing of the Valen language), is sound in the form studied, but its
preservation of T6 is not proved. The rules above are unchanged; the
obligation is T56 (Appendix F, F.9, stated and unproved), and the rule is
adopted only after that lemma is proved in Lean. Relaxing W-PAR-1 is not
sound and is excluded (F.2).

**Read receipt.** What is the name of the example kind used to illustrate error sets?

## 5 (continued). Static semantics: regions, effects and extensions

This section continues the static rules for features that control where
values live and what code may do: *regions* (arenas freed as a block),
concurrency, traits, compile-time code, foreign functions, and the draft 0.5
linear types, device regions and iterators. Example:
`with arena r bound 4096` gives a block its own memory of at most 4096
canonical bytes, freed when the block ends.

### 5.7 Regions (arenas)

`with arena r` introduces region r for the block. A type `τ @r` is allocated
in r.

```
  Σ;Γ,r:region;Δ ⊢ body ⊣ Γ′    r ∉ free-regions(Γ′ restricted to dom(Γ))
  r ∉ free-regions(type of any value assigned to a place outside the block)
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── [Arena]
  Σ;Γ;Δ ⊢ with arena r body ⊣ Γ′ \ r
```

`with arena r bound n` gives r a capacity of n bytes (n : u64, evaluated
once at block entry). Capacity is counted in canonical bytes, the length
of the canonical JSON of each value allocated in r, so the limit is the
same on every implementation. An allocation that would take r past n is
`trap("size limit")`, and the event is refused as for any trap. Without
`bound` the capacity is unlimited except by N9. The reference evaluator
measures the values bound in the region after every statement of the
region's body. So nothing allocated in r escapes the block; copying out (`copy(x)`, or
pushing a Copy element) is how results leave. Each step body runs inside an
implicit region `step` freed when the step returns; state fields are not
region-typed (they live in the state's own storage).

### 5.8 Concurrency

- `chan[τ](n)` creates a channel with capacity n (a comptime or runtime
  usize; 0 means rendezvous) and type `chan τ`; τ must be a data type or a
  `chan`. Channels are Copy handles.
- `c <- v` moves v into the channel. `<- c` has type `τ?` (none when c is
  closed and empty).
- `spawn f(a₁…aₙ)` requires every argument to be a data value or channel
  (not a borrow, not region-typed): arguments are moved into the task
  (W-SPAWN-1). Tasks share nothing but channels and actor handles, so data
  races cannot be written.
- `select` arms: `recv p from c` (c : chan τ, p : τ?), `send v to c`,
  `after n` (n : u64 logical ticks), `default`. At most one `default`, at most
  one `after`.

### 5.9 Traits

A trait declares associated types and function signatures. `impl Tr for T`
must define every member with a signature equal to the trait's after
substituting `Self := T` (W-TRAIT-1). Coherence: at most one impl of a trait
for a type in the whole program, and an impl must be in the module of the
trait or of the type (orphan rule, W-TRAIT-2). Generic functions are
monomorphized (no dynamic dispatch, no vtables), so trait method calls are
resolved statically. Built-in traits: `Eq`, `Ord`, `Hash`, `Show`, `Copy`,
`Data`, derived structurally for every type whose components have them
(f64 is `Eq` and `Ord` with the total order of 6.3, since NaN never exists).

### 5.10 Comptime

An expression or block marked `comptime`, every `const` initializer, every
array length, every state field initializer, and every argument for a
`comptime` parameter is evaluated during compilation by the dynamic semantics
of section 6 (with the same edge semantics). A comptime evaluation that traps
or exceeds its fuel (6.7) is a compile error. A `comptime fn` may only be
called at comptime. Comptime results become constants in the Form IR.
Comptime evaluation cannot read files, clocks, environment or network
(W-CT-1), so compilation is deterministic.

### 5.11 Foreign functions

`extern "C" fn f(p₁: τ₁, …) -> σ` declares a function implemented outside
RCE with the platform C calling convention. It has no body. Rules (W-FFI-1):

- The ABI string is `"C"`. A foreign function is not `comptime`, not generic
  and has no `self`.
- Each parameter type is `bool`, an integer type, `f64`, `&text` (passed as
  a pointer to UTF-8 bytes and a byte length), `&[τ]` or `&mut [τ]` with τ one
  of those scalars (pointer and element count). Borrows are second class
  (5.6), so the foreign callee holds them for the duration of the call only;
  no copy is made.
- The result type is a scalar or `()`. No memory allocated by foreign code
  is ever owned by RCE, and no RCE allocation is freed by foreign code, so
  the two sides never need to agree on an allocator.
- A foreign function may be called only from `fn main` and task functions
  (W-EFF-1), never from a pure function, a step, a handler or comptime, and
  it cannot be spawned (W-SPAWN-1). δ therefore never calls foreign code.
- A foreign function is not a value: its name may appear only as the
  callee of a direct call (W-FFI-1). The context rule above is checked at
  the call, so a value would let a pure function receive a foreign
  function from `main` and call it.
- Each call is recorded in the log as `Foreign(f, arguments, result)`.
  Replay supplies the recorded result instead of calling f, so the run of a
  command remains a function of its inputs and its log (T1, T3), with
  foreign results counted as inputs.
- The memory behaviour of the foreign code is outside the language: T6
  holds for the RCE side on the assumption that the callee touches only the
  buffers it was given, writes only through `&mut` buffers, and keeps no
  pointer after it returns. This is the trust boundary; it is named by the
  `extern` keyword at the one place it occurs.

### 5.12 Linear types (draft 0.5)

`linear struct H` declares a type whose values must be used exactly once.
It is meant for handles to outside resources (a file, a socket, a device
buffer) that must be released once and only once. Rules (W-LIN-1):

- A linear value is moved, never copied: `copy(h)` is refused, and the type
  is not Copy whatever its fields are.
- Every linear local, parameter included, is consumed (moved into a call,
  returned, or sent into a foreign function) exactly once on every path:
  a linear local still live at the end of its block, at `return` or at
  `fail` is refused, and so is one consumed on some branches of an `if` or
  `match` but not others.
- A linear value is not moved inside a loop body unless it was created in
  that iteration.
- A linear type may not appear inside a collection, an array, an option,
  a channel, a state or actor field, an event or error payload, a struct
  field or an iterator's element type. So no data structure can hide a
  second copy or drop one.
- A foreign function (5.11) may take and return a linear struct whose one
  field is an integer or `bool`; the C side sees that scalar. This is how
  `open`/`close` pairs are typed.

Reading a field (`h.fd`) does not consume the value. Lean:
`RCE/Linear.lean` (`linear_exactly_once`).

### 5.13 Device regions (draft 0.5)

`with device d [bound n]` is a region (5.7) whose contents an implementation
may place in accelerator memory. In addition to the arena rules, a device
region holds fixed-size values only: no `List`, `Map`, `Set`, `text`,
slice, channel or iterator may be bound in it, and its body may not `emit`,
`spawn`, send, `select`, `yield` or call a foreign function (W-DEV-1). The
body is therefore pure arithmetic on scalars, tuples, structs of those and
arrays (with lane-wise operators), which is what accelerators run. Its
meaning is the same as the block run on the CPU, so the region is only a
placement hint; `bound` counts canonical bytes as for arenas.

### 5.14 Iterators (draft 0.5)

A function whose result type is `iter τ` is an iterator function. Its body
is a block that produces values with `yield e` (e : τ) and ends by falling
off the end or by `return` with no value. Rules (W-ITER-1):

- An iterator function is pure (no `chan` parameter, no effects), and
  `yield` appears only in one.
- A value of type `iter τ` may only be the operand of `for` or the receiver
  of `.collect()` (which returns `List[τ]`). It cannot be stored, passed or
  returned, so an iterator is never shared or resumed twice.

The meaning is the push model of Go 1.23 range-over-func: the loop body runs
at each `yield`, `break` in the body stops the iterator, and `return` in the
body returns from the enclosing function. The number of yields per run
counts against the loop limit (6.7), so `yield` number LOOP_LIMIT + 1 is
`trap("loop bound")`, and an iterator always terminates. Python generators
and Rust iterators are pull-based and can be resumed from anywhere; the push
form keeps delta total without any suspended state.

### 5.15 Standard library, effects and I/O

**Standard library (normative).** The standard library is closed: it is
exactly the builtin methods below plus the concurrency methods of 5.8 and
Appendix C (`close`, `join`, `offer`, `put`, `wait`, `freeze`, `pscan`,
`pscan_incl`) and the num.rs primitives of 6.3. A method not in the table
is W-NAME-1 at check time, so no program reaches an unknown method at run
time. Every method in the table is pure and deterministic: it reads its
receiver and arguments, and a method that "changes" a receiver (`push`,
`insert`, `sort`, ...) updates only that receiver variable; none performs
I/O. The table is checked
against the reference evaluator (`spec/checker/tests/stdlib_costs.rs`).

| Receiver | RCE type | Methods |
|---|---|---|
| `Int` | integers (iN, uN, usize) | `abs`, `checked_add`, `checked_div`, `checked_mul`, `checked_sub`, `max`, `min`, `saturating_add`, `saturating_mul`, `saturating_sub`, `tostr`, `wrapping_add`, `wrapping_mul`, `wrapping_sub` |
| `F` | f64 | `abs`, `ceil`, `floor`, `max`, `min`, `round`, `sqrt`, `tostr` |
| `Bool` | bool | `tostr` |
| `Text` | text | `chars`, `contains`, `endswith`, `isalpha`, `isdigit`, `isempty`, `isspace`, `join`, `len`, `len_bytes`, `len_chars`, `lines`, `lower`, `raw`, `reverse`, `sha256`, `split`, `startswith`, `strip`, `toint`, `tostr`, `upper`, `words` |
| `F32` | f32 | `abs`, `tostr` |
| `Gen` | iter τ | `collect` |
| `List` | List[τ], [τ; n] | `append`, `clear`, `contains`, `filter`, `fold`, `get`, `isempty`, `len`, `map`, `pop`, `push`, `reverse`, `sort`, `sum`, `utf8`, `with` |
| `Map` | Map[k, v] | `contains`, `get`, `insert`, `keys`, `len`, `merge`, `remove`, `values` |
| `Set` | Set[τ] | `contains`, `insert`, `inter`, `len`, `tolist`, `union` |
| `Opt` | τ? | `isnone`, `issome`, `or` |

`raw` exists only in a version 0.8 module and only on `Text[C]` (5.16). `len_bytes` and `len_chars` exist only in a version 0.9 module, where `len` on text is refused (W-LEN-1, F.5.2).

**Sets and map merge (normative).** A `Set[τ]` is its own value, not a
`List[τ]`: it holds its elements in canonical order without duplicates
(7.1), so two sets with the same elements have the same representation
(`RCE.Canon.set_canon`), and list methods do not apply to it. It is
shown and embedded in the Form (7.1) as that list. `set_of(xs)` makes
one from a `List[τ]`. `s.len()` is the number of elements and
`s.contains(x)` whether x is one of them. `s.union(t)` is the set of the elements of either,
`s.inter(t)` of the elements of both, `s.insert(x)` sets `s` to
`s.union(set_of([x]))` (a `var` receiver), and `s.tolist()` is the
elements as a list in that order. `m.merge(n)` on two `Map[k, v]` has
the keys of either; a key in both maps to `m[k] ⊔ n[k]` by the `Merge` of
`v` (a user `impl Merge`, or the built-in instance, C.11.5), and the
result is in canonical key order. `union`, `inter` and `merge` borrow
their argument. These are the join (and, for `inter`, the meet) of the
set and pointwise map lattices, so a `merge` written from them is
certified (C.11.5).

**Hashing (normative).** `t.sha256()` on a `text` t is the SHA-256
digest (FIPS 180-4) of the UTF-8 bytes of t, written as 64 lowercase
hexadecimal digits, as a `text`. It is pure, total and the same on every
target; it is the digest 6.1 and 6.8 apply to canonical JSON, so a
program given the canonical JSON of a value as text computes the same
hash as the Form log and the content-hash ids. It is in the linear class of C.6.4.

**Bytes to text (normative).** `b.utf8()` on a `List[i64]` b is the `text` whose UTF-8 encoding is exactly the bytes of b. It traps, and so refuses the event it runs in (T8), when an element is outside 0..255 or the bytes are not well-formed UTF-8 (RFC 3629: no overlong forms, no surrogates, nothing above U+10FFFF); it never substitutes characters, since that would change content silently. A leading byte-order mark is kept. It is pure, total on well-formed input, the same on every target, and in the linear class of C.6.4.

**Effects and I/O (normative).** By derivation from least privilege, a
program has no ambient authority: there is no file, clock, network,
environment or randomness primitive. The only ways values enter are the
events of E (6.1) and, in `fn main` and task functions, channel receives
and foreign calls (5.11); the only ways values leave are `emit` (λ) and
sends. Each of these is an effect of the context table above, so the
checker, not run-time behaviour, decides which code may do I/O. Inputs
that are not events (a `select nondet` choice, a foreign result) are
logged, so replay is deterministic (T1, T21). A capability that is not in
this list cannot be added by a library, because the library is closed.

**Cost semantics.** Each standard library call costs `c_call`; in a
version 0.7 module it costs in addition the work of its complexity class
on the sizes of its receiver and argument (C.6.4, C.15); see C.6 for the
budget rules.

### 5.16 Indexed values (version 0.8)

In a module declaring `# rce-version: 0.8` four type names and four
contexts belong to the language: `Text[C]`, `Secret[τ]`, `Cap[A]`,
`Guarded[τ, A]`, and `Html`, `Url`, `Sql`, `Json`. A 0.8 module may not
declare an item with one of these names (W-NAME-2). Each is a type
*index*: the value is a value of the base type (text, τ, `()`, τ), and
the index is a static fact the checker carries. Indices are erased at
run time, so δ, the log and the emitters are unchanged except for the
encoders. Derivation (`spec/proposals/CORE-PROPERTIES.md`, P1): one
meaning per construct requires that a text which is HTML in one place
and SQL in another be two types; least privilege requires that
authority be a value, not an ambient fact; soundness requires that the
checker, not a convention, enforce both. The three indices are one
mechanism: a value carries an index, and it crosses an index only by a
named, total, costed construct.

**Context-typed text (W-CTX-1).** `Text[C]` for C one of the contexts
is text whose structure (markup, query syntax) is fixed by the program.
It is made only by `C.lit(s)`, where s is a string literal (program
text is trusted: its author wrote it), and by `C.encode(t)` for a `text`
t, which escapes every metacharacter of C. `a + b` joins two values of
one context; any other operator, or `+` with plain text or another
context, is W-CTX-1. `x.raw()` gives the text of a `Text[C]` as `text`
(going back only re-enters through `encode`). An event payload carries
plain text only (W-CTX-1): context text cannot come from outside.
`emit` may carry `Text[C]`; a host sink for C takes exactly that type.
The encoders (normative, every runtime): `Html` maps `&` `<` `>` `"` `'`
to `&amp;` `&lt;` `&gt;` `&quot;` `&#39;`; `Url` percent-encodes every
UTF-8 byte except `A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~` with uppercase hex; `Sql` gives
a standard SQL string literal, the text between single quotes with each
`'` doubled; `Json` gives a JSON string literal with `"` `\` newline,
return and tab escaped and other code points below U+0020 as `\u00xx`.
Consequence (T36): every structural metacharacter of a `Text[C]` value
comes from a literal, so untrusted text cannot form markup or query
syntax. SQL injection and cross-site scripting are not expressible.
Example: `Sql.lit("WHERE name = ") + Sql.encode(b)` with b = `O'Brien`
is `WHERE name = 'O''Brien'`; `Sql.lit("WHERE name = ") + b` is W-CTX-1.

**Secrets (W-SEC-1).** `Secret[τ]` is opaque. A secret value comes only
from an event payload field of a `Secret` type: there is no constructor
and no literal of a secret type, so a credential cannot be written in
the program (hard-coded credentials are not expressible; comparing a
secret with a literal is W-TY-1). The only operations are binding,
storing (in a state field, a struct, an option), passing and `==`/`!=`
between two secrets of one type, whose boolean is the one release. Any
other operator or method on a secret is W-SEC-1. A value that can hold a
secret may not be emitted, sent on a channel, carried by an error
payload (a refusal is an output, 6.1) or passed to a foreign function
(W-SEC-1). So λ never carries a secret (T36, noninterference up to the
equality bits). The log D holds admitted events with their payloads, as
any store of the program's inputs does; it is not an output.

**Capabilities (W-CAP-1, W-CAP-2).** `Cap[A]`, for A a declared struct,
is the authority A as a value. It appears only as the type of an event
payload field or of a parameter (W-CAP-1): it cannot be stored in a
state, struct, collection, option or channel, so authority lives for one
event and is never ambient. It cannot be constructed by an expression:
the host that admits an event attests the capability (written `()` in an
event list or `example`), exactly as it supplies every other input, and
the attested event is logged. `Guarded[τ, A]` is the type of a state
field only (W-CAP-1); reading it gives a τ, it keeps τ's range checks
(6.3), and a step that writes it (assignment, `&mut` borrow, a mutating
method, or the arrow form of its only field) must match only events
whose payload has a field of type `Cap[A]` (W-CAP-2). So a missing
authorization check is not expressible: a log of events without the
capability never changes the guarded field (T36).

**Read receipt.** What kind of channel does a capacity of 0 give? (one word)
