## 9. Design decisions for review

This section lists the design choices the spec makes, each with a one-line
reason, and the changes made in each draft. Each decision can be reviewed
and reversed on its own. Example: decision 45 makes text indexed by UTF-8
byte, as in Go, Rust and Zig.

Gaps in SURFACE.md that this spec decides. Each is one line of rationale;
each can be reversed independently.

1. **Layout by indentation, spaces only, tabs refused** (Python), with
   brackets suspending layout. Keeps SURFACE.md's look; tabs removed to make
   layout unambiguous.
2. **`#` comments only**, matching the prototype; no block comments.
3. **Case-sensitive event names in examples.** The prototype wrote
   `example inc` for event `Inc`; the spec requires `Inc` (no hidden case
   mapping).
4. **Several `state` regions per program**, each step reading only its own
   region (pre-state, ASM), events atomic across regions. Matches Form law 2
   and the "rules read their own sink" limit.
5. **Totality = every event is handled somewhere; unmatched regions are
   unchanged.** Stricter than "every (region, event) pair", looser than "every
   event in every region"; catches typos without boilerplate.
6. **Errors refuse the event and leave state unchanged** (`example … ->
   refused: X`), and are logged and output, never thrown.
7. **Traps (overflow, division by zero, non-finite, index, size, loop bound)
   are Form errors, not part of declared error sets**; `catch` cannot hide
   them.
8. **Recursion only where it provably ends** (revised in 0.4 and later: a
   self-call passes a constructor field of a matched parameter, or a measure
   falls in layers, including mutual recursion, or the cycle carries a
   declared `bound`; 6.7 says exactly which) and **every loop bounded**
   (default 1,000,000, `bound n` to change), so δ is total by construction.
   (Originally structural recursion only, with mutual recursion refused.)
9. **Second-class borrows, no lifetime syntax.** Borrows only in parameters,
   receivers, loop/match operands and short `let`s, plus borrow returns tied to
   a parameter. Simpler than Rust, still no GC and no aliasing of mutable
   state.
10. **`struct` only, no `class`**; value semantics, explicit `copy()` for deep
    duplication of non-Copy values.
11. **Integer types checked against their own range**, lowered to the
    Form's i64, except u64, which uses the Form's unsigned operations and is
    exact over [0, 2^64) (6.3 N2, T14; draft 0.5). No implicit widening; no
    literal suffixes. (Originally u64 results at or above 2^63 trapped.)
12. **f64 is the Form's float.** f32 was added in draft 0.5 (decision 42): it
    is computed in f64 and rounded once. (Originally f64 only.)
13. **Bitwise operators bind tighter than comparisons** (unlike C/Python's `&`
    vs `==` in C), so `x & 1 == 1` means what it reads as.
14. **`if … then … else …` as the expression conditional**; no Python
    `a if c else b` (it collides with `try … else`).
15. **`try e`, `try e else E`, `e catch d`, `e catch |x| h`** as the error
    vocabulary (Zig plus the prototype's `else`).
16. **Option is `T?` with `some(x)` / `none`.**
17. **Generic arguments in square brackets** (`List[T]`, `f[T](x)`), Go-style,
    resolved by name resolution; impl parameters need `forall`.
18. **Argument labels** Swift-style (`fn move(from src: u8)`), optional when the
    label equals the parameter name.
19. **`comptime`** for consts, array lengths, state initializers, comptime
    parameters, and `comptime` blocks/expressions; comptime is pure and
    deterministic.
20. **Arenas are lexical** (`with arena r`), region-typed values cannot escape;
    each step has an implicit per-step arena.
21. **Concurrency is deterministic by construction:** ticks, staged delivery,
    content-hash ids, select takes the first ready arm from a rotating start (decision 48),
    bounded channels with held sends and Backpressure logs (no silent drop),
    `after n` in logical ticks, Deadlock is a defined outcome. (Originally
    select chose the least ready arm; it rotates its starting arm since draft
    0.5, decision 48 and T11. `par` and the rest of C.4 are in version 0.6.)
22. **Pure functions cannot emit, spawn or use channels**; only steps,
    handlers, `main` and task functions (those with a `chan` parameter) have
    effects (revised by S2).
23. **Actors are regions with mailboxes and handlers** (`on M(…)`), one message
    per tick.
24. **A program with `fn main` and no state is a command**: one event
    `Start(args)`, outputs are its emits.
25. **Examples and checks are part of admission** (the gate), and the outcome
    of a multi-field example is a boolean over the final state.
26. **Kind variants encode as `{"$v": name, …}` records** in Form values;
    maps/sets as sorted lists, so canonical JSON hashing stays well-defined.
27. **Identifiers are ASCII**; text values are full Unicode, case operations
    ASCII-only (as num.rs).
28. **No macros, no exceptions, no null, no inheritance, no operator
    overloading beyond traits `Eq`/`Ord`/`Show`**: kept out to keep one
    meaning per text.
29. **The grammar artifact is the EBNF of section 3, checked LALR(1)** by
    `rce-spec-check`: a deterministic LR table with mechanical conflict
    detection, with a tree-sitter port checked against it. (Originally a
    Lark file, `rce.lark`, now retired.)

30. **Tail values** in block-bodied functions (S5).
31. **A trapping guard refuses the event** (S1).
32. **Keywords reserved everywhere except after `.`** (S3).
33. **`std.text`, `std.collections`, `std.math` are built-in modules** (S4).
34. **Loop elements of non-Copy type are borrows**; storing one needs
    `copy(x)`; lists, constructors, channels and vars cannot hold borrows
    (W-OWN-3, made explicit by the checker). Map `get` returns `V ! Missing`.
35. **Structural recursion admitted** (R1). Bound: calls ≤ nodes of the
    value recursed on.
36. **C-ABI `extern` functions** (R2): scalars and borrowed buffers in,
    scalars out, no allocator crosses the boundary, callable only from
    `main` and task functions, results logged for replay. Unwinding across
    the boundary does not exist because RCE has no unwinding.
37. **Arena capacity** `with arena r bound n` in canonical bytes (R3).
38. **Explicit `wrapping_*` and `saturating_*` methods** (R4); `+ - *` stay
    checked in every build (there is no build profile that changes meaning).
39. **`&Box[τ]` coerces to `&τ`** (R5).
40. **Effects stay inferred from context** (5.2), with no effect annotations
    and no `async`/`await`; a task function is an ordinary function that
    has a channel parameter.
41. **Ownership stays affine, not linear**, except for types declared
    `linear` (decision 46): ordinary values drop with no observable effect
    (O4).
42. **f32 computed in f64, rounded once** (N3). Bit-identical on every
    target; the cost is one extra rounding instruction per operation.
43. **Lane-wise arithmetic on fixed arrays** instead of a separate vector
    type; the array length is the lane count.
44. **Device regions** are placement hints with CPU meaning; only
    fixed-size, effect-free code may run in them.
45. **Text indexed by UTF-8 byte**, with character-boundary checks on slices.
46. **Linear structs** for outside resources, consumed exactly once.
47. **Full-range u64** through dedicated unsigned Form ops.
48. **select rotates** its starting arm per execution instead of choosing at
    random (Go) or always the least (draft 0.4).
49. **LOOP_LIMIT is a per-program constant** with default 1,000,000.
50. **Push iterators** (Go 1.23) rather than pull generators (Python, Rust):
    no suspended state, so δ stays total and replay needs nothing new.
51. **Floats derived from IEEE 754-2019 and totality** (6.3 N3, F1 to F9):
    correctly rounded basic operations only, one rounding per operator,
    subnormals kept, non-finite results trap because NaN and infinities
    break equality, order and JSON encoding, and transcendentals only as
    correctly rounded RCE code in the `math` module (F9), so every target
    runs the same algorithm instead of its platform library.
52. **Unicode 18.0.0 pinned, no tables read at run time** (6.3 N7): the
    whitespace set is enumerated, so a toolchain upgrade cannot change a
    result.

53. **Draft 0.9 is a new version** (number 0.9, never reuse 0.6), because it
    refuses programs 0.8 accepts and changes `&mut` after a failed call
    (C.15 rule).
54. **A failed call restores its `&mut` arguments** when every effect since
    entry is undoable; a function that could fail after a non-undoable effect
    is refused (F.4.4).
55. **Contracts are always enforced** and a violation is one defined refusal
    with fixed fields; no switchable contracts (F.2, F.6.2).
56. **Information flow is checked by labels with a refusal channel and robust
    declassification**; labels are erased at run time (F.4.2).
57. **`World` is a borrowed capability**, not a threaded value (F.4.1).
58. **The definition hash covers everything that affects meaning and nothing
    else** (F.4.3).
59. **`decreases` is required only where 6.7 does not already admit the
    recursion, and never replaces the loop bound** (F.6.4).
60. **Unused values, dropped results and shadowing are refused** in 0.9 (F.3).
61. **The four constructs that would break a theorem are written as
    non-goals**: effect handlers, switchable contracts, mutable aliasing
    across `par`, runtime reflection (F.2).
62. **The relaxed sequential borrow rule is not adopted** until its T6 lemma
    (T56) is proved (5.6).
63. **New theorems T42 to T56 are numbered after T41 and are stated,
    unproved**; the survey's "T17" for noninterference became T42 because
    T17 is the `par` diamond lemma (F.9).

### 9.1 Changes made while mechanizing (draft 0.1 → 0.2)

- S1 (6.4) A guard that traps refuses the event. Draft 0.1 did not say; δ
  was not total on that case.
- S2 (5.2) Task functions. Draft 0.1 decision 22 made every function except
  `main` pure, so `spawn f(…)` could never be well-typed; a function with a
  `chan` parameter may now use effects and be spawned.
- S3 (2.4) Keywords are reserved (the Lark grammar now uses a basic lexer, so
  the machine grammar agrees with the text), except as member names after
  `.`. Example 25 now uses labels `source`/`target` since `from` is a keyword.
- S4 (4.1) Built-in standard modules, so `use std.text` resolves.
- S5 (5.3) Tail values in block-bodied functions; examples 05, 06, 23 and 29
  relied on this reading.
- Examples were made whole programs: declared errors (18, 19, 22) and the
  emitted records (04, 31), defined `report` (07) and `depth_shallow` (29),
  added `shop_pricing.rce` for 26, parenthesized `(try …) as u32` (07) and
  `(m.get(w) catch 0) + 1` (21, which previously meant `catch (0 + 1)`),
  `copy(i)` in 16, and 08/09 declare their own trait
  `Describe` (the built-in `Show` cannot be re-declared or given an orphan impl).

### 9.2 Changes in draft 0.3

- The admission gate of 6.9 is implemented: `rce-check` evaluates every
  `example` and `check`, every comptime block and every constant and state
  initializer, and refuses a program on W-INT-1 or W-CT-1. W-LEX-3 (an
  integer literal outside its type's range) is checked.
- `rce.lark` tree shapes (the language is unchanged): `T?` now yields an
  `opt_type` node, negative and `true`/`false`/`none` literal patterns, the
  three receiver forms (`self`, `&self`, `&mut self`), the two ends of a slice
  and `e()` versus `e` in example event lists are distinguishable in the
  tree. Draft 0.2 trees dropped these; found while porting to tree-sitter.

What the mechanized models simplify (stated so the coverage is clear):
within a tick, sends are staged but receives consume in task-id order;
`select` is modelled over channel ids only; actor state is a number; the
borrow model's static context has the shape of the run-time state; H is an
arbitrary function (no collision or SHA-256 model); concurrency is not
evaluable at comptime.

### 9.3 Changes in draft 0.4 (from `spec/LANGUAGE-REVIEW.md`)

- R1 (6.7, W-REC-1) Structural self-recursion is admitted; mutual recursion
  and every other cycle stay refused. Checker: `structural_violation`, since
  replaced by `lex_measure` (6.7: one fixed position, or layers).
  Lean: `RCE/Struct.lean`.
- R2 (5.11, W-FFI-1, `extern`) A C-ABI foreign function interface: scalar
  and borrowed-buffer parameters, scalar results, callable only from `main`
  and task functions, results logged and replayed. `extern` is a new keyword.
- R3 (5.7) `with arena r bound n`: an arena capacity in canonical bytes,
  exceeded by `trap("size limit")`. The checker types `n` as u64; the
  reference evaluator does not yet count arena bytes.
- R4 (6.3 N2) `wrapping_*` and `saturating_*` integer methods; the default
  stays checked.
- R5 (5.1) `&Box[τ]` coerces to `&τ`, which structural recursion over
  `Box` fields needs.

Draft 0.4 deferred the changes in 9.4 because each changes the Form or the
emitters.

### 9.4 Changes in draft 0.5

- f32 (5.1, 6.3 N3): new type, Form ops `f32add f32sub f32mul f32div` and
  prim `tof32` in `form/num.rs`, `form_core.py` and `form_core.js`.
  Lean: `RCE/F32.lean`.
- Lane-wise array arithmetic (5.1, W-SIMD-1). It lowers to Form `Map` over
  the zipped lanes, so the Form needed no change.
- Device regions (5.13, W-DEV-1, keyword `device`).
- Byte-indexed text (5.1, 6.3 N7): Form prims `blen`, `bget`, `bslice`.
- Full-range u64 (6.3 N2): Form ops `uadd usub umul udiv urem`.
  Lean: `RCE/U64.lean`.
- select rotation and bounded wait (6.8). Lean: `RCE/Select.lean`.
- Linear structs (5.12, W-LIN-1, keyword `linear`); `extern` may take and
  return linear structs with one scalar field. Lean: `RCE/Linear.lean`.
- `const LOOP_LIMIT: u64 = n` (6.7, W-LOOP-1).
- Iterators (5.14, W-ITER-1, keywords `iter` and `yield`). The reference
  evaluator runs the iterator with a yield cap, delivers values to the loop
  body, and re-runs with a doubled cap only when the body asks for more;
  `gen_prefix` shows this equals the push model. Lean: `RCE/Iter.lean`.
- R3 completed: the reference evaluator counts arena and device bytes
  (canonical JSON of the values bound in the region, after every statement)
  and traps "size limit".
- `lalr` is no longer reserved (2.4).
- The four Form runtimes (Rust crate and WASM through `num.rs`, Python,
  JavaScript for XState and SCXML) agree on the new ops; the
  `tests/form_num_v05.rs` cross-runtime test compares them on about 6,600
  cases.

Known open questions (not decided here): the standard library surface beyond
the num.rs primitives; foreign interfaces other than the C ABI (WASM
component model, GPU kernels); how an RCE module is used as a fit (the
handler spec and fit formats themselves are now Appendix D); whether emitters should lower device
regions and lane-wise operators to real accelerator or vector code (today
they run them on the CPU, which 5.13 allows).

### 9.5 Changes in draft 0.7

- Version 0.7 (2.7, C.15): version 0.6 with size-scaled standard library
  method costs (C.6.4). Versions 0.5 and 0.6 keep their meaning.
- Errata for every version, listed in C.15: closed standard library and
  no ambient I/O (5.15), `&mut` write-back on `fail` in the emitters (6.2,
  T33) with nested calls flattened by an order-preserving ANF pass (T34),
  exact u64 at or above 2^63 (6.3 N2), the fallible-return literal fix
  (5.1), saturating budget arithmetic (C.6), the hash-chained Form log
  (6.1).
- Refined types (5.1, W-REF-1, T35): `type R = τ where p` with p in a
  decidable fragment, checked where the declared integer range is
  checked. Derived from soundness and one meaning per construct
  (`spec/proposals/CORE-PROPERTIES.md`, P2). Closes the replacement-matrix
  rows "improper input validation" (defined: refused at entry) and
  "dependent specifications" (defined for the decidable fragment;
  undecidable obligations excluded by derivation). An extension for
  every version (C.15).
- `sha256` text method (5.15): SHA-256 of the UTF-8 bytes as 64 lowercase
  hex digits, linear cost class (C.6.4), in the reference evaluator and the
  Rust, Python and JavaScript runtimes. Derived from self-hosting: the
  hash-chained log (6.1) and content-hash ids (6.8) must be computable by
  an RCE program. An extension for every version, since it only admits
  programs refused before (C.15).

### 9.6 Changes in draft 0.8

- Version 0.8 (2.7, 5.16, C.16): 0.7 plus indexed values, context-typed
  text `Text[C]`, opaque `Secret[τ]`, capabilities `Cap[A]` and
  `Guarded[τ, A]` fields, with W-CTX-1, W-SEC-1, W-CAP-1, W-CAP-2 and T36.
  A new version because the names it takes (`Text`, `Html`, ...) could be
  a 0.7 program's own declarations, whose meaning would change. Derived
  from one meaning per construct, least privilege and soundness
  (`spec/proposals/CORE-PROPERTIES.md`, P1). Closes the replacement-matrix
  rows SQL injection and XSS (excluded), missing authorization
  (excluded), hard-coded credentials and information exposure (excluded).

### 9.7 Changes in draft 0.9

Version 0.9 (2.7, Appendix F) is specified and not yet implemented. Each item
below is applied in the tier order of its dependencies; the derivation is in
Appendix F next to the rule, and every theorem is stated and unproved (F.9).

- **Tier 0.** Stale text corrected (errata for every version): decisions 8, 11,
  12, 21 and 29, the Copy list of 5.5 (f32 added), W-VER-1 and 2.7 (0.8 and
  0.9 named), the overview status and its checker figures. Version 0.9 refuses
  unused values, dropped non-unit results and unused stores (F.3.2), and
  adds lexical hygiene: hidden and bidirectional characters, shadowing of any
  enclosing local, qualified variants, longest-token lexing (F.3.3).
- **Tier 1.** `World` capability for foreign calls (F.4.1); information-flow
  labels with the refusal channel and robust declassification (F.4.2, T42,
  T43); definition hashes and `rce api-diff` (F.4.3, T50); transactional
  calls (F.4.4, T47).
- **Tier 2.** File-system capabilities and caretaker revocation (F.5.1, T51);
  typed shell and prompt output and strict input (F.5.2, T44); the hash-pinned
  manifest (F.5.3, T54); `ct fn` (F.5.4, T45); declared budgets (F.5.5, T52).
- **Tier 3.** Templates `t"..."` (F.6.1); `requires` and `ensures` (F.6.2,
  T46); `ghost` (F.6.3, T49); `decreases` (F.6.4, T48); `if let` (F.6.5);
  trait laws, tested not proved (F.6.6).
- **Tier 4.** The broker contract for the lethal trifecta (F.7, T55).
- **Rules derived from the sources' later items** (F.8): closures, types,
  calls, operators, containers, indexing, classes, errors, reflection and
  derive, compile-time code, linear values, tooling, release gate.
- **Non-goals** (F.2): effect handlers, switchable contracts, mutable
  aliasing across `par`, runtime reflection, and the other constructs listed
  there, each with its reason.
- **Not adopted until proved:** relaxed sequential borrows (5.6, T56).
- **Version number.** The proposal list was drafted under the name "draft
  0.6"; 0.6, 0.7 and 0.8 are taken, so this is 0.9 (C.15: a version number
  is never reused).

### 9.8 Decision log for draft 0.9 (open questions, decided by derivation)

Each row decides one question left open by the survey and security study. The
principle named is one of the five in Appendix F: least privilege (a),
soundness (b), determinism (c), totality (d), one meaning per construct (e).
No row rests on taste: where no principle decides, the existing text stays.

| Q | Question | Decision | Derivation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which effects are undoable for a transactional call | Writes to owned values and `emit` into the pending output are undoable; send, receive, `spawn`, foreign calls, `World` operations, host entries and consuming a linear handle are not; a path from a non-undoable effect to a `fail` is refused (W-TX-1) | (c): a restore must be total and need no handler; (b) T8 |
| 2 | Measure for mutual recursion | One lexicographic tuple for the whole group (F.6.4) | (d): one well-founded order for the group, as 6.7 already uses |
| 3 | Is tool metadata hashed | No. Comments, formatting, declaration order and attributes are not hashed; the version, signature, contracts, measure, ghost clauses, labels and referenced hashes are | (c) and T7: a hash is the meaning, nothing else |
| 4 | `?` in `par` arms | Refused | T16: `?` leaves the arm early, so an arm is not an expression with one result |
| 5 | Advisory format | Canonical JSON object signed with Ed25519 over its SHA-256 | (c): reuse the canonical JSON of 6.1; Ed25519 signatures are deterministic |
| 6 | Map iteration order | Ascending canonical key order of 7.1 | already 6.7 and the C.15 erratum; (c) |
| 7 | Half-open slices and inclusive ranges | Unchanged: slices as in 6.3 N8, ranges keep `..` and `..=` | (e): both already have one meaning; no principle favors removing one |
| 8 | Comparison-chain sugar | Not adopted; a chain is refused (W-OP-1) | (e): one meaning, and a chain would need a second reading of the operator |
| 9 | NaN payload and libm strategy | Neither exists: non-finite results trap, transcendentals are RCE code in `math` (F9) | already decision 51; (c) |
| 10 | Value-indexed types | Not adopted beyond comptime array lengths and the type indices of 5.16 | (d): a value in a type needs a decidable fragment, and none is specified |
| 11 | Linear types in the spec | They are (5.12, W-LIN-1, T12); a linear handle is not undoable | already in the spec; (b) |
| 12 | Inductive predicates | Not adopted; a predicate is a `ghost` pure total `bool` function | (d): inductive definitions need positivity and continuity checks no theorem needs |
| 13 | Are doc comments hashed | No doc comments exist (decision 2, `#` comments only), so nothing is hashed | decision 2; (e) |
| 14 | Maximal-munch token rule | Adopted as a requirement on the lexer, checked in F.11 | (c): the same text must tokenize the same everywhere |
| 15 | First-class type invariants | A refined type has `R.check(v) -> R?`; no witness clause; no implicit conversion; opaque outside its module | (b) T35: a value of R is only made by a checked path |
| 16 | Argument labels | Kept (decision 18) and checked: a wrong label is refused | (e): a label that is not checked has two meanings, the written and the real one |
| 17 | Constant conditions | An `if`, `elif`, `while` or guard on a comptime constant is refused (W-UNUSED-2) | (e): one branch is dead code; P8 |
| 18 | Display trait | `Show` of 5.9; a template field of a non-text type must implement it | (e): one display conversion, explicit; no new trait |
| 19 | Map equality independent of order | Yes, because the representation is canonical | (c): equality and iteration agree by construction |
| 20 | User-definable `derive` | Not offered; `derive` is the built-in closed set of 5.9 | T7: a user derive needs reflection |
| 21 | Literal default type when unconstrained | Unchanged: integer literals default to i64, float literals are f64 (5.3, 5.1) | (c): the default is a fixed rule; refusing adds no safety |
| 22 | Expression fields and nested quotes in `t"..."` | Not allowed: a field is an identifier or a field path, no quotes inside a field | (e) and S8: a field needing a nested lex has two readings |
| 23 | Inductive type syntax and its `decreases` rule | No new syntax: a recursive `kind` with `Box`, strictly positive because `fn` types cannot occur in data (W-TY-2) | (d): positivity follows from W-TY-2 |
| 24 | Is `refuse` the empty enum | No: `refuse` is not a value and has no type | (e): a bottom type brings subtyping, which RCE does not have |
| 25 | Fixed-size arrays as value parameter or ghost length | Array length stays a comptime constant `[τ; n]`; contracts may use `len` | (d): no value-indexed types (Q10) |
| 26 | Spelling of the `Copy` and `Discard` bounds | No new spelling; `Copy` is the built-in of 5.5 and generics stay affine (decision 41); a type parameter is not instantiated by a linear type | (b) T12 |
| 27 | Canonical form of propositions | A contract is hashed as the canonical parsed tree of its expression; no rewriting or solver normalization | (c): a hash must not depend on a solver |
| 28 | Source span in the refusal record | No; the record has the rule or clause, the definition hash and the clause index | (c) and T7: a span depends on whitespace |
| 29 | Layout-sensitive vector types | Not adopted; lane-wise fixed arrays only (decision 43) | no principle decides; the existing text stays |
| 30 | Any foreign boundary in 0.9 | Yes, the C ABI of 5.11 as a `World` operation, declared in the manifest | (a): authority is a value; (c) T32 |
| 31 | Big integer or ghost mathematical integer | `mathint`, ghost and contract code only; no runtime big integer | (d): an unbounded integer has size-dependent cost, which budgets cannot bound |
| 32 | Wording for reactive programs | A total step function driven by the host (6.1, Appendix E); no `while true` | (d) |
| 33 | Unsatisfiable contracts: static or first call | Static in the decidable fragment (W-CON-1); otherwise enforcement refuses every call | (b), (d): decide what is decidable, never succeed vacuously |
| 34 | Comment forms | Only `#` line comments | decision 2; (e) |
| 35 | Implication spelling in contracts | None; write `not a or b` | (e): `or` short-circuits, so the form is already guarded |
| 36 | Digit separators in literals | One `_` between digits, as 2.5 already says | (e): one canonical form, already specified |

The published text and the engine development tree were joined at draft 0.9.
No version number was reused or redefined: versions 0.7 and 0.8 keep the
meaning they had in the published text, and 0.9 is the version of Appendix F.
Where both trees had reworded the same stale sentence (decisions 8, 11, 12 and
29 above), the wording that states the original rule and then its revision was
kept, because it says what the rule was and what it is now. The canonical JSON

**Read receipt.** The decisions list says it decides gaps in which file?

## 10. Tooling: the `rce` command and the language server

This section defines the tools that read RCE programs: the `rce` command
and the language server it contains. It adds no rules to the language; it
says what each tool prints and returns for a given input. Example:
`rce run counter.rce "Inc, Dec, Dec"` prints the state after each event
and stops at the refused third event with exit status 1.

### 10.1 Principles

1. **Determinism.** Every subcommand of 10.2 to 10.10 is a function of its
   arguments and the bytes of the files it reads. Two runs on the same input
   give the same output bytes and the same exit status. None of them reads
   the clock, the network, environment variables or random numbers. The same
   binary also carries the host commands (`rce host ...`) and `rce db`,
   defined by Appendix E; the host loop reads the clock (the frame period
   of `Tick`) and the network by design, and logs what it reads as inputs
   (HC-2, HC-14), so this item does not describe them. The handler-spec
   staleness rule W-HS-CUR-2 takes a time as an input and is part of the
   engine profile (D.9, D.10), not of these subcommands.
2. **No model in the loop.** No subcommand and no language server request
   calls a language model, a remote service or any learned component. A
   diagnostic, a run, a test verdict, an emitted file and a formatted file
   come only from the rules of sections 2 to 7.
3. **One checker.** `rce check`, `rce test`, `rce run`, `rce emit` and the
   language server all use the same parser, type checker and admission gate
   (6.9) as the reference checker `rce-check`. A file accepted by one is
   accepted by all.
4. **Exit status.** 0 means success. 1 means a program was refused, an
   example or check failed, a run reached a refused event, or `fmt --check`
   found a file to change. 2 means a usage error: unknown subcommand, wrong
   number of arguments, unreadable file, or an unknown emit target or
   construct an emitter does not translate (10.5).

`rce` is one binary, built from the reference checker crate in
`spec/checker` (crate `rce-spec-check`, `cargo build --release --bin rce`).
The language commands of this section are implemented in
`spec/checker/src/cli.rs` (entry point `cli::main`), with their tests in
`spec/checker/tests/`. This `rce` carries the language commands only; the
Form command line (`rce form ...`), which reads the Form spec format rather
than RCE programs, is not part of this build, and `rce form` exits with
status 2.

The tables of 5.15 (which methods each receiver has) and C.6.4 (the work
class of each method) are not typed into the checker a second time: it
reads them from `spec/data/spec-data.json`, which `rce-spec-data`
generates from this book. The two tables are cut from it into
`spec/data/spec-tables.json`, the file compiled into `rce`, the checker
and its wasm build; `rce-spec-data --check` fails when either file
differs from what the book gives.

### 10.2 `rce check FILE|DIR...`

All FILEs form one program: `use` resolves among them (4.1). A DIR is a
package: it stands for its `.rce` files, recursively, in sorted order,
and reads nothing outside it (the multi-module example is the package
`spec/examples/26_use_module/`, so `rce check spec/examples/26_use_module`
checks it alone). Each file is
parsed, type checked (section 5) and admitted (6.9: every `const`,
`comptime` block, `check` and `example` is evaluated). For each file, in
the order given, one line is printed:

```
ok FILE
REFUSED FILE: line N: RULE message[; line M: RULE message ...]
```

Every refusal names its rule from section 7. Exit status 1 if any file is
refused, else 0.

### 10.3 `rce run FILE [EVENTS]`

The file must pass `rce check` alone; otherwise one `REFUSED` line is
printed and the status is 1.

**With EVENTS.** EVENTS is written exactly as the event list of an
`example` line (3.2, `EventRef { "," EventRef }`), for example
`"Inc, Inc, Dec"` or `"Deposit(amount: 50), Withdraw(amount: 20)"`.
Let s₀ be the initial state (6.1) and e₁ … eₙ the events. For k = 1 … n the command computes

```
(sₖ, oₖ) = δ(sₖ₋₁, eₖ)
```

where δ is the step function of 6.4 and oₖ is the sequence of values the
step emitted (λ). It prints line 0 as `0 (initial) STATE`, then for each k
the line `k EVENT STATE` followed by one line `  emit VALUE` per element of
oₖ, in order. STATE lists every region as `Region { field = value, ... }`,
regions separated by `; `, in declaration order. If δ refuses eₖ, the line
is `k EVENT refused: ERROR`, no later event is applied, and the status is
1. Otherwise the status is 0. An event name that is not declared is a usage
of a wrong event list: one `REFUSED` line, status 1.

For the counter `spec/examples/01_counter.rce`:

```
$ rce run 01_counter.rce "Inc, Inc, Dec, Dec, Dec"
0 (initial) Counter { n = 0 }
1 Inc Counter { n = 1 }
2 Inc Counter { n = 2 }
3 Dec Counter { n = 1 }
4 Dec Counter { n = 0 }
5 Dec refused: Underflow
```

**Without EVENTS.** The module must declare `fn main()` with no
parameters. The command evaluates its body by the rules of section 6 and
prints `emit VALUE` for each value emitted, in order. If the body traps or
fails, the last line is `refused: REASON` and the status is 1. Calls to
foreign functions (5.11) are not executed by the reference evaluator and
trap. If there is no `fn main()`, the command says so and the status is 1.

The evaluator is the reference interpreter of the checker, with the fuel bound
of 6.7 and the VALUE_LIMIT of 6.3. It is a definition of meaning, not a fast
runtime.

### 10.4 `rce test FILE|DIR...`

The test cases of a module are its `example` lines and its `check` items,
including those inside `intent` blocks. `rce test` admits the files as
`rce check` does, which evaluates every case (6.9, W-INT-1). It prints, per
file,

```
ok FILE (E examples, C checks)
FAIL FILE: line N: RULE message[; ...]
```

with E and C the numbers of cases in that file, then a total line
`P passed, F failed`. Exit status 1 if F > 0. A test verdict therefore
equals the admission verdict: a module whose examples do not hold is not a
program (section 7).

### 10.5 `rce emit TARGET FILE`

TARGET names an output. The file must pass `rce check` on its own.

| TARGET | Output |
|---|---|
| `form` | the Form P = (S, E, δ, D, λ) as one line of JSON (6.1), then a line end |
| `rust` | one Rust 2024 source file with a `main` |
| `python` | one Python 3 source file |
| `js` | one JavaScript module (ES2020 or later, BigInt) for Node |
| `scala` | one Scala 3 source file with a `@main` for the JVM (Java 19 or later) |

The Form JSON lists objects in canonical order (6.1), so it is a
deterministic function of the program text.

**The program emitters.** `rust`, `python`, `js` and `scala` translate the checked
module, not the Form. Each output is self-contained. It starts with a
runtime that defines the values of 6.3 and their operations, following the
reference evaluator (`spec/checker/src/interp.rs`) value by value. That
includes the integer range checks, the trap messages, canonical map key order
and the display of floats and text. After the runtime comes one target
function per RCE function, method, step and constant. An expression becomes
calls to runtime helpers with its operands in evaluation order; `if`,
`while`, `loop`, `for` and `match` become the target's own control flow,
with one counter per loop against its bound. Values are never changed in
place: an assignment to `a.f[i]` rebuilds the value, as the reference
evaluator's `assign` does.

The Rust output follows the shape of the verified emitter of T9
(`spec/lean/RCE/Emit.lean`): one value type, `Result` with `?` for traps
and refusals, and i128 arithmetic checked against each integer type's
range. The theorem of T9 is about the Lean model of that emitter. The
emitter in `rce` is tested against the reference evaluator; it is not
proved.

The Scala output is the functional-language target. Its values are the
same dynamic values as the JavaScript output's (integers as `BigInt` with
their type, floats as JVM `Double`, whose arithmetic is IEEE 754 binary64
with round to nearest even and no contraction since Java 17, and whose
`toString` is the shortest round trip since Java 19). Loops are `while`
loops, and `break` and `continue` are control exceptions caught at the
loop, so no RCE loop grows the stack; the observations run on one thread
with a 2 GiB stack.

**What an emitted program does.** Run it, and it prints the module's
*observations*: one line per constant, per `check`, per function without
parameters (other than `main`), per event of each example (the state after
it, its outputs, or the refusal), and finally the outputs and result of
`fn main`. These are the lines `emit::observe` computes with the reference
evaluator, so that a target and the reference can be compared line for
line.

**How the emitters are tested.** `spec/checker/tests/emit.rs` emits all 59
programs of `spec/examples/` (the 57 files and the 2 of `26_use_module`) in
all three targets. To exercise function
bodies, it first adds *probes*: for each function and method, up to three
calls on small sample arguments built from the parameter types, plus one
example that sends every event. It then runs each output (`rustc`,
`python3`, `node`) and requires its output to equal the reference
evaluator's, line for line. On 2026-10-16, with rustc 1.98.1, Python 3.13.5
and Node 20.19.2, all 58 agree on all three targets, with 474 observation
lines per target. (The dated runs below were made when the corpus was 51
programs, and 55 for Scala, with 299 and 361 observation lines.) Four programs (14, 15, 34, 47) contain only
concurrency and give no observation. A separate program
(`tests/emit_edge.rce`) covers range traps, loop bounds, `&mut` write-back,
closures and float display. The Scala target has its own test in the same
file: on 2026-10-14, on the Apple M5 Max below, with Scala 3.10.0 run by
scala-cli 1.18.0 on OpenJDK 27, all 55 programs of the current corpus
(with the package files of example 26) agree with the reference, 0
refused, 361 observation lines, and the edge program agrees on all four
targets. Its oracle is `RCE_SCALA` (default `scala-cli`). That agreement is for this examples corpus only. On the larger `rce-conformance` suite the Scala emitter passes 52 of 1,845 results (its README gives 1,189 failures and 604 unsupported), so the Scala target does not yet agree with the reference on that suite.
When `rustc`, `python3` or `node` is missing,
its test prints `SKIPPED` and the reason; a skipped target is never
counted as a pass. The oracles used were Python 3.13.5 and Node 20.19.2.
The test reads the oracle paths from `RCE_RUSTC`, `RCE_PYTHON` and
`RCE_NODE` (default `rustc`, `python3`, `node` on the path) and prints each
oracle's version. On 2026-10-12 the same tests were also run on an Apple
M5 Max (macOS 27.0.1, arm64) with rustc 1.98.1, Python 3.14.5 and Node
26.11.1: 51 of 51 agree on each of the three targets, 0 refused, 0
skipped, 299 observation lines per target, and the edge program agrees on
all three.

**Fuel.** Each emitted program counts fuel (6.7) at the reference
evaluator's charge points: one tick per evaluated expression, per
executed statement, per call of a user function or method, and per
element of a list comprehension and of `map`, `filter` and `fold`. A
temporary introduced by the emitter's own lowering is not charged. The
limit is 50,000,000; it is reset before each observation, as the reference
starts a new evaluator for each, and running out traps with the message
"comptime fuel exhausted". The argument `--fuel=N` sets the limit to N and
`--fuel-trace` prints `fuel K` after each observation, K being the ticks
used. These two arguments exist for the test below; the default program
takes no argument.

`spec/checker/tests/fuel.rs` compares the ticks used, line for line, on
the 50 programs of the emitter tests (with probes) against
`emit::observe_fuel` of the reference evaluator, in all three targets. It
then runs ten programs at every limit from 0 up to 300 and at 400 evenly
spaced limits above, up to one more than the program uses, and requires
each target to trap at the same observation with the same output as the
reference run at the same limit. Within one observation, the emitted
order of ticks can differ from the reference where the emitter evaluates
arguments before entering a call; the trap observation and the total are
what the test fixes. The Scala target is in the same test (the emitted
file is packaged once into a jar and run with `java -jar`); on 2026-10-14
it agreed on all 54 programs of that corpus and at all 1,366 swept limits
(`RCE_FUEL_LANGS=scala`).


**Running `fn main`.** Run with the argument `--run`, an emitted program
instead evaluates `fn main` with tasks, channels, `select`, actors and
`par` on a runtime of its own: every task is a thread (a worker in
JavaScript), and one scheduler admits their moves tick by tick in the
order of `conc::run_main`, the reference of `rce run` without EVENTS. It
prints `emit VALUE` per output and the line `outcome Done`,
`outcome Deadlock` or `outcome Refused: REASON`. A module without
`fn main()` prints the reference's message ("nothing to run") on standard
error and exits with status 1, as `rce run` does. Fuel follows the reference's
pools: each task has its own, starting full (its first ticks are the call
of its function and one per argument); actor handlers share the
scheduler's pool; a `par` branch or `for ... par` chunk starts from its
parent's remaining fuel, and the branches are charged back in source
order, so the trap falls where the reference's sequential run puts it.

`spec/checker/tests/emit_run.rs` compares the three runtimes with
`conc::run_main` on a corpus of task programs. Among them are the four
concurrency examples 14, 15, 34 and 47, each run with a `fn main` from
`spec/checker/tests/drivers/` appended to its unchanged text.
`spec/checker/tests/fuel_run.rs` runs seven of these programs at every
fuel limit where the reference's result changes and at the limit before
it (258 runs over the three targets), and requires the same outputs and
outcome.

**Limits of the emitters.**

- In the observations, channels, `spawn`, `select`, actors and `extern`
  functions trap with the same message as in the reference evaluator
  ("not available at comptime"); they run only under `--run`. `extern`
  functions trap there too.
- A `par` whose branches wait on an lvar runs its branches at the same
  time in the reference (`ParMode::Threads`). Derivation. The governing
  law is schedule independence: a `par` must be observationally equal to
  one fixed sequential order, source order (C.4). Fuel is additive over
  sequential composition, so the sequential run traps at the first
  branch i where the uses of branches 1..i sum past the fuel left at the
  fork. The reference therefore gives each branch a copy of that fuel,
  sums the branches' uses in source order after they finish, and traps
  with "comptime fuel exhausted" at the first branch whose running sum
  passes it, before that branch's own result is taken. The trap point is
  the sequential one. A split of the fuel before the fork would make the
  set of programs that trap depend on the split rule and would agree
  with no sequential order, with no gain in soundness, so it is not
  used. The cost of running branches ahead is bounded: at most k times
  the fuel left at the fork is evaluated for a `par` of k branches, of
  which the excess over the sequential run is discarded. A wait charges
  no fuel while blocked, so a branch's use does not depend on the
  schedule. The emitters run such a `par` by restart and restore the
  fuel and the budgets of an abandoned attempt (`par_snap`,
  `par_restore`), so each branch is charged once, for its completing
  attempt. `spec/checker/tests/fuel_run.rs` checks this at every change
  point on two programs (`lvarpar`, and `lvartrap`, where a late
  division by zero must lose to the fuel trap when fuel runs out first).
- Deep recursion ends with the target's own stack error.
- A call that writes back its receiver or a `&mut` argument (`xs.push(x)`,
  `f(&mut a)`) is translated only as a whole statement or as the right side
  of `let`, `var`, an assignment, `return`, `emit` or `fail`. Elsewhere,
  `rce emit` refuses the program with status 2 and names the construct. No
  example program is refused.
- When a function whose result is a union fails, its `&mut` arguments are
  not written back. The reference evaluator writes them back.
- The Python output has been checked with Python 3.13.5 and 3.14.5, and
  the JavaScript output with Node 20.19.2 and 26.11.1. Other versions have
  not been run.
- The Scala output has been checked with Scala 3.10.0 on OpenJDK 27 only.
  It has no `--run` runtime yet: with `--run` it prints that `--run` is not
  available on this target and exits with status 2. A `par` runs its
  branches in source order on one thread (by restart when they wait on
  lvars), as the JavaScript output does when a local cannot go to a worker.


For an unknown target, or a program that one of these emitters does not
translate, `rce emit` prints nothing on standard output, prints the reason
on standard error, and exits with status 2. It never prints a partial file.

### 10.6 `rce fmt [--check] FILE...`

`rce fmt` rewrites each file into canonical layout. Let tok(t) be the token
sequence of text t produced by the lexer and layout pass of 2.6, with line
numbers dropped. The formatter is a function fmt on texts with:

1. **Meaning preserved.** tok(fmt(t)) = tok(t). The formatter checks this
   equality on every file before writing it; if it would fail, the file is
   left unchanged, a `REFUSED` line is printed and the status is 1.
2. **Canonical layout.** In fmt(t): a block that is k levels deep starts its
   lines with exactly 4k spaces; no line has trailing spaces; there are no
   blank lines before the first line, no two blank lines in a row, and the
   file ends with exactly one line end. A comment-only line takes the
   indentation of the next code line. A line that continues inside an open
   bracket keeps its position relative to the line that opened it.
3. **Idempotence.** fmt(fmt(t)) = fmt(t). This is tested on every program
   in `spec/examples/` and on the formatter's tests; it is not proved.

A text the lexer refuses (2.6, W-LEX-1, W-LEX-2) is refused by `fmt` with
the same reason. `fmt` does not type check: a file that is refused by
`rce check` can still be formatted. With `--check`, no file is written;
each file that would change is printed as `would reformat FILE` and the
status is 1. Without it, each changed file is written and printed as
`formatted FILE`.

### 10.7 The language server: `rce lsp`

`rce lsp` speaks the Language Server Protocol 3.17 over standard input and
output (JSON-RPC 2.0 messages framed by `Content-Length` headers). It keeps
the full text of each open document; it does not read other files.

| Message | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `initialize` | replies with capabilities: full-text sync (`textDocumentSync` = 1), formatting, hover, definition, document symbols, and completion triggered by `.` |
| `textDocument/didOpen`, `didChange` | stores the text and publishes diagnostics for that document |
| `textDocument/didClose` | forgets the text and publishes an empty diagnostic list |
| `textDocument/formatting` | returns one edit replacing the whole text with fmt(t) (10.6), or no edit if t is canonical or refused |
| `textDocument/hover` | the type or declaration of the name at the position, or `null` |
| `textDocument/definition` | the location of that name's binding or item, or `null` |
| `textDocument/completion` | the names that can be written at the position |
| `textDocument/documentSymbol` | the document's items, each with its fields, variants or methods |
| `shutdown` | replies `null` |
| `exit` | ends the server: status 0 after `shutdown`, 1 without it |
| any other request | error -32601, method not found |

**Diagnostics.** For a document with text t, the published diagnostics are
exactly the refusals `rce check` gives for t, one per refusal, with severity
Error and source `rce`. A refusal `line N: ...` covers line N − 1 in the
protocol's 0-based numbering, from column 0 to the start of the next line.
`use` resolves among the module paths of all open documents.

**Names.** Hover, definition, completion and symbols all read one index of
the document. The index is built from the parsed module and from the
bindings the type checker declares while it checks the module: each local
binding, with its line and its inferred type. A document that does not
parse has an empty index, so these requests answer `null` or an empty list.

- *Hover* on a local binding shows `name: T`, with the type T the checker
  inferred. On an item it shows the item's declaration: the line of a
  function, constant, event or alias, or the whole block of a kind, struct,
  state or trait. On a variant, field or method it shows that line.
- *Definition* gives the line of the binding or item, and the column where
  the name appears on it.
- *Completion* after `.` offers user methods, fields and the builtin
  methods of the reference evaluator. Elsewhere it offers the local
  bindings of the enclosing item, the module's items, variants and fields,
  and the keywords. Each list is filtered by the part of the name already
  typed.
- *Document symbols* list the items in order, with fields of structs and
  states, variants of kinds and methods of impls as children.

Limits: the AST has no columns, so a name is found by scanning its line,
and columns are counted in Unicode scalar values rather than the UTF-16
units of the protocol; the two counts differ only on a line with a character outside
the Basic Multilingual Plane. A local is visible from its line to the end
of its enclosing item: block scope is not tracked, so a binding of a closed
block is still offered. Names are resolved within one document, not across
`use`.

Because diagnostics come from the same checker, an editor shows a program
as clean exactly when `rce check` accepts it (10.1, principle 3).

### 10.8 What is not yet implemented

- The program emitters do not run concurrency or actors in their
  observations, only under `--run`, and never run `extern` functions
  (10.5).
- The language server resolves names within one document, without block
  scope, and counts columns in Unicode scalar values (10.7). It has no
  rename, references or semantic tokens.
- `rce run` uses the reference interpreter; there is no compiled runtime.
- Idempotence of `fmt` is tested, not proved.
- Version 0.9 (Appendix F) is implemented in part (F.12). `rce hash`,
  `rce api-diff OLD NEW` (F.4.3) and `rce v09-status` exist: `rce hash FILE|DIR...`
  prints the definition hash, kind and name of every named item (`pub` marks an
  export), `rce api-diff OLD NEW` prints one row per change of the exports
  (`compatible` or `breaking`, then kind and name, then the change; status 1 when
  any row is breaking) and `rce v09-status` prints the implemented and the
  unimplemented rules. The broker contract (F.7), the manifest and pin check
  (F.5.3) and the emitter refusals of F.5.4 do not exist yet. Results are
  reproducible from the inputs alone (10.1).

### 10.9 `rce trace --json FILE [EVENTS]`: reference traces (informative)

The trace format lets an independent projector (another compiler or
runtime of the same Form) show that it agrees with the reference
evaluator step by step. It adds no meaning: every field is a field of the
log D of 6.1, so a trace is the log, and conformance to 6.1 implies
conformance to the trace.

`rce trace --json FILE` prints one trace per `example` of the module, in
source order (the same logs `rce emit form` puts in `logs`); with EVENTS
(the syntax of an `example` line, as in 10.3) it prints one trace of that
event list. A module that is refused, or a trace of EVENTS that yields no
step, is status 1. The output is one JSON object (format `rce-trace/1`),
compact, with sorted keys:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `format` | `"rce-trace/1"` |
| `file` | the file name, without directories |
| `events` | the EVENTS argument, or null |
| `genesis` | the first `prev_hash`: 64 zeros (6.1) |
| `traces` | list of {`source`, `steps`}; `source` is `"example@L"` (the example's line) or `"events"` |
| `steps[i].seq` | required: 0-based index in the trace |
| `steps[i].event` | required: {`type`, `payload`}, payload values as in 6.1 |
| `steps[i].state_hash` | required: SHA-256 (lower-case hex) of the canonical JSON of the state after the step |
| `steps[i].prev_hash`, `steps[i].hash` | the 6.1 chain: `hash` is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of {event, prev_hash, seq, state_hash} |
| `steps[i].outcome` | `"applied"` or {`refused`: error name}; derived, not hashed |

A refused event is the last step of its trace, with the unchanged state's
hash (T8). A projector conforms on a module when, for every trace, its
steps have the same `seq`, `event` and `state_hash` as the reference, in
order and with none missing or extra; when it also emits `prev_hash`,
`hash` or `outcome` they must be equal too. Since `state_hash` covers
the whole state, equal hashes mean equal states without exchanging them.

`spec/traces/` holds the reference traces of the example corpus: one
file per top-level example (the package `26_use_module/` has no state
machine), plus two event-list traces, `01_counter.events.json` (the
counter on a longer list) and `16_multi_region.events.json` (two regions
stepped by one event, which has no `example` lines). Examples without a
state machine have an empty `traces` list. `spec/traces/rce-trace-diff.py REFERENCE OTHER` (Python 3,
standard library only) compares two trace files or two directories of
them and prints `exact match` or the first divergence (trace, `seq`,
field, both values); exit 0 on full match. `spec/checker/tests/traces.rs`
checks that the fixtures are current, that every step is on the 6.1
chain, and that the runner finds a planted divergence.

### 10.10 `rce index [--vectors N] FILE|DIR...` and `rce search CATALOG QUERY`: the brick catalog (informative)

`rce index` checks the files as one program (10.2) and prints one JSON
object (format `rce-catalog/1`, compact, sorted keys) with one entry per
top-level function of each module (the `pub` ones when the module marks
any `pub`, else all; methods are not bricks), sorted by module and name.
Library dependencies are resolved first: a `# uses: a/b` line adds
`a/b.rce` from the nearest ancestor directory that has it; a `#!lib NAME`
line checks the module with the items of module NAME in front (its checks
dropped, its own items winning), as the rce binary does; and a module
refused only for unknown names that exactly one single-segment module of
the program declares is checked again with that module as its `#!lib`.
`resolved` records each resolution and whether it was a directive or
inferred.
An entry holds `module`, `name`, `file`, `line`, `generics`, `params`
(name and type), `ret`, `key` (the type with generic parameters renamed
`t0`, `t1`, ... in order of first occurrence), `hash` (SHA-256 of the
module path and the canonical text of the function alone, so layout and
position do not change it), `checked` (the verdict of its file) and
`lowering` (`{"term": T}`, the D.7 lowering, or `{"refused": reason}`).
The catalog's `hash` is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of its entries;
`refused_files` maps each refused file to its diagnostics. With
`--vectors N`, `vectors` maps a lowered brick's hash to up to N
`{"args", "out"}` or `{"args", "trap"}` records of the reference
evaluator on inputs generated from the parameter types by a fixed rule
(an input that needs more than 200000 interpreter steps gives none, as the
store-passing terms do more work than the interpreter); they are outside the catalog
hash. `rce-brick-verify CATALOG` (`src/form/brick.rs`) evaluates each
lowered term on its vectors and reports, per brick, agreement or the
first disagreement: a result must be equal, a trap must be an error.

`rce search` reads a catalog and a query `A -> R` or `(A, B) -> R`, where
one-letter lowercase names are type variables, and prints `RANK
module.name : key` per match, best first. A brick matches when its
arguments and result unify with the query's, in some order of the
arguments. RANK is 0 for a type equal up to renaming of variables, 1 for
an instance, plus 2 when the arguments match only in another order. Ties
break by module and name. Both commands are deterministic: equal inputs
give equal output bytes.

**Read receipt.** Which JSON-RPC error code does the language server return for a request it does not know? (a number)

## Appendix C. Draft 0.6 and 0.6b concurrency (normative for version 0.6 and 0.7 modules)

This appendix defines the draft 0.6 language: structured parallelism
(`par`, `for ... par`), budgets, deadlines, nondeterministic select and
priorities (0.6), and the 0.6b extensions: workgroups, session types,
structured spawn, cross-actor transactions, supervisors, nodes,
interrupts, LVars and replicated state. It applies only to a module that
declares `# rce-version: 0.6` or `# rce-version: 0.7` (2.7); everything
said here of a 0.6 module holds for a 0.7 module, except where C.6.4 and
C.15 say otherwise. A 0.5 module never sees any of it:
its words are ordinary names there, and none of its rules apply. The
text is written from what the reference checker (`spec/checker`,
`check.rs`, `check06b.rs`, `conc.rs`, `link.rs`) and the Lean files
(`spec/lean/RCE/Par*.lean`, `Models06b.lean`, `Session*.lean`,
`TickClock.lean`, `VClock.lean`) actually enforce and prove; where the
two differ from an intended design, the checker is what is described.
Example: in a 0.6 module, `par` with two branches that write different
variables gives the same result as running the branches in source order.

### C.1 Version and keywords

The 23 words below are reserved in a version 0.6 module, in addition to
the 0.5 keywords of 2.4, except directly after `.` (so `c.offer()` and
`c.choose(L)` remain method calls):

```
par       branch    nondet    budget    deadline  priority
replicated interrupt session  lvar      group     lanes
barrier   scope     atomic    protocol  offer     choose
node      supervisor strategy child     restart
```

In a 0.5 module they are names (`fn f(node: i64)` is valid 0.5). The
reference checker keeps them in `parse::DRAFT06_KEYWORDS`, separate from
`parse::KEYWORDS`, and reserves them only when the module is version 0.6 or 0.7.

### C.2 Grammar

These productions extend section 3 for version 0.6 modules. They are the
productions of the tree-sitter port (`spec/tree-sitter/grammar.js`) and of
the Rust parser. A rule below with the name of a section-3 rule replaces
it for a 0.6 module; the others are new. The machine check of 3.12 also
builds the LALR(1) tables of section 3 with these rules applied
(`lalr::book_grammar_06`), lexing with the keywords of C.1 reserved, and
fails on any conflict; it runs that machine over the 0.6 corpora
(`spec/conc06`, `spec/conc06b`). So T10 (one parse per program) holds for
version 0.6 modules too.

```
Item         = UseDecl | IntentDecl | ExampleDecl | CheckDecl
             | [ "pub" ] ( ConstDecl | TypeDecl | StructDecl | KindDecl
                         | TraitDecl | FnDecl | ActorDecl | ProtocolDecl )
             | StateDecl | EventDecl | ErrorDecl | StepDecl | ImplDecl
             | ExternDecl | NodeDecl | SupervisorDecl .
StateDecl    = [ "replicated" ] "state" NAME NEWLINE INDENT Field { Field } DEDENT .
EventDecl    = [ "interrupt" ] "event" NAME [ Payload ] [ "priority" Expr ] NEWLINE .
StepDecl     = "step" NAME "on" Pattern [ "if" Expr ] [ "deadline" Expr ] StepBody .
ProtocolDecl = "protocol" NAME NEWLINE INDENT ProtoStep { ProtoStep } DEDENT .
ProtoStep    = "send" Type NEWLINE | "recv" Type NEWLINE
             | "offer" NEWLINE INDENT ProtoArm { ProtoArm } DEDENT
             | "choose" NEWLINE INDENT ProtoArm { ProtoArm } DEDENT
             | "loop" NEWLINE INDENT ProtoStep { ProtoStep } DEDENT
             | "break" NEWLINE .
ProtoArm     = NAME NEWLINE [ INDENT ProtoStep { ProtoStep } DEDENT ] .
NodeDecl     = "node" NAME "{" NAME { "," NAME } "}" NEWLINE .
SupervisorDecl = "supervisor" NAME "strategy" NAME NEWLINE INDENT SupChild { SupChild } DEDENT .
SupChild     = "child" NAME ":" TypePath [ "restart" Bound ] NEWLINE .
BaseType     = TypePath | "(" ")" | "(" Type "," [ Type { "," Type } [ "," ] ] ")"
             | "(" Type ")" | "[" Type "]" | "[" Type ";" Expr "]"
             | "chan" BaseType | "iter" BaseType
             | "fn" "(" [ TypeList ] ")" "->" BaseType
             | "session" TypePath | "lvar" BaseType .
Stmt         = SimpleStmt | LetStmt | VarStmt | IfStmt | WhileStmt | LoopStmt
             | ForStmt | MatchStmt | ReturnStmt | BreakStmt | ContinueStmt
             | EmitStmt | FailStmt | SpawnStmt | SelectStmt | ArenaStmt
             | DeviceStmt | YieldStmt | ComptimeStmt | CheckDecl | PassStmt
             | ParStmt | BudgetStmt | DeadlineStmt | GroupStmt | BarrierStmt
             | ScopeStmt | AtomicStmt .
ForStmt      = "for" Pattern "in" Expr [ "par" ] Block .
SpawnStmt    = "spawn" Expr [ "priority" Expr ] [ "->" NAME ] NEWLINE .
SelectStmt   = "select" [ "nondet" ] NEWLINE INDENT SelectArm { SelectArm } DEDENT .
ParStmt      = "par" NEWLINE INDENT Branch { Branch } DEDENT .
Branch       = "branch" NAME Block .
BudgetStmt   = "with" "budget" Expr Block .
DeadlineStmt = "with" "deadline" Expr Block [ "else" Block ] .
GroupStmt    = "with" "group" NAME "lanes" Expr Block .
BarrierStmt  = "barrier" NEWLINE .
ScopeStmt    = "scope" Block .
AtomicStmt   = "atomic" Block .
```

### C.3 Footprints

The footprint of a statement is the set of place paths (5.6) it reads and
the set it writes. Two branches are disjoint when no path written by one
is a prefix of, or has as prefix, a path read or written by the other.

### C.4 `par`

`par` runs its branches; each branch is a block. The result equals running
the branches in source order (T16). Rules:

- W-PAR-1: the footprints of two branches overlap (write/write or
  write/read), including through a `&mut self` method call.
- W-PAR-2: a branch has an effect other than its own writes (`emit`,
  channel operations, spawn, foreign calls), or returns, breaks or
  continues out of the `par`.
- W-NAME-2 also refuses two branches with one name.

Derivation of the rules (confluence). Determinism of a parallel
composition is a confluence property: every way of interleaving the
branches' steps must reach one result, which is then the result of any
fixed order, source order among them. By the Church-Rosser method it is
enough to show the diamond: one step of branch a and one step of branch
b, taken from the same configuration in either order, reach the same
configuration. A step changes only its write set and depends only on
its free variables, so the two steps commute exactly when neither writes
what the other reads or writes. That is W-PAR-1, derived, not chosen: it
is the weakest footprint condition under which the diamond holds for
every store. Termination of each branch (T19) and the diamond give
confluence (Newman's lemma), so every complete interleaving gives the
source-order store (T16). An effect that leaves the store (`emit`,
channel operations, spawn, a foreign call) is observed in the order it
happens, so it would make the observation depend on the interleaving
even when the store does not; W-PAR-2 removes these. Traps follow the
same law: a trap is observed at the first branch in source order that
traps, because that is where the sequential run traps; the reference
and the emitters place both arithmetic traps and resource traps (fuel,
budget) at that branch (book/12-tooling.md 10.5). Mechanized in
`spec/lean`: the diamond on a core with `par` (`RCE.ParSem.diamond`),
determinism of complete runs (`RCE.ParSem.par_det`), refinement to a
model of the reference evaluator including overflow traps
(`RCE.ParSem.refine`), and the fuel account, whose sum-checked trap
point equals the sequential one and whose evaluated work is at most k
times the fuel left at the fork (`RCE.ParFuel.sumcheck_eq_seq`,
`RCE.ParFuel.overrun_bound`). LVars weaken the diamond to
quasi-determinism (C.11.8, T29q). Open: the core has no loops, calls or
data structures, so the link from the core to the full evaluator rests
on the generated vectors (`ParVectors.lean`) and the differential tests,
not on a proof.

### C.5 Budgets, deadlines and nondeterminism

- `with budget n` runs the block with a cost budget n: every Form
  operation charges its cost (C.6.4) and the operation that takes the
  total past n is `trap("budget")`, at the same operation on every
  target. The cost table is the reference evaluator's (`interp` and
  `conc.rs`, `charge`), listed in C.6.4.
  W-TY-1 if n is not an integer.
  `with budget n Block else [as e] Else` makes exhaustion a value.
  Derivation. Totality (T2) asks every step to end in a value; a trap
  that refuses the event is an outcome of the step, not a value the
  program can act on. To act on it the program needs a point where the
  trap is caught, and the state at that point must be one that some
  sequential execution reaches at a well-defined place, or Else observes
  a state no specification of Block describes. The only such states are
  the entry of Block and its completion; the trap rules out completion,
  so a caught trap restores the entry state. Block is therefore atomic:
  all of its writes or none (the same law as T30 for `atomic`).
  Normative rules:
  - A `trap("budget")` raised while Block runs, by this budget or any
    enclosing one, is caught by the innermost enclosing budget that has
    an `else`. Every write Block made (locals, struct fields, state
    fields, `self`) is undone, then Else runs.
  - `as e` binds `e: Exhausted`, the builtin
    `struct Exhausted { limit: u64, used: u64 }`, where `limit` is n and
    `used` is the units this frame had spent before the operation that
    would have passed a limit.
  - Charges stay. Cost counts operations performed (C.6.1), so the
    units spent in Block remain on every enclosing budget. When the trap
    came from an outer budget, Else charges that budget, its next charge
    traps again, and the trap reaches the next budget out with an
    `else`, or refuses the event.
  - W-BUD-1: Block of a budget with an `else` holds an effect that a
    trap cannot undo (`emit`, channel operations, spawn, select, yield,
    lvar `put` or `freeze`), or returns, breaks or continues out of it.
  - A budget without `else` behaves as before: the trap refuses the
    event.
  - The charge rule itself is in the proved kernel
    (`crates/rce/src/kernel.rs`, `budget_charge`), verified with Kani for
    stacks of up to three frames: a charge is all or nothing, leaves no
    frame past its limit, and is additive (`budget_all_or_nothing_within_limits`,
    `budget_charge_is_additive`). Every runtime's `charge` implements the
    same rule; the link from the kernel to those copies is the
    differential tests, not a proof.
  The trap falls on the same operation on every target, so whether Else
  runs, and the value of `e`, are functions of the program and its
  inputs, and replay re-derives them. The emitters save every local the
  block writes at entry (struct fields and state fields are locals of
  the emitted step) and restore them on the trap. Checked by
  `spec/checker/tests/conc06_run.rs` (`budget_else_catches`,
  `budget_else_refuses_undoable_effects`), `emit_run.rs`
  (`budget_else_*`, reference against the Rust, Python and JavaScript
  runtimes) and `emit06b.rs` (`budget_else_is_atomic_on_every_target`,
  the limit swept across the block's cost on all four targets).
- `with deadline n` runs the block with an expiry n logical ticks after
  entry; if the block has not completed by then, the `else` block runs
  instead (T22). W-DL-1: outside `fn main` or a task
  function.
- `select nondet` may take any ready arm; the choice is an input and is
  logged, so replay reproduces it (T21). W-ND-1: outside `fn main` or a
  task function. `select` without `nondet` keeps the rotation rule of 6.8.
- `spawn f(...) priority p` and `event E priority p`: admission prefers
  the highest pending priority (T25). W-TY-1 if p is not an integer.

### C.6 Cost semantics

C.6.1 A cost is a non-negative integer number of units. Cost is a
deterministic accounting of Form operations, the same on every target;
it is not a measurement of time or energy (est_j is separate).

C.6.2 Charging point. An operation charges its cost after its operands
are evaluated and before it acts. If the charge would take any
enclosing budget past its limit, the operation is `trap("budget")` and
does not act; otherwise every enclosing budget is charged. So nested
budgets see the same operation trap, and a budget n admits exactly the
operations whose running total stays at most n.

C.6.3 `par` and `for ... par` charge `c_fork` per branch (or chunk),
then each branch's own costs. The branches' costs are summed in source
order, and exhaustion is placed where the sequential run would hit it
(C.4, T16), so the trap does not depend on scheduling.

C.6.4 The cost table (normative). Operations not listed (literals of
scalars, variable reads, assignment, control flow, `let`) cost 0. The
table is checked against the reference evaluator, and the emitted Rust,
Python and JavaScript runtimes charge the same costs
(`spec/checker/tests/stdlib_costs.rs`).

| Operation | Cost |
|---|---|
| `c_call`: call of a user function or a closure | 4 |
| standard library method (5.15) on receiver size n, first-argument size k | 0.7: 4 + work(m, n, k), below; 0.5 and 0.6: 4 |
| `c_chan`: channel send or receive | 8 |
| `c_spawn`: `spawn` | 32 |
| `c_fork`: one `par` branch or `for ... par` chunk | 16 |
| list literal `[a, b, ...]`, map literal, comprehension with n results | 4 + n |
| `[x; n]` | 4 + n |
| index `a[i]`, slice `a[i:j]`, member `x.f`, tuple member `t.0` | 1 |
| unary `-`, `~`, `not` | 1 |
| `and`, `or` | 1 |
| binary operator on integer, bool or text operands, comparisons | 1 |
| float (f64, f32) `+`, `-`, `*` | 2 |
| float (f64, f32) `/` | 8 |

**Method work (normative for version 0.7).** In a version 0.6 module a
standard library method costs `c_call` whatever its sizes, as draft 0.6
defined it; a budget there bounds the number of operations. In a 0.7
module it costs `c_call` plus work(m, n, k). A budget is a proxy for energy, and energy
scales with the operations performed, so a method's cost must track its
work. Sizes: text is its UTF-8 byte length, a list its length, a set its number of
elements, a map its number of entries, any other value 0. n is the receiver's size and k the
first argument's (0 when there is none). work(m, n, k) is fixed by the
method's complexity class in the reference evaluator:

| Class | Methods | work |
|---|---|---|
| linear, text receiver | `strip`, `upper`, `lower`, `reverse`, `tostr`, `chars`, `words`, `lines`, `split`, `isdigit`, `isalpha`, `isspace`, `contains`, `startswith`, `endswith`, `toint`, `join`, `sha256` | n + k |
| linear, list receiver | `reverse`, `contains`, `sum`, `map`, `filter`, `fold`, `utf8` | n + k |
| linear, map receiver (maps are ordered association lists) | `get`, `contains`, `insert`, `remove`, `keys`, `values`, `merge` | n + k |
| linear, set receiver (a set is held as its elements in canonical order) | `union`, `inter`, `insert`, `contains`, `tolist` | n + k |
| n log n, list receiver | `sort` | n · ⌈log₂ n⌉, with ⌈log₂ n⌉ = 0 for n ≤ 1 |
| constant | every other method of 5.15 | 0 |

The calls a `map`, `filter` or `fold` makes to its function argument are
charged as calls in addition (`c_call` each, plus their bodies). The
arithmetic saturates at the largest i128, so it cannot overflow; no
reachable size comes near it, so the Python and JavaScript runtimes,
whose integers are unbounded, give the same numbers. work is monotone:
it never decreases when n or k grows. The reference evaluator
(`conc::method_work`) and the Rust, Python and JavaScript runtimes
compute the same function, and the budget boundary falls on the same
operation in all of them (`spec/checker/tests/method_costs.rs`, which
also checks monotonicity).

### C.7 Device kernels

Inside a device region (5.13), a version 0.6 module may use `par` and
`for ... par` with the same rules; the device rules of W-DEV-1 still
apply.

### C.8 `for ... par`

`for x in e par` runs the iterations as if in order. It is encoded in the
reference checker as the marker region `$forpar` (the AST has no new
variant). Rules:

- W-PAR-3: the body writes a place other than as a reduction (`+= *= &=
  |= ^=` on a variable never read in the body) or as slot `[i]` of a range
  loop over `i`.
- W-PAR-4: the body has an effect, or returns, breaks or continues.

A reduction is evaluated on a fixed tree, which equals the left fold for
an associative operation with an identity (T18). The tree is normative,
since a float operation is not associative and the bits depend on it:
for m >= 2 contributions, the left subtree takes the first h, where h is
the largest power of two below m, and the right subtree the rest; one
contribution is itself; none is the identity. Derivation: placement must
give the same bits on every fabric (HC-12), and the reductions that
vector units and GPUs execute are complete binary trees over
power-of-two blocks. With this split every left subtree is complete, so
the tree decomposes into such blocks and a fabric can evaluate it
natively. `pscan` uses the same split for its up-sweep and down-sweep.
One definition, `host::tree_split`, serves the reference evaluator and
the placement executor (`place_par`, `place_sum`), and every runtime
computes the same h. Checked by `spec/checker/tests/host_place.rs`
(`forpar_reference_and_placement_share_the_tree`: a non-associative
float sum gives the same bits from `run_main` and from the placement
executor for every length up to 40) and by the emitter parity tests.
Before 2026-10-15 the reference and runtimes split at ceil(m/2) while
the placement executor split at the power of two; the two disagreed in
the last bits of float reductions from five contributions on.
The Lean model defines the same split, `RCE.Par.split m = 2 ^ log2 (m -
1)` (checked against `host::tree_split` on sample lengths), and proves
`tree_eq_foldl` for the tree built with it, so T18 is proved for the tree
the code runs. `RCE.ParFuel` reduces branch uses in that tree:
`tree_use_eq_sum` (the tree total is the source-order sum) and
`tree_work_eq` (the threaded work reduced in the tree is the work of
`overrun_bound`, at most k·F).

### C.11 Draft 0.6b

- C.11.2 Workgroups. `with group g lanes n` runs n lanes in phases
  separated by `barrier`. W-GRP-1: a group not directly inside a device
  region. W-GRP-2: `barrier` other than as a statement at the top level of
  a group body. W-GRP-3: a lane reads another lane's slot in the same
  phase, or lanes share a scalar written in the phase.
- C.11.3 Sessions. `protocol P` declares a session type; a value of type
  `session P` is an endpoint. W-SES-1: an operation not allowed by the
  protocol state, an unknown label, `offer()` not matched over its labels,
  a match that does not handle every label, or branches leaving the
  endpoint in different states. W-SES-2: an endpoint not at the end of
  its protocol when it goes out of scope or is closed. W-SES-3: a label
  that appears twice, a protocol loop with no message before it repeats,
  or `break` outside a protocol loop. W-TY-1: a payload of the wrong type.
  The two endpoints of `chan[session P]` have the types P and dual(P),
  where dual swaps send with receive and choose with offer (duality).
  W-SES-4 (linearity): an endpoint is a capability that exactly one
  name holds. A protocol operation consumes the endpoint at one state
  and yields it at the next. A bare use of the name (an argument, a
  spawn argument, a payload sent on another endpoint, a rebinding) moves
  the endpoint, and `close` consumes it; after either the name holds
  nothing, and a further use is refused (no use after move, send or
  close). Paths that join must agree on whether an endpoint was
  consumed, so a branch that moves it while another keeps it in use is
  refused, as is a loop body that moves an endpoint the loop does not
  create. With W-SES-2 this makes endpoints linear (affine plus
  must-close): on every path to the end of its scope each endpoint is at
  the end of its protocol, closed, or moved to a holder that takes the
  obligation over. `let m = x` moves the endpoint to `m`, which owes the
  rest of x's protocol; a name bound inside a block goes out of scope at
  the end of that block, so its endpoint must be finished or passed on
  there. The checker's protocol automaton (`check06b`, `ProtoCursor`) is
  linked to T28 by vectors (C.13). Linearity is a typing judgment
  (`SessionLin.Ty`): the checker's W-SES-1, W-SES-2 and W-SES-4 for
  bodies of send, receive, close, move and branch are proved sound
  against it, and a typed body never uses a gone endpoint, never closes
  an unfinished one and ends with every endpoint gone or done, on every
  path (T28l).
  W-SES-5 (session graph a tree): a `spawn` passes at most one session
  endpoint, and a body that holds both ends of one channel acts on
  neither until it has passed one on. The session graph has processes
  as nodes and channels as edges. A spawn with one endpoint adds one
  edge to a new node, and sending an endpoint to the holder of the
  other end of the carrying channel moves an edge along a path, so the
  graph stays a tree. On a tree, if every channel's two ends are
  compatible, either every process has finished or some channel has
  both ends waiting on it and they can step (T28d). Two channels
  between the same two processes break this: each can wait on a
  different channel.
  W-SES-5 by priorities: a program the tree rule refuses is accepted when
  its session graph has a priority order. Each exchange on a channel is
  an action (channel, step), shared by both ends, and a spawn is a
  one-step action between spawner and spawned. Each process's actions in
  program order must strictly increase in priority, and each channel's
  ends must make the same number of exchanges; the checker finds such
  priorities exactly when the order the processes impose on actions is
  acyclic. Then every reachable state is finished or can step, on any
  session graph, cycles included (T28p): the waiting action of least
  priority has its partner waiting on that same action. A cycle of
  waits, as in two channels between two processes used in opposite
  orders, is a cycle in the order and is refused. The checker reads
  priorities from programs whose endpoints are created, sent on,
  received on and passed to spawns at the top level of bodies, over
  protocols of messages; outside that fragment the tree rule decides.
  Multiparty global types (T28g): a global type says which role sends
  to which and in what order, with binary choices; its projection on
  each role uses plain merge (roles not told of a choice must have the
  same local type in both branches). Every configuration reachable from
  the projections of a global type is finished or steps, and a step
  lands on the projections of a global type again. A global type of
  messages only gives priorities by event order, so its projections pass
  the priority rule and compose with the other channels of a program.
  The checker's projection equals the Lean projection on 200 generated
  global types (C.13).
  Full merge and asynchrony (T28a): a role not told of a choice may
  receive differently in the two branches; its projection merges them
  into one branching that accepts the labels of both (sends must still
  agree). Sends never block: each ordered pair of roles has one FIFO
  queue, so two messages from one sender to one receiver arrive in
  sending order, and the global type records which labels are in
  flight. Each role's local type need only accept at least what the
  projection of the current global type accepts (association). Every
  asynchronous step of an associated configuration is a step of the
  global type and stays associated; every receiver accepts the label at
  the head of its queue; and every configuration reachable from the
  projections with empty queues is final (all roles done, all queues
  empty) or steps. The checker's full-merge projection equals the Lean
  projection on 300 generated global types, and its exploration of the
  asynchronous runs from each fully projecting one finds no stuck or
  refusing configuration (C.13).
  Convergence notes. Honda, Vasconcelos and Kubo (ESOP 1998) keep
  channels in a linear realm and pass them by delegation; their type
  soundness theorem gives subject reduction and the absence of run-time
  communication errors, and does not claim deadlock freedom. Gay and
  Hole (Acta Informatica 2005) give each end to exactly one process by
  environment addition, end a derivation only at a completed
  environment (as W-SES-2 does), prove their typechecking algorithm
  sound for the declarative rules (the shape of `chkBody_sound`), and
  for polarity inference forbid using one end of a channel while the
  same thread holds the other (as W-SES-5 does); they show a typable
  process over two channels between two processes that deadlocks.
  Wadler (Propositions as Sessions, ICFP 2012) composes processes by a
