  cut on exactly one channel, which gives deadlock freedom; a cut on two
  channels admits loops that may deadlock, and he notes that a primitive
  that creates a channel and returns both ends in a pair may suffer from
  deadlock. RCE's `chan[session P]` is such a primitive; W-SES-5 keeps
  its uses to the one-channel shape at spawns. Kobayashi (CONCUR 2006)
  annotates each channel use with an obligation and a capability level
  and proves that a well-typed process is deadlock free (and with time
  tags, lock free); Padovani (CSL-LICS 2014) gives the linear pi-calculus
  one priority per channel type, requires each process to use its
  channels in increasing priority, and proves deadlock freedom, encoding
  multiparty sessions so that a global type's events give the
  priorities (his App. C). T28p is this rule on RCE's networks, with one
  priority per exchange. Honda, Yoshida and Carbone (POPL 2008) introduce
  global types, projection and the progress of a single well-formed
  session; T28g is the synchronous, plain-merge form of their result,
  and T28a keeps their order-preserving queues (their Sec. 2) with the
  full merge and association of Hou, Yoshida and Kuhn (arXiv:2402.16741,
  Def. 3.1 and 3.7).
  The reading ledger is spec/proposals/session-reading-ledger.md.
  Open: an endpoint and its dual sent separately to the same third
  process close a loop that W-SES-5 does not see; T28d assumes the tree
  and the preservation of the tree under delegation is argued above,
  not mechanized (the priority rule closes this loop when the program is
  in the fragment it reads); T28p and T28g model rendezvous, and T28a
  models buffered delivery for global types without recursion or
  payloads; the checker reads priorities only for straight-line
  bodies over message protocols, and priorities for global types with
  choice or recursion are not derived; `SessionPrio.decideP` is proved
  sound, not complete (the checker's acyclicity test is the complete
  decision, linked by vectors); there is no surface syntax for global
  types; T28l covers message steps and local branching, not
  choose/offer, loops or recursion (those are covered by the automaton
  vectors of T28).
- C.11.5 Merge. `impl Merge for T` declares a join. Its laws
  (associative, commutative, idempotent) are an admission obligation
  (W-CRDT-1, `conc::crdt_gate`), discharged by a certificate and never by
  sampling. `bottom()` is the initial state; the states an LVar can reach
  are the up-set of it, which the join preserves, so the laws on that
  up-set are the laws of the type. For a kind of nullary variants the
  gate evaluates every triple, which decides them
  (`MergeLaws.laws_of_enum`). Otherwise the gate reads the body of
  `merge` as a term over proven combinators (`conc::merge_certs`): per
  field, `max` or `min` on an integer, `or` or `and` on a bool,
  `union` or `inter` on a `Set[τ]`, `merge` on a `Map[k, v]` (pointwise,
  certified when the `Merge` of `v` is: an integer, a bool, a set, a map
  of such, or a type with a certified impl), or `.merge` of a field whose
  type has a certified impl (componentwise product); on a record of one integer field, a selection that keeps
  `o` when `o.k > self.k` and `self` otherwise (max, or min when the
  smaller side is kept); and lexicographic on an integer key: `self` when
  `self.k > o.k`, `o` when `o.k > self.k`, and otherwise the key with the
  other fields merged by the rules above. Each term is a `Cert` of
  `MergeCert.lean`, and `Cert.semi` turns every certificate into a proof
  of the three laws, so they compose by construction. The lexicographic
  rule needs its key to be a chain (a total order); without that it is
  not a join (`MergeCert.lex_needs_chain`), which is why the key must be
  an integer. Any other impl is refused, also a lawful one written
  differently (for example bitwise `|`), with a message naming the
  combinators; a search on a finite sample runs first and, when it finds
  a counterexample, the refusal names it. The built-in
  instances (integers under `max`, `bool` under `or`, sets and lists
  under union, maps pointwise, tuples and records componentwise, `none` as
  bottom) have the laws by `MergeLaws.lean`; that sorted lists without
  duplicates represent sets and maps canonically is `Canon.set_canon` and
  `Canon.map_canon`, and that the canonical order they are sorted by is a
  strict total order is `ValOrder.lt_total`. A componentwise instance
  exists only when every component has one: a map needs a `Merge` on its
  value type, an option on its payload, and a struct without its own
  `impl Merge` on every field, recursively through nested structs and the
  struct's type arguments (a struct reached again through itself adds no
  condition). Otherwise `lvar_new`, `lvar T` and `Map.merge` are refused
  (W-CRDT-1) with the path to the first field that has none. Sets and
  lists merge by union, which needs only equality, so their element type
  needs no `Merge`.
- C.11.6 Prefix scan. `xs.pscan(f, e)` and `xs.pscan_incl(f, e)` take a
  list of T, `f: (T, T) -> T` and `e: T` (W-TY-1 otherwise) and return a
  list of the same length. Element i of `pscan` combines xs[0..i] and
  element i of `pscan_incl` combines xs[0..=i]; `pscan` gives `e` at
  index 0, the empty prefix, and the empty list scans to the empty list.
  Evaluation is on a fixed tree (the up-sweep and down-sweep of
  Blelloch) of C.8: the range [lo, hi) splits at lo + p, with p the
  largest power of two below hi - lo (`host::tree_split`). The
  up-sweep stores the combination of each node's range, left operand
  before right. The down-sweep gives each node an offset: none at the
  root; the parent's offset to the left child; to the right child the
  left child's sum, combined after the parent's offset when there is
  one. Element i of `pscan` is the offset of leaf i, or `e` when it has
  none; element i of `pscan_incl` is xs[i] combined after that offset.
  The tree depends on n alone, so every run and every target applies f
  to the same operands in the same bracketing and order, and the result
  is bit-identical for an f that is itself deterministic on each target,
  floats included. Law: if f is associative, every bracketing of a
  prefix has the same value, so element i equals the left fold of its
  prefix. No identity law is needed: `e` is never combined, it only
  stands for the empty prefix. If f is not associative (float addition)
  the result is still fixed, but can differ from the left fold, as for a
  reduction on the fixed tree (C.8, T18). Work: fewer than 2n applications
  of f for `pscan` and fewer than 3n for `pscan_incl`; depth O(log n).
  The reference (`conc.rs`) and the runtimes of every emitter (rt.rs,
  rt.py, rt.js, rt.scala) use the same split.
- C.11.8 LVars. `lvar T` requires `T: Merge` (W-CRDT-1). An LVar holds a
  value, the optional top of `lvar_new(bottom, top)`, and a frozen bit.
  `put(d)` sets the value `v` to `v ⊔ d` with the program's `Merge`; it
  is `trap("lvar conflict")` when the result is the top, and
  `trap("lvar put after freeze")` when the LVar is frozen and the result
  differs from `v` (a put that changes nothing is allowed). `freeze()`
  sets the bit and returns the exact value. `wait(Q)` returns the `t` in
  `Q` with `t ⊔ v = v`, in the same `Merge` order as `put`, and blocks
  until there is one. The threshold tests charge no fuel and no budget,
  so the cost of a `wait` does not depend on how often a schedule
  rechecks it. A `Q` with more than one element must be pairwise
  incompatible: distinct elements join to the top. Every `wait` checks
  this before it reads the value and is otherwise
  `trap("lvar thresholds are not pairwise incompatible")`; the check does
  not read the value, so its outcome does not depend on the schedule. A
  trap is a defined result, so δ stays total. W-LVAR-1: inside the
  branches of one `par`, or the body of a `for ... par`, a `freeze`
  while some branch may `put`, where a call to a function or method that
  puts to (or freezes) an LVar it did not create counts as a put (or a
  freeze). An LVar a branch creates with `lvar_new` and does not rebind is
  its own and does not count. The rule does not match the name of a put
  with the name of a freeze, so an
  alias, a parameter or a helper cannot hide a freeze. W-LVAR-2: an empty
  threshold list, or a list with two elements that are, or on some input
  can be, one below the other in the program's `Merge` (`conc::lvar_gate`).
  This is decided at admission when every element takes finitely many
  values: a constant, or `if c then a else b` over such, with every
  combination checked, since two thresholds where one is below the other
  are compatible for any top. A parameter whose declared type is finite
  (a kind of nullary variants, or `bool`) and which the body never
  rebinds ranges over every value of its type, so it is decided too;
  since every value of such a type is at or above its bottom, a list
  with such a parameter and another element is refused whenever the
  bottom is below that element. Where an element is not finite in this
  sense (a parameter of an unbounded type, a computed value),
  incompatibility depends on the input, and the check every `wait` makes
  against the top, with its trap, is the defined behaviour. Model: T29q,
  T29s, T29a; the rule table
  `conc::LVAR_RULES` ties each rule and trap to its Lean declaration
  (see T29s).
- C.11.8 convergence notes. The frozen bit, and the rule that only a put
  that would change a frozen LVar is an error, follow Kuper, Turon,
  Krishnaswami and Newton (POPL 2014, Sec. 3.3 and 4.2). Threshold sets
  and their `incomp` premise follow Kuper and Newton (FHPC 2013, Sec.
  3.3). T29q has the shape of the POPL 2014 Theorem 1 for this fragment.
  Their proof goes through an Independence lemma and quasi-confluence;
  the one here uses an invariant (the value joined with the puts still to
  come is the join of all puts), which suffices because there is no
  allocation: T29s takes a store of many LVars as the product lattice
  over locations and proves the invariant per location, and T29a adds
  `lvar_new` as a step that allocates a location named by a
  deterministic counter (thread i's k-th allocation is `(i, k)`), so
  locations do not depend on the schedule and the POPL 2014 permutation
  of locations is not needed. Their library marks code that freezes as
  `QuasiDet` in its type. RCE instead refuses, by W-LVAR-1, the freezes
  that could race with a put, so an admitted program is deterministic,
  and the frozen bit turns a race the rule misses into an error instead
  of a different answer. FHPC 2013 suggests validating user lattices
  with QuickCheck; the sample search here is that kind of test, and is
  used only to find counterexamples.
- C.11.9 Structured spawn. `spawn f(...) -> h` gives a join handle. In a
  version 0.6 module a task function may spawn only inside `scope`; `fn
  main` is an implicit scope (W-SCOPE-1). A join handle cannot leave its
  scope (W-SCOPE-1). A 0.5 module keeps the rule of 5.8: any task
  function may spawn.
- C.11.10 Transactions. `atomic` applies all its actor sends or none
  (T30). W-ATOM-1: `spawn`, a receive, `select` or another wait inside
  `atomic`. W-ATOM-2: actors of one `atomic` on different nodes.
- C.11.11 Placement and supervision. `node N {A, B}` places actors on a
  node. W-NODE-1: a placed name that is not an actor, or an actor placed
  twice. `supervisor S strategy k` with k one of `one_for_one`,
  `one_for_all`, `rest_for_one` (W-SUP-1); each `child` must be an actor
  (W-SUP-2), and W-NAME-2 refuses a duplicate child.
  Run-time meaning (normative). A supervisor declaration is one static
  supervisor; it supervises every actor whose type is one of its
  children, so the set an actor belongs to is fixed by the program, not
  by spawn order. When a handler of such an actor refuses its message
  (a trap or a `fail`), the run log records `Refused(reason)`, then
  `Restart(child, instance, reason, tick t, k)`, where `instance` is the
  actor's id (6.6) and k counts this child's restarts in the window
  below. The strategy then resets the region of the failed actor
  (`one_for_one`), of every actor of the supervisor's child types
  (`one_for_all`), or of those whose child is declared at or after the
  failed one (`rest_for_one`), to the actor's initializers. Intensity is
  measured in logical ticks, never wall time: with `const
  RESTART_WINDOW: u64 = W` only restarts at ticks t' with t - t' < W
  count, otherwise every restart of the run counts; more than the
  child's `restart bound` stops the supervisor with `Stopped(supervisor
  S)` and the run ends `Refused`. Mailbox policy: a restarted actor keeps
  its mailbox, since Form law 3 drops no message; only the message that
  failed is consumed, and it is logged as refused. A handler that fails
  inside `atomic` (C.11.10) leaves every handler of the batch
  uncommitted (T30), and the failing actor is then supervised as above.
  Restart as input. Derivation. The state of a run is the fold of its
  log (T3). A restart changes actor state without a message, so it must
  be an entry of the log that the fold applies, or the state is not a
  function of the log. The decision is therefore an input of the run:
  at a crash the run records `RestartIn{tick, sup, child, id, reset,
  stop}` (`RunResult.restarts`), and a replay given these inputs
  (`RunCfg.restarts`) applies each logged decision at its crash without
  consulting the supervisor's policy. A log thus replays under the
  decisions it records even after the strategy, bound or
  `RESTART_WINDOW` in the source has changed (the resolver rule of
  Appendix D, applied to supervision). A replayed decision for another
  actor or supervisor than the one that crashed is `replay diverged`.
  Checked by `spec/checker/tests/conc06b_run.rs`
  (`supervisor_restarts_then_stops`,
  `restart_is_an_input_replay_consumes`: replay reproduces the log,
  logged decisions govern under a changed bound, an edited decision is
  applied as logged, a mismatched one diverges) and `emit_run.rs`
  `actor_refusals_match` (the Rust, Python and JavaScript runtimes take
  the same decisions as the reference, with and without a window) and
  `restart_inputs_replay_on_every_target` (each runtime prints its
  decisions with `--restart-log`, replays a logged list given as
  `--restart=TICK|SUP|CHILD|ID|STOP|RESET,...` under a changed bound
  exactly as the reference does, and diverges on a mismatched decision).
  Stable ids and upgrades. Derivation. A logged decision names actors
  by id, and replay applies it to the actor with that id, so a log
  replays on an upgraded program exactly when the upgrade maps each
  logged id to the same instance. An id built from source text (a line,
  a count of unrelated creations) changes under edits that do not touch
  supervision, and T7 forbids identifiers in ids. What both an upgrade
  that keeps supervision and a renaming preserve is the position of an
  instance: its place in the supervisor tree and its order among its
  creating task's creations at that place. Ids are therefore those paths
  (6.6): `i.j`, creating task, ordinal for a supervised actor; `-`, task,
  ordinal for an unsupervised one; parent and ordinal for a task. Since
  ids are positional, a log is meaningful only against the tree it was
  recorded under, so the tree is the log's schema: version 1 of the
  restart log is a header `restartlog v1 tree=S/c,...` (every position
  by its declared supervisor and child names, in declaration order;
  `RunResult.tree`, `conc::sup_tree`) followed by the `restartin`
  lines. Migration rule (normative): a version 1 log replays on a
  program in which every recorded position still holds the same
  declared supervisor and child, that is the recorded supervisors are
  the program's first ones in order and each keeps its recorded children
  as its first ones in order; new children may follow a supervisor's
  recorded ones and new supervisors may follow the recorded ones, since
  neither moves a recorded position. Any other change (a position
  removed or renamed, a supervisor or child inserted before a recorded
  one, a reorder) is detected before the first step: the run refuses
  with `trap: upgrade removed supervisor position S/c` or `trap: upgrade
  reordered supervisor position S/c` for the first recorded position
  that fails, and nothing is replayed (`conc::tree_migrates`,
  `RunCfg.restart_tree`). A log without a header is version 0: its
  decisions replay with each decision's position checked when it is
  taken, so a decision whose position is gone refuses with the removed
  trap at that crash, and a decision for another actor is `replay
  diverged`; neither is ever applied to a different instance. A log
  whose tree does not migrate is converted by recording it again under
  the new program; no rule rewrites positional ids across a moved
  position, because the instance a moved position denotes is not
  determined by the log. Checked by `conc06b_run.rs`
  (`restart_log_schema_migration_rule`,
  `actor_and_task_ids_survive_structure_preserving_edits`) and
  `emit_run.rs` `restart_replay_survives_upgrades_and_traps_on_tree_changes`
  (a log recorded on one program replays on an upgrade that shifts every
  line and adds a function, an actor type and a supervisor; removal and
  reorder traps; the version 0 per-decision check; on the reference and
  on the Rust, Python, JavaScript and Scala runtimes, which print the
  header with `--restart-log` and take it as `--restart-tree=S/c,...`).
  The run log of `fn
  main` is not D: actors run by `rce run`, not by the host of Appendix E
  (HC-6).
- C.11.12 Real time. `interrupt event E priority p` with p an integer
  literal in 0..=255 (W-INTR-1). `step ... deadline n` with n a positive
  integer literal in ticks, and `const TICK_NS: u64 = n` when declared
  (W-RT-1). TICK_NS only relates logical ticks to a nominal duration for
  reporting; no construct reads a wall clock (6.3 N11).
- C.11.4 Replicated state. `replicated state R` is a region whose log is
  shared by replicas; a replica that applied a prefix of the log holds the
  fold of that prefix (T31).

### C.12 Rules that are not draft 0.6

The reference checker also raises three rules that belong to the 0.5
language and are now listed in section 7: W-MOD-3 (an imported name that
clashes with a declaration or with another import; names are not
renamed), W-VIS-1 (use of a name private to its module, the form W-MOD-1
takes in `link.rs`) and W-TRAIT-3 (a type used with `==`, `<` or a
generic bound that does not implement the required trait).

### C.13 Theorems

Status is stated exactly. "Proved on a semantics" means a Lean proof over
a small-step semantics of a core of RCE. "Model" means a Lean proof about
an abstract model that is not connected to the RCE semantics or to the
reference evaluator. "Vectors" means the reference evaluator's results on
generated programs are checked against the model by the Lean kernel; that
is a correspondence on samples, not a proof about the evaluator.

| | Statement | Status | Lean |
|---|---|---|---|
| T16 | under W-PAR-1 every interleaving of `par` gives the source-order result | proved on a semantics (core: integer variables, assignment, sequence, `if`, binary `par`; no loops, calls, data or traps); refinement to a model of the evaluator with i64 traps; vectors | `par_det`, `refine`, `ParVectors` |
| T17 | steps of two well-formed branches commute | proved on a semantics | `diamond` |
| T18 | a fixed reduction tree equals the left fold | model | `tree_eq_foldl` |
| T19a | `par` neither deadlocks nor diverges | proved on a semantics | `progress`, `steps_bound` |
| T19b | acyclic waits-for leaves a task that waits on none | model | `t19b` |
| T20 | every complete run of `par` has the same length | proved on a semantics | `steps_count`, `work_par` |
| T21 | logged nondeterministic choices replay | model | `t21` |
| T22 | a deadline block has exactly one outcome, time bounded | model | `t22` |
| T23 | a workgroup gives the phase-then-lane result | proved on a semantics | `group_det` |
| T24 | happens-before iff vector clocks are ordered, for the tick rule | proved on a model of runs (both directions) | `vc_iff`, `TickClock.hb_iff` |
| T25 | priority admission takes a maximal pending priority | model | `t25` |
| T26 | a scope ends after every child | model | `t26` |
| T27 | an actor answers as its sequential specification | model; vectors | `t27`, `ModelVectors` |
| T28 | session duality, subject reduction and progress, with recursion | proved on a session calculus; encoding of surface protocols mechanized; the checker's dual and protocol automaton equal the model's on 60 generated protocols along a joint run (enabled actions at each point, and the end); linearity is T28l | `t28r_preserve`, `t28r_progress`, `enc_comp`, `SessionVectors.lean`, `checker/tests/lean_session.rs` |
| T28l | linear endpoints: the checker's W-SES-1, W-SES-2 and W-SES-4 are sound for a linear typing judgment, and a typed body runs every path without using a gone endpoint or closing an unfinished one, and ends with every endpoint gone or done | proved on a calculus of bodies (send, receive, close, move, branch over message protocols); the checker agrees with the model's `chkBody` (accept, or the rule refused) on 120 generated bodies, which found that the checker did not track an endpoint moved by `let m = x` (fixed) | `SessionLin.chkBody_sound`, `ty_safe`, `chkBody_safe`, `SessionLinVectors.lean`, `checker/tests/lean_session_lin.rs` |
| T28d | deadlock freedom: on a tree-shaped session graph with compatible ends, every process has finished or some channel has both ends waiting and they step | proved on a model of networks (processes blocked on one endpoint or finished); the tree is enforced by W-SES-5 at spawns and argued for delegation | `SessionDead.deadlock_free` |
| T28p | deadlock freedom by priorities: if each process's actions strictly increase in priority and both ends of a channel share each action, every reachable state is finished or steps, on any session graph (cycles included); the checker's W-SES-5 accepts a program the tree rule refuses when the order on its actions is acyclic | proved on a model of networks (rendezvous, spawns as one-step channels); priorities computed by relaxation are proved to satisfy the rule, and a cycle in the order refutes every priority assignment; the checker agrees with the model (tree rule or priorities, else W-SES-5) on 150 generated programs, 9 of them cyclic and accepted only by priorities | `SessionPrio.deadlock_free`, `decideP_sound`, `cycle_chk_false`, `SessionPrioVectors.lean`, `checker/tests/lean_session_prio.rs` |
| T28g | multiparty global types: the projections of a well-formed global type (plain merge) step only to projections of a global type, and every reachable configuration is finished or steps; a global type of messages only satisfies the priority rule with priority = event index | proved on a synchronous calculus of global and local types with messages and binary choice; the checker's projection equals the model's on 200 generated global types, and its priority decision accepts every message-only one | `SessionGlobal.sr`, `progress`, `deadlock_free`, `global_prio`, `SessionGlobalVectors.lean`, `checker/tests/lean_session_global.rs` |
| T28a | multiparty global types with full merge and asynchronous, order-preserving delivery: every step of a configuration associated with a global type is a step of that global type and stays associated; a receiver accepts the label heading its queue; every configuration reachable from the projections with empty queues is final or steps | proved on an asynchronous calculus of global and local types with binary choice and one FIFO queue per ordered pair of roles; the checker's full-merge projection equals the model's on 300 generated global types, and its exploration of their asynchronous runs finds no stuck or refusing configuration | `SessionAsync.sr`, `safe`, `progress`, `deadlock_free`, `SessionAsyncVectors.lean`, `checker/tests/lean_session_async.rs` |
| T29 | LVar puts commute; one-threshold reads are order independent | model; vectors | `lvar_interleave`, `t29_perm` |
| T29q | LVars over any join-semilattice with an absorbing top, threshold reads in the same order, and a frozen bit: two runs that complete every thread without error end in the same configuration (value, frozen bit, every result); without `freeze`, a program with a completing run has no erroring run; with `freeze`, whether a run errs can depend on the schedule | proved on a calculus (put, get with incompatible sets, freeze, on one LVar shared by any number of threads); runs that block forever are not covered; the built-in Merge instances are semilattices | `LVarQD.quasi_det`, `det_no_err`, `quasi_not_det`, `MergeLaws` |
| T29s | A store of many LVars shared by any number of threads (the product lattice over locations, a frozen bit per location): two runs that complete every thread without error end in the same store, frozen bits and results; without `freeze`, no run errs if one completes. W-CRDT-1 certificates are lawful by construction. Each row of `conc::LVAR_RULES` (rule, trap, Lean declaration) and the certificate of each certified test program is generated into `LVarRules.lean`, which `lake build` elaborates, and the same test checks each trap string in the evaluator and every emitter runtime | locations allocated before the threads start (T29a adds allocation); the generated table checks that the named declarations exist and the certificates elaborate, not that the evaluator refines the calculus | `LVarStore.store_quasi_det`, `store_det_no_err`, `MergeCert.cert_laws`, `LVarRules`, `checker/tests/lvar_rules.rs` |
| T29a | The store of T29s with dynamic allocation: `new l` allocates `l` (only once; operations on `l` wait for it), locations from a deterministic counter (`counter_owner`). Two runs that complete every thread without error reach the same store, frozen bits, allocation map and results; without `freeze`, no run errs if one completes. An executable semantics `stepAt` / `exec` is proved sound and complete against the relation: every step `stepAt` takes is a `Step` (`stepAt_sound`, `exec_sound`), and from a configuration with no value at top every `Step` is `stepAt c i` for some thread index i (`stepAt_complete`), so the schedules of `exec` are exactly the runs of the relation. The sorted representation of a `Set[τ]` and the key-sorted one of a `Map[k, v]` are unique: equal membership (equal lookup) implies equal lists (`Canon.set_canon`, `Canon.map_canon`), so the Merge laws stated on membership and lookup (`MergeCert.unionS`, `mapS`) hold of the runtime values. 60 runs extracted from `stepAt` over the lattice 0..6 under max are replayed sequentially on the evaluator and the Rust, Python and JavaScript emitters, which must give the same `wait` and `freeze` results and the same error; every schedule of every vector (each interleaving of the threads' operations in program order in which each wait is enabled, 221 in all) is run on the evaluator's deterministic sequential execution, explored depth first with the evaluator deciding enabledness: without `freeze` every schedule gives Lean's results, or every one errs when Lean's run does; with `freeze` all complete schedules agree and Lean's outcome is among them. All 60 are also run as a threaded `par` on OS threads, one branch per Lean thread, with each `freeze` sequenced after the join, where W-LVAR-1 accepts it; the frozen value is then the join of all puts to the cell, and Lean's mid-run frozen value is at most that | the vectors cover `put`, single-threshold `get`, `freeze` and allocation on integer cells, with at most 9 operations each; the explorer enumerates every interleaving with no partial-order reduction, and allocation is placed before the other operations; `ValOrder` proves the order of `cmp_canon` on Form values (rank null < bool < int < float < text < list < record, IEEE 754 totalOrder on floats, lexicographic text, lists and record entries), and its `cmp` is written from that definition, not extracted from the code | `LVarAlloc.alloc_quasi_det`, `alloc_det_no_err`, `stepAt_sound`, `stepAt_complete`, `exec_sound`, `Canon.set_canon`, `Canon.map_canon`, `ValOrder.lt_total`, `ValOrder.set_canon_val`, `ValOrder.map_canon_val`, `LVarVectors`, `checker/tests/lean_lvar.rs` |
| T30 | an atomic batch applies all or none | model; vectors | `t30` |
| T31 | replicas agree on equal prefixes | model (the statement is close to trivial) | `t31` |

None of T16 to T31 is a proof about the Rust reference evaluator. The
checker rules W-PAR-1 to 4 and W-GRP-1 to 3 are not linked to the Lean
footprints beyond the core of `ParSem.lean` (W-PAR-1 on variables).

### C.14 Emitters and running

`rce run` runs version 0.6 programs on the reference evaluator
(`conc.rs`). The program emitters (`emit/conc06.rs`) run the branches of a
`par` with more than one branch at the same time where the target allows
it (Rust and Python threads, JavaScript workers) and in source order in
Scala; in every case the store, the outputs and the trap point are those
of source order (C.4, T16), the branches' results and costs being merged
in source order after they finish; a `par` whose branches
wait on LVars is run by restart (a repeated attempt puts nothing new,
since puts are joins and W-CRDT-1 makes every join idempotent), and budgets charge the same costs as the
evaluator, so `trap("budget")` falls on the same operation on every
target. Workgroups run lane after lane per phase. The 0.6b actor, session
and node constructs follow the limits of 10.5.

### C.15 Version 0.7

`# rce-version: 0.7` declares version 0.7. Its syntax, keywords, static
rules and evaluation are those of version 0.6, with one difference: a
standard library method costs `c_call + work(m, n, k)` (C.6.4) instead
of `c_call`. The rule that decides what needs a new version: a module's
meaning (its outputs, states and outcomes, including where a budget
traps) must be determined by its declared version, so a change that
gives a valid program of an existing version a different meaning that
the old text defined is a new version; a change that makes the
implementations meet text that already defined the meaning, or that
only touches artifacts outside a program's meaning, is an erratum and
applies to every version.

**Which version governs a cost (normative).** A program may join modules
of different versions (2.7). The cost of a standard library method call
is fixed by the declared version of the module that contains the call
expression, not by the version of the module that declared the function
being run, of its caller, or of the program's first module. A call
written in a 0.7 module, including one inside a closure written there,
costs `c_call + work(m, n, k)` wherever it is executed from, and a call
written in a 0.5 or 0.6 module costs `c_call` even when a 0.7 module
calls the function around it. The rule is lexical, so linking modules
changes no cost. Every other cost of C.6.4 is the same in 0.6 and 0.7.
Example: a 0.6 function that holds `with budget B` and calls an imported
0.7 function whose body sorts an 8-element list is charged 24 more than
the same call to an identical function declared in a 0.6 module.

| Change since draft 0.6 | Versions | Why |
|---|---|---|
| size-scaled method costs (C.6.4) | 0.7 only | draft 0.6 defined each method as `c_call`; where a 0.6 budget traps would change |
| saturating budget arithmetic (C.6) | all (erratum) | changes nothing reachable: no program reaches a sum near the largest i128 |
| closed standard library, no ambient I/O (5.15) | all (erratum) | states what the checker already enforced (W-NAME-1 on an unknown method); no valid program changes |
| `&mut` write-back on `fail` (6.2, T33) | all (erratum) | the reference evaluator already updated in place; the emitters now agree with it (and T34 flattens nested calls without changing order) |
| u64 values at or above 2^63 exact in order, min/max and f64 ops (6.3 N2) | all (erratum) | N2 has defined full-range u64 since draft 0.5; the runtimes now meet it |
| literals take the success type of a fallible return (5.1) | all (erratum) | a checker bug against `τ <: τ ! ε`; it admits programs the text already admitted |
| canonical D entry and hash-chained Form log (6.1) | all | the log format, not a program's meaning |
| `sha256` text method (5.15) | all (extension) | admits only programs that W-NAME-1 refused before, so no valid program of any version changes meaning |
| mutual recursion with a decreasing summed measure (6.7, W-REC-1) | all (extension) | admits only programs whose call graph has a cycle of two or more functions, which W-REC-1 refused before; the rule for a function that calls only itself is unchanged, so no valid program of any version changes meaning |
| maps iterate in canonical key order (6.7, 7.1) | all (erratum) | 6.7 has always said a map iterates in canonical order; the reference evaluator and the four emitter runtimes kept insertion order. They now keep every map sorted by the canonical order of its keys, so `for`, `keys()`, `values()` and display follow 6.7. A program whose output depended on insertion order was relying on behavior the text never gave it; tests/map_order.rs checks all targets |
| self-recursion needs one fixed shrinking position, or layers (6.7, W-REC-1) | all (erratum, and extension for layers) | 6.7 has said since draft 0.4 that the value at one position i shrinks along any chain of calls, and T2 that every run ends; the checker took a different position per call, which admitted functions that never return. Refusing them makes the checker meet the text. Every function the text admitted is admitted by one layer, and layers admit only programs refused before, so no program the text admitted changes meaning |
| a parameter typed by an alias of a channel type makes a task function (5.1, 5.2) | all (erratum) | the type grammar of 5.1 has no nominal alias, so `type A = chan τ` already named the channel type; the checker tested the written type, not the type it names, and refused such functions with W-SPAWN-1 or W-EFF-1. Only programs refused before are admitted |
| declared recursion bounds `fn … bound n` (6.7, W-REC-1) | all (extension) | `bound` after a signature was W-SYN-1, and a cycle it admits was W-REC-1, so only programs refused before are admitted; no valid program of any version changes meaning |
| est_j receipts | all | measurement records outside the language (C.5: est_j is separate from budgets) |
| `i64.MIN % -1` traps; `toint` traps outside i64 (6.3 N2) | all (erratum) | N2 already defined both; the reference and runtimes returned 0 and an out-of-range i64 |
| canonical float text in `tostr` and display (6.3 N3) | all (erratum) | N3 already defined it (`1e+300`, `1.5e-7`, `-0` is `0`); the implementations printed Rust's long decimal form |
| `x op= y` charges the cost of `op` (C.6.4) | all (erratum) | C.6.4 already charges every binary operator; compound assignment was charged 0, so a budget could be exceeded |
| 6.3 N2, N3, N8 and 6.2 state the trap texts, `usize` indices and trapping slices the implementations have always had; float `%` removed from N3 and C.6.4 | all (erratum) | the text contradicted the checker and every runtime; no accepted program changes, since the text described behaviour no program could reach (negative usize, float `%`) or contradicted what every implementation did |
| f64 `min`/`max` (6.3 N5, 5.15) evaluate | all (erratum) | the checker accepted them and N5 defined them, but the evaluators trapped; a program that trapped now computes what the text defined |
| f64 `pow` refused (W-NAME-1) | all (erratum) | not in the closed library of 5.15, which already made it W-NAME-1; the checker accepted it and every evaluator trapped on it, so no accepted program computed a value with it |
| refined types `type R = τ where p` (5.1, W-REF-1) | all (extension) | `where` after a type was W-SYN-1 and stays an ordinary identifier, so only programs refused before are admitted; no valid program of any version changes meaning |
| a foreign function is not a value (5.11, W-FFI-1) | all (erratum) | 5.11 already forbade a pure function calling foreign code; the value route was a checker hole |
| host contract (Appendix E: one admitter, durable append per OS, fatal barrier, verify on open, inputs as events, capabilities, fabric entries, automatic placement) | all | constrains hosts and the log, not programs: a host entry has a `host.` type that no program can declare and δ is the identity on it, so the fold of every log of every valid program is unchanged |
| host bindings (E.8: a host result delivered as an event the program declares) | all | the bound event is an ordinary declared event, admitted and typed as any other; a program that declares no binding target sees no new input |

So a 0.6 program keeps its meaning, a 0.5 program is unaffected (it has
no budgets), and a 0.7 program differs from the same program declared
0.6 only in where a `with budget` block traps. Checked by
`spec/checker/tests/method_costs.rs` (0.6 charges `c_call` alone, 0.7
charges the table, in the reference and every runtime) and
`spec/checker/tests/draft06_gate.rs`, and the per-call-site rule by
`spec/checker/tests/call_site_cost.rs` (0.5, 0.6 and 0.7 modules joined
by `use`, in the reference evaluator and the Rust, Python and JavaScript
emitters on the linked program); the tree-sitter port and the
LALR(1) check treat 0.7 as 0.6, since the grammar is the same.

### C.16 Version 0.8

`# rce-version: 0.8` declares version 0.8: the syntax, keywords, rules,
evaluation and costs of 0.7, plus 5.16. It reserves no keyword, so the
grammar, the LALR(1) check and the tree-sitter port treat it as 0.7. It
is a version, not an extension, by the C.15 rule: the eight names of
5.16 are ordinary names in 0.7, and a 0.7 program that declares one
(`struct Text`, `struct Html`) would change meaning if 5.16 applied to
it. In a 0.8 module `C.lit(s)` costs `c_call`, `C.encode(t)` costs
`c_call` plus the size of t (the linear class of C.6.4) and `.raw()`
costs `c_call` (the text is not copied), in the reference evaluator and
every runtime; the indices are erased, so nothing else in C.6 changes. A 0.5, 0.6 or 0.7 module never
sees 5.16 (`spec/checker/tests/indexed.rs`, gate test), and modules of
different versions may `use` each other (2.7).

### C.17 Version 0.9

`# rce-version: 0.9` declares version 0.9: the syntax, rules, evaluation and
costs of 0.8, plus Appendix F. It is a version by the C.15 rule because it
refuses programs that 0.8 accepts (unused values, shadowing, dropped
results, flows to lower labels) and changes the value of a `&mut` argument
after a failed call. It is specified and not yet implemented: until it is, a
conforming implementation refuses the declaration (W-VER-1), and no cost of
C.6 is defined for it beyond the costs F.10 names.

**Read receipt.** How many words does a version 0.6 module reserve in addition to the 0.5 keywords? (a number)

---

## Appendix D. The engine profile: handler specs and fits (normative)

This appendix defines the second input language of the engine: the
*handler spec*, a line-oriented `.rce` file that `rce check`, `rce
compile`, `rce run`, `rce auto` and `rce form` read (`src/spec/parser.rs`),
and the JSON *fit* that says what each node of the compiled graph does
(`src/form/fit.rs`). It is a profile tied to the language spec, not a
second programming language: a handler spec declares a graph and its
contracts; the behaviour of each node is a fit entry, and the compiled
result is a Form P = (S, E, δ, D, λ) as in 6.1, with S, E and δ given by
D.6. A file is a handler spec when its first non-blank, non-comment line
starts with `spec`; otherwise it is a module of sections 2 to 10. Example:

```
spec "orders-form" v0.1.0
reason "Demo for the Form compiler" by "david"
currency max_age=24h
```

**Implementation status.** This appendix describes the engine profile. The
code it names (`src/spec/`, `src/form/`) belongs to the engine crate, which
is not in this repository. The reference checker in `spec/checker` has no
`src/spec` or `src/form`, `rce-spec-check` does not read handler specs, and
no file under `spec/checker/src`, `spec/checker/tests`,
`spec/checker/examples` or `spec/examples` mentions a W-HS rule. So nothing
in this appendix is checked by the tools published here; the rules below are
a specification of the engine, tested there.

### D.1 Lexical rules

- The file is UTF-8 text read line by line. A line that is blank after
  trimming, or whose first non-space characters are `#` or `//`, is
  skipped.
- A *top-level line* starts in column 0. A *body line* starts with a space
  or a tab and belongs to the nearest preceding top-level block. A blank
  line ends a body.
- Tokens are separated by white space. A token that starts with `"` runs
  to the next `"` (no escapes); its value is the text between the quotes.
- Durations: hours are `N` or `Nh`; milliseconds are `Nms`, `Ns`
  (seconds) or `N`. N is a decimal integer.

### D.2 Grammar

```
File        = SpecLine { TopLine } .
SpecLine    = "spec" STRING VERSION .                VERSION = [ "v" ] MAJOR "." MINOR "." PATCH
TopLine     = ReasonLine | CurrencyLine | Objective | Constraint | Acceptance
            | Deliverable | Role | Dependency | Escalation | Flow | ChangeControl .
ReasonLine  = "reason" STRING [ "by" STRING ] .
CurrencyLine= "currency" { "max_age=" HOURS | "last_checked=" RFC3339
            | "toolchain." NAME "=" VALUE | "dep." NAME "=" VALUE } .
Objective   = "objective" ID STRING Body( "metric" NAME "target" VALUE | ReasonLine ) .
Constraint  = "constraint" ID ( "substrate" | "performance" | "regulatory"
            | "resource" | "compatibility" ) STRING Body( ReasonLine ) .
Acceptance  = "acceptance" ID "validates" ID
              Body( "property" STRING | "error_budget" NUMBER | ReasonLine ) .
Deliverable = "deliverable" ID "fulfills" ID
              Body( "schema" STRING | "description" STRING | "blast_radius" NAME | ReasonLine ) .
Role        = "role" ID STRING ( "execution_node" | "coordinator" | "ai_foreman"
            | "order_giver" ) Body( "blast_radius" NAME | ReasonLine ) .
Dependency  = "dependency" ID ( "node" | "crate" | "service" | "data" ) STRING
              Body( "input_schema" JSON | ReasonLine ) .
Escalation  = "escalation" ID { "from" ENDPOINT | "to" ENDPOINT | "timeout" MS }
              Body( ReasonLine ) .
Flow        = "flow" ID "from" ENDPOINT "to" ENDPOINT Body( ReasonLine ) .
ChangeControl = "change_control" { "approvers" LIST | "review_period" HOURS | "frozen" } .
```

`Body(X)` is zero or more body lines each of the form X. `error_budget`
must lie strictly between 0 and 1. `input_schema` is JSON that may span
body lines until its brackets balance. An unknown top-level keyword, an
unknown constraint, role or dependency kind, a flow without `from` and
`to`, a missing `spec` line, an `error_budget` out of range, a
`last_checked` that is not RFC 3339 and invalid `input_schema` JSON are
refused at parse time. The reference parser ignores unknown body keywords
and unknown `change_control` words, and reads an unparsable duration as
its default (24 h, 30 000 ms).

### D.3 Meaning of each declaration

- `spec NAME VERSION`: the name and version of the spec. The version is
  recorded in the compiled graph's metadata (`spec_version`) and in the
  Form IR (`FormIr.version`). The version is not yet checked.
- `reason WHY by AUTHOR`: why an artifact exists. A top-level reason
  belongs to the spec; a body reason belongs to its block. A reason is
  recorded on the node or edge it explains and enters the log with every
  mutation that creates it. Reasons are data: they never change δ.
- `currency`: when the spec's toolchain and dependencies were last
  verified (`last_checked`), the versions seen then, and the maximum age
  `max_age` in hours. Parsing is not a check: without `last_checked` the
  record is *unchecked*. `rce currency FILE --mark` records a check by
  writing `last_checked` back into the file. A record is stale when it was
  never checked or is older than `max_age`; the promotion gate records a
  stale spec, and blocks on it when the engine's `enforce_currency`
  policy is on (off by default).
- `objective`, `constraint`, `acceptance`: requirements. Acceptance
  properties and their error budget are not inputs of δ: no step reads
  them. They decide whether a candidate passes the promotion gate, and
  so which δ is installed next (see the versioning of δ below).
- `deliverable D` compiles to the node `del_D` (an executor and a sink),
  `role R` to `role_R` (kind executor, decision, escalation or source),
  `dependency P` to `dep_P` (a source). `flow F from A to B` compiles to
  the edge `flow_F`; `escalation E from A to B timeout t` to `esc_E`. An
  endpoint names a node id, a node name or a declared id; an unknown flow
  endpoint is refused by the compiler, an unknown escalation endpoint is
  a diagnostic.
- `change_control`: who may approve changes to the spec, the minimum
  review period, and whether the spec is frozen. These bind the engine's
  promotion path (spec mutations are logged and need an approver). They
  are not inputs of δ; they govern which δ may be installed, and by
  whom.

δ is versioned. A promotion that passes the gate is committed as a
RESOLVE entry of D (`PromoteEscalation` with a `resolve` stamp) that
records the log height h of the entry, the version of δ at its node
(raised by one at each RESOLVE for that node), and the sha256 digests of
the installed HandlerSpec and of the fit evidence the gate accepted. The
new handler governs every entry after h, and every entry before h was
computed under the previous one. A tick is one step and no input can be
committed inside it, so a step in flight when a RESOLVE is requested
finishes under the δ it started with. The state after n entries is the
fold of D under the δ in force at each height: s(i+1) = δ_v(i)(s(i),
D(i)), where v(i) is the version set by the last RESOLVE before i. A
fold applies each RESOLVE at the height it records and refuses one whose
height, version or spec digest differs from the fold's; the fit digest
is recorded and not refolded, since the fit evidence is not in D. The
handler installed is the one the entry carries; only an opaque handler
(no spec) runs as the live object, and every result it returns is in D
(`ExternalResult`).

### D.4 Fits

A fit is a JSON object:

```
{ "handlers": { NODE: HandlerSpec | {"kind": "term", "term": TERM}
                       | {"kind": "recorded", "contract": C, "table": {SHA256: RESULT}} },
  "types":    { SOURCE_NODE: TYPE },
  "keys":     { SINK_NODE: [COLUMN, ...] },
  "reads":    { SINK_NODE: {"key": [FIELD, ...], "into": FIELD} },
  "joins":    { SINK_NODE: [ {"relation": REL, "key": [FIELD, ...], "into": FIELD,
                              "scan": BOOL}, ... ] } }
```

An object with any of the five fields above is a full fit, even when it
holds only `reads` or `joins`; any other object is a bare map of handlers
and is read as `handlers` alone. NODE is a
compiled node id (`role_R1`, `dep_DEP1`, `del_D1`). `types` gives the
input contract of a source; `keys` the key of a sink's relation (default:
the input number `seq` and the index `n` within the step). A recorded
entry is an oracle: a recorded input replays its result and an unseen one
escalates as "oracle miss".

### D.5 Reads, joins and scans

Each is applied before the body of every rule that writes the sink, to
the state at the event's entry (pre-state, as in 6.4), in this order:
the read, then the joins in list order.

- `reads[S] = {key, into}`: the row of S's own relation whose key is the
  payload fields `key` (in key-column order) is put into the input as
  field `into`, or null when there is none. The relation must exist and
  its key must have as many columns as `key` names.
- `joins[S]`, an entry without `scan`: the row of relation `relation`
  keyed by the payload fields `key`, or null, into field `into`. The
  relation must exist and its key arity must match.
- an entry with `"scan": true`: every row of `relation` as an array, in
  canonical key order (code point order of the canonical JSON key);
  `key` is ignored.
- A payload that is not a record is passed unchanged. Joined rows and
  scans are typed as JSON. Each read or join is covered by the rule's
  SHA-256 id, and a rule with a read or a join is not monotone (CALM,
  `form/laws.rs`). A `joins` entry for a sink no rule writes is refused.
- Every target (reference δ, Rust, Python, JavaScript for XState and
  SCXML) applies them identically.

**CALM tags (normative).** Each rule's `monotone` tag is derived by
`form::laws::calm_reason`, never declared, and `laws::check` refuses an
IR whose tag differs. A rule is monotone only when it has no resolve, no
read, no join and no scan. The reasons, by derivation:

| Rule has | Tag | Why |
|---|---|---|
| none of the below | monotone | its writes only add keys and grow counters |
| resolve | not monotone | it deletes escalation rows |
| read | not monotone | read-modify-write of its own sink |
| keyed join | not monotone | the joined row may be null now and present later, or overwritten |
| scan | not monotone | it observes the whole relation, so also what is absent |

The tag is conservative (sound, not complete): a join against an
insert-only relation would be monotone in principle, but the profile
does not prove insert-only, so it is not claimed. A Form is
coordination-free (`laws::coordination_free`) iff every rule is
monotone. Because every read, join and scan sees the entry state, the
post-state of an input event does not depend on the order in which
rules for different sinks run; only the output order does, and that is
fixed by content hash (law 2). Tested in `tests/form_joins.rs`.

### D.6 The compiled Form

Σc has one region per node, `Ready | Escalated`. Σd has the logical clock,
an input count and the typed relations of the sinks plus `escalation` and
`error`. E is `IN_<source>`, `TICK` and `RESOLVE_<node>`. An input event
normalizes the payload (6.3 N1), checks the source's contract (a mismatch
is a `reject` output and an `error` row, not a refusal of the event) and
runs the rules in content-hash order. A `timeout` is converted to ticks of
a nominal 100 ms, rounded up; the clock is logical (6.3 N11). D is the
canonical log of 6.1: entries {seq, event, prev_hash, state_hash, hash}
chained by SHA-256. Every event is applied (no `outcome` field is
needed), since a contract mismatch is an output, not a refusal. The numeric
edges are those of 6.3, with one recorded difference: in this profile an
integer above i64::MAX is "integer out of range" (D.10).

### D.7 Relation to the language

A handler spec and a module of sections 2 to 10 both denote a Form, but
the profile has no expressions of its own: node behaviour comes only
from fits. A fit `term` is a term of the Form IR (`form/ir.rs`), not an
RCE expression. A function of a module is used as a fit through its
lowering (`rce index`, `spec/checker/src/brick_lower.rs`): a function
f(p1: T1, ..., pn: Tn) -> R lowers to the term t with
t({"p1": v1, ..., "pn": vn}) = f(v1, ..., vn), values in the Form's JSON
embedding (lists and tuples as arrays, structs as objects). A trap of f is
an error of t at the node `module.f`. A function that calls others lowers
to a Form IR format 2 program (`spec/proposals/form-ir-2.md`): each callee
is a definition keyed by the SHA-256 of its term's canonical JSON, and a
call is a `ref` to that key; a function that calls nothing lowers to a bare
format 1 term.

Statements lower store-passing: each is a term from an environment record
(the variables in scope and the control fields `$done`, `$ret`, `$brk`,
`$cnt`) to the next one, skipped once the function has returned or the
iteration has been left. `let`, `var`, assignment (also compound and to a
list item), `push` and `pop` statements, `if`, `while c bound n` (the
iteration count traps past n, after the condition holds, as in 6.7),
`loop`, `for x in e` (a range or a list), `break`, `continue`, `return`
anywhere and `check` lower. Expressions: literals, constants (their
values, by the reference evaluator), arithmetic (`+` as `plus`: integers
add, texts and lists concatenate), bit operations (`band`, `bor`, `bxor`,
`shl`, `shr`, `bnot`; a shift amount outside 0..64 is an error, as it
traps), comparisons, `and` and `or` (as `cond`), `if`, list and tuple
literals, `[v; n]`, indexing (`at`: a text is read as its UTF-8 bytes, as
in 6.3; a negative index traps), fields, struct construction, the methods
`len` (`size`, bytes of a text), `chars`, `tostr`, `toint`, `upper`,
`lower`, `contains`, `startswith`, `endswith`, `split`, `join`, casts to
i64 and usize, shared borrows, `copy`, and calls of other lowerable
functions (by `ref`). A function with `&mut` parameters lowers by
state-passing: its term returns `[result, final values of the &mut
parameters in parameter order]` (the result is null for a function
without one), and a call of it, as a statement, a `let` or `var`
initializer or the right side of `=`, writes those values back to the
borrowed places; such a call inside a larger expression is refused.
`match` lowers arm by arm (variants by their `$v` tag, `some`/`none`,
literals, ranges, tuples, alternatives, guards; no arm traps), and a
variant value is its fields with `$v`. A function with result `T ! E`
lowers with its errors as values: `fail e` returns `{"$err": e}`, `try x
[else e]` (as a `let`/`var` initializer, an assignment's right side, a
statement or a `return` value) tests `x` with `has(x, "$err")` (`none`
for an optional) and returns the error, and `x catch |e| h` tests the
same and evaluates `h`; a call of such a function anywhere else is
refused. A recursive group (a cycle of the call graph) lowers to one
`fix` term of its members' bodies, a call inside it being `rec` of the
callee's index; `bound n` is a counter of active calls passed by every
`rec`, trapping past n as in 6.7. The evaluator bounds `rec` nesting at
20000 (the reference evaluator's nesting limit) and calls per evaluation
at 50000000 (its fuel); past either is an error, and an input on which
the reference evaluator meets its own limits gives no vector. Integers
are i64 or usize (a usize variable that would become negative traps);
floats, narrower integers and closures are refused. A generic function
lowers to one term for every instance, since the IR is untyped over JSON.
A term over 1 MiB of JSON, not counting its definitions, or a program
nested over 1000 levels is refused (catalog readers parse past JSON
libraries' usual 128 levels, with a stated bound). Every refusal is recorded in the
catalog with its line and construct, never approximated.

`rce index --vectors N` records the reference evaluator's results on N
generated inputs per brick; `rce-brick-verify` (`src/form/brick.rs`)
evaluates each term on them and reports agreement. Agreement is tested on
vectors (`spec/checker/tests/brick.rs`, `tests/brick_lowering.rs`), not
proved.

### D.8 Lift guarantees (normative)

A brownfield lift (`rce scan DIR --form`, `brownfield/lift.rs`) reads
existing Rust, Python, TypeScript or Go into a Form schema. Its
guarantees are exactly these, each enforced by code and tests, and no
other is claimed:

- L1 Labeled: every relation, region, event and transition carries a
  label that starts with "unproven"; a lifted element is never presented
  as checked.
- L2 Fail closed: a guard the lift cannot read is opaque, and
  `Lifted::step` refuses to step through it rather than guess.
- L3 Generated code agrees with the lift: code emitted from a lifted
  machine (`--emit-machine`) steps as `Lifted::step` (tested,
  `tests/lift_emit.rs`).
- L4 Evidence, not proof: agreement of the lift with the original
  program is tested on seeded runs of the original
  (`tests/brownfield_lift.rs`); its level is tested (8). A lift is an
  input to a gate, never an authority: what it proposes is admitted only
  through the checker and the gate, like any other proposal.

### D.9 Rules (normative)

These are checked by `crate::spec::rules` (`src/spec/rules.rs`) in the engine
crate (see the implementation status above), run by the engine's `rce check`,
and each diagnostic names its rule.

- W-HS-VER-1: the `spec` version is not `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` of decimal
  integers (an optional leading `v` is allowed).
- W-HS-VER-2 (compatibility, between an old and a new revision of one
  spec, `rce diff`): the version must not decrease; a revision that
  removes or modifies a declaration must increase MAJOR, or MINOR when
  MAJOR is 0; a revision that only adds declarations must increase at
  least MINOR; a revision with no change may keep the version. Flows are
  declarations here: a flow whose endpoints change is modified.
- W-HS-CUR-1: a `max_age` that is not a positive integer number of hours
  (`N` or `Nh`, N ≥ 1).
- W-HS-CUR-2 (staleness): at check time `now`, the currency record is
  stale when it was never checked or `now - last_checked` exceeds
  `max_age` hours. A stale spec is refused by `rce check --strict` and by
  the promotion gate when the engine's `enforce_currency` policy is on;
  otherwise it is reported as a warning naming W-HS-CUR-2. This is the one
  rule of the appendix whose verdict depends on a time given as an input
  (see D.10).
- W-HS-REASON-1: the spec, or a declaration that compiles to a node or an
  edge (deliverable, role, dependency, flow, escalation), has no `reason`
  line, or a reason whose text is empty or `unspecified`.
- W-HS-DUR-1: a duration that is not a decimal integer with an allowed
  suffix (D.1).
- W-HS-KW-1: an unknown body keyword or `change_control` word.

### D.10 Recorded differences and open items

- Integers in [2^63, 2^64) are u64 values, as in the language (6.3 N2):
  the u64 operators compute on them exactly, comparisons, `sort`,
  `lmin`, `lmax`, `min` and `max` order them exactly, and the f64 and
  f32 operators convert them to f64. The signed operators refuse them
  ("integer out of range"), which no well-typed program reaches, since a
  signed value is never at or above 2^63. A JSON integer beyond u64 is
  read as a float (`form::num`); no integer type of the language holds
  one.
- W-HS-CUR-2 takes `now`. 10.1 item 1 says the subcommands of section 10
  read no clock; the staleness check is outside them, but a verdict that
  depends on `now` is a function of its recorded inputs only if `now` is
  recorded with the verdict. Whether it must be is not decided.
- The cost model of extraction (est_j) and the gate's certificate are
  outside this appendix, except the break-even receipt of D.11.
- `InstallHandler` and `RetireHandler` also change δ at the height of
  their entry and carry the same RESOLVE stamp as a promotion: height,
  the next δ version at the node (versions count every install,
  promotion and retirement there), the digest of the installed spec
  (for a retirement, the digest of the stub, distinct from an opaque
  install) and a fit digest. A fold refuses one whose stamp does not
  match. Entries written before the stamp existed carry none and fold
  as before.

### D.11 Promotion break-even (receipt)

Each promotion record (promoted or refused) carries a break-even
receipt `break_even` with three terms and n\* =
J_build / (J_model_path - J_handler), the number of inputs after which
the promoted handler has paid back its build:

- J_build: the est_j of the gear resolution that wrote the handler plus
  the coverage shadow run of the promotion path. Static checks (proof,
  kernel) are not priced and not included, so J_build and n\* are lower
  bounds.
- J_model_path: joules per input on the model path, the est_j of one
  gear resolution (the price the retirement rule uses for savings).
- J_handler: joules per input of the handler, the shadow run's priced
  operations per sample plus one dispatch.

Each term is {`j`, `basis`} with basis one of `est` (a model of the
work, including a model provider's own figure), `reported` (an OS or
on-chip energy counter: RAPL, NVML, IOReport), `measured` (a wall or
shunt meter on a named rail) or `unpriced` (no figure; `j` is null,
never 0). The terms the engine fills today are est or unpriced: a gear
receipt's `est_j` is an estimate by schema and is never relabeled from
its free text. A figure
without a basis is refused when a record is read, and the type that
holds a term has no constructor from a bare number. `n_star` is
{`kind`: `unpriced`} when any term is unpriced (it is never computed
from the other terms or from a default), {`kind`: `never`} when
J_model_path - J_handler <= 0, and otherwise {`kind`: `value`, `n`,
`inputs` = ⌈n⌉}; its basis is the weakest of the three
(unpriced < est < reported < measured). The promotion path's last step
records the same figures as text. Implemented in
`src/runtime/break_even.rs`, tested there and in the engine's promotion
tests.

**Readings: provenance, boundary and amortization (normative; P4, P5,
P6 of the receipt field proposals of 13 Oct 2026).** These rules apply to every
term labeled `reported` or `measured`, in every receipt that holds one,
and are checked where a term is built and where a record is read:

1. A reading carries `provenance` = {`sampler`, `counter`, `interval_s`,
   `idle_baseline_w`, `machine`, `boundary`}: the four names non-empty,
   `interval_s` finite and > 0, `idle_baseline_w` finite and >= 0 (0 when
   no baseline was subtracted). `boundary` says what the joules include
   (`package`, `package+dram`, `rail:VDD_GPU`). A reading without a valid
   provenance is refused; unknown fields in it are refused. Derivation:
   the label `reported` or `measured` claims that something was read; a
   reading that cannot be reproduced or compared (which counter, over what
   interval, against which baseline, on which machine, inside which
   boundary) does not support that claim, so a term that lacks it is not
   a reading, and labeling it one would be unsound.
2. A term labeled `est` or `unpriced` carries no `provenance` (nothing was
   read); one that does is refused.
3. A reading carries `amortization`, one of {`kind`: `per_call`},
   {`kind`: `batch_mean`, `n` >= 1}, {`kind`: `per_solved_task`}. An
   `est` term may carry one; the engine's own estimates omit it.
4. Figures of different kinds are never added or subtracted: a sum of two
   terms whose `amortization` differs (absent counts as its own kind) is
   refused, and so is a break-even whose J_model_path and J_handler differ
   in kind (n\* divides by their difference) or whose J_build is a mean
   (`batch_mean` or `per_solved_task`; J_build is a one-off total).
   Derivation: a batch mean added to a per-call figure, or a per-task
   figure subtracted from a per-input one, is arithmetic on different
   units; no result of it is a figure of either kind.
5. A sum of two readings keeps the weaker label only when both come from
   the same sampler, counter, machine and boundary (the intervals add);
   otherwise it is refused. A sum with an `est` term is `est` with no
   provenance (unpriced < est < reported < measured, as for n\*).
6. A stored break-even receipt is re-derived from its terms when read; a
   stored n\* that disagrees with them is refused.

The `est` wire form is unchanged (`{"j": 2.5, "basis": "est"}`), so no
stored receipt changes meaning; no receipt in the repository holds a
reading today. Implemented by `Term`, `Provenance` and `Amortization` in
`src/runtime/break_even.rs` (no constructor makes a reading without
provenance and amortization), tested there (`p4_*`, `p6_*`).

The receipt is a measurement record. It is not an input to δ, to any
check, or to the decision to promote, so it does not change the meaning
of any program or handler spec in any language version (C.15:
receipts are version-independent).

**Read receipt.** Which compiled node id does `deliverable D1` become? (for example role_R1)

---

## Appendix E. The host contract (normative)

This appendix states what a host must do to run an RCE program. A *host*
is everything outside δ and λ: the code that admits events, appends the
log D (6.1), runs λ's outputs as effects, answers foreign calls and talks
to devices. The language defines meaning; the host is conforming when
every run it performs is the fold of its own log (T3) and the log it
leaves on storage can be replayed with every adapter disconnected (T37).
The appendix applies to every version (C.15): it constrains hosts and the
format of D, and it gives no valid program a different meaning.

![Host contract: five primitives, adapters, one admitter, log D, replay](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openIE-dev/rce/main/docs/figures/host-contract.svg)

*Figure (informative). The five primitives, adapters, the single admitter (HC-1), typed results (HC-3) and replay with adapters disconnected (HC-8, T37). Source: [docs/figures](https://github.com/openIE-dev/rce/tree/main/docs/figures).*

The rules were derived from a survey of operating systems, embedded
kernels, browsers, language runtimes, replay systems, storage engines and
compute fabrics. A primitive is in the contract only when (a) every
surveyed target can supply it and (b) its result is a pure function of
logged data or is itself logged. What fails (b), because it depends on
timing, ordering, hardware or another process, enters as an event, as
5.15 already requires. Every target supplies: pure computation on bytes
with integer operations and binary64 round-to-nearest-even, append-only
storage, SHA-256 as pure code, one input queue and one output queue, and
a monotonic counter read only by the admitter. Everything else is an
adapter.

### E.1 Terms

- **Admitter.** The one component that orders inputs into E and appends
  entries to D.
- **Adapter.** Host code that turns one outside source (a keyboard, a
  socket, a file, a clock, a GPU, a foreign library) into events, or one
  output request into an effect and a result event.
- **Host entry.** An entry of D whose event type starts with `host.`
  (E.5). No RCE identifier contains a dot, so no program declares such an
  event, and δ is the identity on it: δ(s, e) = (s, []) and the entry's
  `state_hash` equals the previous entry's (or that of s₀ for the first).
  The fold law of 6.1 is unchanged.
- **Durable.** An entry is durable when the barrier of E.3 for its
  storage returned success.

### E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)

- **HC-1 One admitter per term.** At any log height a program instance
  has exactly one admitter, the holder of the current term (E.2b). Every
  input reaches δ only after the admitter appended it to D, in D's order.
  The admitter is a role, not a machine: when it fails, another host takes
  the role for a higher term and continues the same D (E.2b). A host
  without replication holds term 0 for its lifetime, which is the single
  admitter of earlier versions.
- **HC-2 Only the admitter reads clocks.** Wall time and monotonic time
  enter only as events (`Tick(n)`, and `host.WallTime` when an adapter
  supplies it). Time inside the language is logical (6.3 N11, C.11.12).
- **HC-3 Typed output requests.** Each effect requested by λ (a write, a
  send, a draw, a foreign call) has exactly one result event: delivered,
  failed, timed out or unreachable. A race inside the adapter (for
  example a file checked and then opened) is resolved by the adapter;
  the program sees one atomic outcome.
- **HC-4 Foreign code.** Foreign code runs only through 5.11, with its
  arguments copied or borrowed for the call only, under fuel, and its
  result or trap logged as `Foreign(f, arguments, result)`. An isolated
  component boundary (a WebAssembly component per call) is the
  recommended adapter; it does not change the rule.
- **HC-5 Capabilities.** Authority comes only from capabilities minted by
  logged events (5.16 `Cap[A]` in a version 0.8 module). The host holds no
  ambient authority on the program's behalf. This is the sandbox, and its
  contract is independent of any OS: the checker admits only programs whose
  effects go through granted capabilities, and the deterministic host
  refuses any effect without one, before any OS layer is involved. The
  same contract then has enforcement targets underneath the host, entered
  at start as strictly as the target allows: WASM (the module imports only
  the granted host functions), bare metal (no OS; the engine is the only
  host and capabilities are the whole I/O surface), Linux (Landlock and
  seccomp), macOS (Seatbelt, `sandbox_init`), Windows (AppContainer, to
  do) and other OSes (FreeBSD Capsicum `cap_enter`, OpenBSD
  pledge/unveil, iOS, Android: to do). The contract is planned to conform
  to OpenIE's Sandbox v0.1 standard (https://sandbox.transaction.science:
  S0-S7 tiers, §5 Grants, §6 energy and §7 attestation receipts) and to
  JCP v0.3 (https://jcp.transaction.science); see REMAINING-PLAN W1h-std.
  The program loses nothing,
  since 5.15 gives it no ambient authority.
- **HC-6 Tick scheduler.** Concurrency runs under the tick semantics of
  6.8. The host runs `fn main` (tasks, actors, supervisors; C.5, C.13)
  with its scheduler as a live task whose every transition is an entry
  of D. `host.MainStart` {links, max_ticks, seed} starts the task;
  `host.MainInput` {a, b, partition, tick} logs an input to it (a link
  change), and `host.MainInput` {event, tick} feeds it a program event
  (canonical event JSON): at that tick the scheduler logs `Input(..)`
  and delivers the event to every live actor whose type has an `on`
  handler for it, in actor-id order, or logs `Unhandled(..)` when there
  is none (an input event has no addressee, so its receivers are the
  program's handlers of it, as for the steps `on E` of a Form;
  `Host::main_event`, `conc::RunCfg.events`,
  `tests/host_sched.rs` `program_events_feed_the_live_task_and_replay`,
  `tests/conc06b_run.rs` `program_events_feed_the_running_task`; the
  emitted runtimes take the same inputs as `--event=TICK|Name|f=v,...`,
  a field's value given by its declared type as a decimal integer,
  `true`/`false` or text, and log `Input(..)` and `Unhandled(..)` with
  `--actor-log`; a malformed event is an input error, exit status 2,
  not a program trap; `tests/emit_run.rs`
  `program_events_agree_on_every_target` on the Rust, Python,
  JavaScript and Scala runtimes); `host.Step` {cause, i, node, tick, what} logs one scheduler
  step, including the arm the environment chose at each `select nondet`;
  `host.MainEnd` {choices, outcome, ticks} ends it. Program inputs to δ
  may be admitted between any two of these entries. While the task is
  live its state (the start entry, the inputs logged so far, the number of
  steps logged and a hash chain over them) is part of the state D folds
  to, and the `state_hash` of every entry covers it, so the state after
  each entry is the fold of D up to that entry and a host rebuilt from any
  prefix continues the same run. Replay re-runs the scheduler on the
  logged inputs and refuses an entry unless the step it logs is the next
  step the scheduler takes and the end agrees in outcome and choices
  (T21). An input whose tick is not after the last logged step is refused
  before it is logged, and an input is also refused if re-running on it
  would change a step already in D, so an input never rewrites the past.
  No snapshot is taken while a task is live. A host may execute tasks in
  parallel only when the result equals the tick semantics (T1, T21).
  Reference: `Host::main_begin`, `main_input`, `main_event`,
  `main_step`, `main_end`, and `run_main` for a run whose inputs are all
  known at the start. Derivation: law 1 of E.2c makes each
  nondeterministic choice of the run an entry of D, and the requirement
  that state be the fold of D at every entry, not only between runs,
  makes the task's progress part of that state. The task's inputs are
  link changes, program events and the environment's choices, each an
  entry of D under the same causality rule. The emitted runtimes do not
  take program events (G14).
- **HC-7 Numerics and limits.** The host reproduces 6.3 bit for bit and
  enforces fuel, SIZE_LIMIT and VALUE_LIMIT (6.7, N9) as the reference
  does, on every run.
- **HC-7a Fuel per input.** A host is event driven, so fuel is charged per
  admitted input: each input (one application of δ, including constructing
  its event) starts with the full fuel of 6.7, and no budget is shared
  across inputs. Every input has its own bound and a session never starves
  however long it runs. The reference trace (`rce trace`), the host and
  replay all reset fuel per input, so a refusal for fuel is a function of
  that input and the state before it, and D is the same on each.
- **HC-8 Replay.** A host offers a replay mode that reads D, disconnects
  every adapter and re-derives every state hash. Replay reads no clock,
  file, network, device or environment (T37).
- **HC-9 Priority admission.** Interrupt sources carry a priority in
  0..255 (T25, C.11.12). Inputs admitted together are ordered by priority,
  highest first. Inputs with a source and sequence number are ordered by
  the window key of HC-15. Inputs given together without source identity
  (`admit_simultaneous`) are ordered by priority, then by the bytes of
  their canonical event JSON, so the order is a function of the set of
  inputs and not of the order the caller passed them in. Either way the
  order chosen is D's order. A real-time bound holds only on a kernel with
  a priority scheduler; a general-purpose OS gives none.

### E.2a Canonical admission (HC-15 to HC-17)

The order of D must not depend on when inputs arrive. Arrival timing may
decide only which window an input lands in, and the window boundary is
defined by logical time, never by a wall clock.

- **HC-15 Windows.** Every input carries its source id (text), a
  per-source sequence number (1, 2, ... with no reuse) and the logical
  tick its source stamped on it. When the module declares
  `event Tick(n: u64)`, a window closes when a `Tick(n)` input not yet in
  D is offered: window k gets `upto = n`, holds every offered input with
  tick at most `upto` that is not already in D, and the `Tick(n)` is its
  last input. The boundary is therefore a logged fact, never a wall clock
  and never a choice of the caller. An input whose tick is at or below the
  `upto` of the last window in D is late: it is admitted in the next
  window and its `host.Input` carries `"late":true`, so whether an input
  was late is decided by D. A host whose module declares no `Tick` closes
  windows by `close_window(upto)` from its own logical time. Apart from the closing `Tick`, the order
  inside a window is the total key (priority descending, source id ascending, sequence ascending).
  So two admitters given the same window contents append the same entries
  in the same order whatever the arrival order, and two hosts given the
  same inputs per window produce byte-identical D.
- **HC-16 Exactly once.** The dedupe key is (source, seq). A (source, seq)
  already in D, or offered twice, is a duplicate and is not appended
  again. Two copies of one (source, seq) with different payloads are
  ordered by their event bytes, and the lower one is admitted, so the
  choice does not depend on arrival. An input after a gap in its source's
  sequence is held for a later window, so each source is admitted in its
  own order and nothing is skipped. A source retransmits until acked, and
  the admitter acks an input only after the barrier (HS-2) that covers
  its window succeeded. A crash before the ack leads to a retransmission,
  which HC-16 turns into a duplicate when the input did reach D.
- **HC-17 Window entries.** Closing a window appends `host.Window` {count,
  id, term, upto}, then, before each admitted input, `host.Input` {late (only when
  true), seq, source, window}. The dedupe state is the fold of these entries: on open
  and on replay the admitter rebuilds, per source, the highest seq in D. A
  `host.Input` counts only when the program entry it announces follows it,
  so a cut between the two (HS-4) admits nothing. These are host entries:
  δ never reads them and they leave the state hash unchanged.

### E.2b Replicated D and admitter failover (HC-18 to HC-20)

A host may keep D on a replicated log so that losing the admitter's
machine neither stops the program for good nor forks D. The reference
implementation is `spec/checker/src/raft.rs` (Raft log replication behind a
`Transport` trait, with a loopback switch and a TCP transport, and
`RaftStore`, the E.3 Store of a host on the leader).
`spec/checker/src/repl.rs` is a smaller model of the same rules on whole
logs.

- **HC-18 Interface.** A replicated log offers the host the Store of E.3
  with two additions: `elect(term)`, which succeeds only with grants from
  a quorum of replicas, each of which then promises not to accept an
  append from a lower term, and returns the most up-to-date log among the
  granting quorum, ordered by (term of the last write, length); and an
  append at a term that a replica accepts only while it has promised no
  higher term. The barrier succeeds only when a quorum accepted every
  entry up to it, so a durable entry (HS-2) is a committed entry.
- **HC-19 Term fence in D.** A host that won `elect(t)` folds the log it
  received (HS-4 verification of the whole chain, then HC-8), then appends
  `host.Term` {leader, term} and makes it durable before admitting any
  input. `t` must exceed every term already in D. Every `host.Window`
  carries the term. A request emitted under an older term with no result
  in D gets one result, `failed` with `interrupted` (HC-3). The term in D
  is the fence token: an entry of D was appended by the holder of the
  most recent `host.Term` before it.
- **HC-18a Transport.** Replication follows Raft's AppendEntries and
  RequestVote: an append carries (prev_idx, prev_term) and a follower
  refuses it unless its log has an entry at prev_idx with that term (log
  matching), deletes a conflicting suffix and appends what is missing.
  The current term and the vote are written to stable storage before a
  candidate asks for votes, before a vote is granted, and before an
  append is acknowledged. A vote goes only to a candidate whose log is at
  least as up-to-date by (last term, last index). The leader advances the
  commit index only over entries of its own term held by a quorum. A
  follower that needs entries the leader has compacted receives the
  leader's snapshot (an HS-5 snapshot of the state at that index) and keeps
  any suffix of its own log that matches it. The transport may lose,
  delay, duplicate or reorder messages. Timeouts are counted in logical
  ticks, so a loopback run is a function of its seed.
  Snapshots travel in chunks of bounded size, each carrying its byte
  offset; a follower accepts a chunk only at the offset it expects,
  acknowledges the next offset it needs, and installs the snapshot only
  when the final chunk arrives, so loss, duplication and reordering of
  chunks cannot install a partial state. Membership changes use joint
  consensus: the leader appends a configuration entry C_old,new; a node
  uses the latest configuration in its log whether or not it is committed;
  while C_old,new is in force, elections and commitment need a majority of
  C_old and a majority of C_new; once C_old,new commits the leader appends
  C_new, and a leader that is not in C_new steps down once C_new commits.
